THE matron's lament,—Let us sweep. I HAD ather undertaik tew be two good doves than one descent sarpent. AnouT!thie hardest thing a phellow kan do is tew sperk tew girls at once and preserve a good average. THERE is only one good substitute for the endearments ov a sister and that is the endear- ments ov sum other phellow's sister. .AT an Irish League meeting some one in the audience got up and moved that no one should vote who was not present. WHY is.a balloon voyager greatly to be .envied Because he tises rapidli in the world, and has most excellent prospects. A MAN of philosophical temperament resembles a 'cucumber—for although he may be completely cut up he still remains cool. "THANK heaven," exclaimed a fond father, as he paced the floor at midnight with his howling heir, " thank heaven you are not twins !" IF a burnt child dreads the fire, why does a per son who has been singed by Cupid's torch, so often have a lingering regaad for the old flame! Titz most gigantic sharks in the world are said to be found near Australia. Of course, this dis eovery, is making .the English lawyers mad, but facts are facts ** WAITER, you can bringme a nice young chicken smothered in onions !" "No sail. We doesn't kill 'era dat way, sah. We cuts off d'er heads. THE English language contains over, 38,000 worts, and yet when a man wishes to stop a street ear he cannot think of anything better to say than " Hi !" .

• SAY, what is a chestnut ?" "Well, it's a joke that is a little stale." " Ah, I see! Then I suppose that a joke that is very old is a horse chestnut." "Well, you ought to know." PICTURE dealer (exhibiting a picture)—" That, Sir, is a genuine Turner." Purchaser—" Yes, I see. You have to turn it around a good many times before you can make out what it is." "What is your patronymic, sir ? " -asked the Civil Service examiner. "lly what!" asked the applicant. • "Your patronymic." 'Oh, yes; I didn't catch your meaning at first; I'm a barber." A SCHOOLMASTER whose wife was one of his pupils had occasion to punish her one day. The next day the schoolhouse door bore this incription: —" School closed for one week owing to the illness of the schoolmaster.". , "I'VE written a new poem," said an msthetio young man, addressing a lady noted for her wit and beauty. " Indeed ; and what is the title ?" she asked. "Before the dawn," said he. "Keep it dark," was her rejoinder. "AND are you glaa to see me, my little man ?" asked the bishop of Bobby. " Yes, sir," replied Bobby. "And why are you glad to see me IP" "Because it s only when you come that we have anything for dinner worth eating." SAID a magistrate to an actress: "Your pro- fission, mademoiselle ?" " Artiste ?" " our age ?" "Twenty-two." "Usher, you can now swear the lady to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth." "DOCTOR, I come to see you about my younger brother." " What is the matter with him ?" " Olie of his legs is shorter than the other, and he limps. Now, what would you do in a case of that kind ?" "I reckon I'd limp, too." "MARY," said a mother to her daughter, "has Henry proposed yet ?" "Not yet, mamma, but I think he will before many days." "What makes you think so ?" "Because he asked me if you expected to live with me -if I married, and I told him no." • "CHARLEY is an unlucky fellow. He has been disappointed in love; he mopes about defeotedly, and has repeatedly threatened to shoot himself." "Disappointed in love? -I didn't hear about it." " Yes ; he asked that liVinnoweird girl to marry him last week." " Well " Well, she said, 4 Yes.'" •

A GENTLEMAN well known in a certain church gave a beautifal window in memory of his wife. About the time of his second marriage some one made the remark—" Suppose this wife were to die ?" At which little Frank said—" Why, then he'd have to put in a double sash." AN ignorant candidate .for medical honours having been thrown almost into a fever from his hicapability of answering the questions, was asked by one of the censors how he would sweat a patient for the rheumatism: "I would send him here to be examined," he replied. • "An, good morning; nice morning," was the salutation of a gentleman to his friend. "How are all the folks ? ' "Oh, nicely. As well as could be expected." "Why, what is the matter ?" "Oh, nothing much. I've been boycotted, that's all." " lioycotted ?" "Yes. My third girl was born yesterday." • AMATEUR Artist (to a friend)—" I was showing Jones my new picture this morning. He was very much struck with it. He got quite enthusiastic, and gave it unqualified praise. You know Jones, of course. What do you think of him ?" Friend— " Jones is one of the kindest hearted, and best natured men I ever met." &arm, landscape painter, hard up: only one pot-boiler sold in six weeks—" I tell you what it is, Brown, old chap, art is a hard mistress to serve What do you say to giving it' up?" Blown, a. figure painter, still harder up !—" You have antici- pated my though; I am going to give up art to-morrow." "And then?" "And then 1 shall paint landscapes." UNDERTAKER (to recent widow)—," The carriages will be 5 dole, a-piece, Madam, if the horses trot. 14 you prefer to have the funeral procession move slowly to the grave, I shall have to charge 7 dole. -60 cents for each carriage on account of the extra time. Widow (very much ditressed) L —let th—them trot. Poor John could never bear t—to ride a—after a h—horse on a w—walk, even when g—going up h—hill." 11E—" See that bird on the upper limb of that tree, Carrie." She (after vainly looking in ths direction indie ite(4—" Why, Charlie, I can't see it." He—" Can't see it? That's funny. It's as plain as the nose on your face." And that is why they do not speak now as they pass by. Her nose is, candour compels meto say, plainness itself. Moral—When you make mod simile, be sure that there can be no unpleasant :features its appli- cation. —Boston Traamcript. "Oii, dear !" exclaimed Mrs. F., after vainly endeavouring to pour hot water out of the empty tea-kettle, "how did I forget to fill it,,l wonder? I'm getting to be a perfect simpleton. I wish I did have a little common .sense." ".But, my dear," interrupted Fogg, "suppose you had, de you think you'd know what todo with it ?" "Do with it 1" echoed Mrs. F..; "many things. I might want to be married again, you know, and it might save me from Making e.lool of myself a, second time." TIM Hyena had Abused the Lion ,for ,several months, to all other Animals, without .Provoking a Retort, and one day met the King of Beasts face to face and said: have been Abusing you for this Many Weeks." " AIL! I hadn't heard of it." "I have called you• All Sorts of names." "Indeed 1" I have Maligned you Profession- ally, and lied about you Personally." "Just so." "And you hadn't heard of it?" -"Not a ~word." "And if I now repeat this abuse to your face ?" "I shall Aeeept it as Comisq from a B.yena,;" said the. Lion. " How old are you, sonny Twelveyears of sage." "You are very small for your age. What ;is your name?" " Johnny Smith. My father is baker on Austin Avenue." "So your father is a baker. I might have guessod it by, your size. You remind me of one of his loaves2l—Texa, faugs• CHARLEY —"I thought Shakespeare wrote ,gCharles the First.'" Alice—" But, you know, Anakespeare died so ninny years before Charles the First was born that—" 04, yes; hut Shakespeare is full of anaehranisms." " WEIL, this is a pretty time for you to get .home, Mr. Crap," carolled his better half as that ,gentlemaan appeared before her in the early morning ,hours. "I should think you would be ashamed of yourself to leave me alone this ,way." "I couldn't help it, my dear. I had to see a man, you know." "Had to see a man, did you 2" " YA32, my dear." Lord Randolph Churchill, has, necessarily, been circumscribed in respect of tke cubic measurement of the library he paay take with him in his expedi- tion to Mashonaland. After much consideration he has fixed upon two books. One is Shakespeare, the other Mohere.

The old parish clerk of Addington has just re- signed his place, in his eightieth year. It is stated that he has dug the graves of four archbishops of Canterbury,three of whom are buried in the church- yard; the other Archbishop Howley, in the chancel of the little church.

In Ministerial circles the belief of a dissolution in the autumn is growing. The position will then be unusually favourable. The Government will have accomplished all their more difficult work in con- nection with Ireland, and they would be able to go to the country on a programme of moderate and rational social reform.

A good story told against Mr. Frank Lockwood at the I-ress Club dinner is having an enormous private circulation, but I have not seen it in print. One of Mr. Lockwood's constituents in York was asked how he liked the member for the city. "Oh, he'll do." was the reply. "But," retorted the inquirer, "I hear at the Law Courts that he is doing-" "Who's he doing'?" was the reply of the sharp Yorker.

A correspondent writes :—Might I suggest that when the well-packed Labour Commission delivers its inevitable anti-labor report, it should adopt the following motto from Bacon's" Essay on Cunning." It would explain much :—" If a man would cross a business that he doubts some other would hand- somely and effectually move, let him pretend to wish it well and move it himself in such sort as may roil it.

Primroses were largely worn on Saturday through- out London, though the real anniversary was on Sunday, and several wreaths were laid by Lord Beaconsfield's statue; but a large wreath appeared at the foot of Lord Byron's melancholy statue in Hamilton Gardens, while during the morning many passers-by noticed the figure of a young lady sitting pensively by its side! Few people nowadays remem- ber that Byron died on April 19th.

Here are a working-man's three reasons (authority Mr. R. W. rftks) for attending not church but a chapel—(l) It was too respectable; (2) it was too expensive; (13) the preaching was too much on the benefits of the world to cc-flue. And here is a servant-girl's reason for preferring the Salvation Army :—" The army are not haughty. With the clergy you have to bow and scrape, and if you please' and by your leave.' But I don't hold with the General." He is too select, we suppose.

Mr. Smith announced on Monday night that the Government have resolved to take the case of James Sadleir, M.P., for Tipperary, as a precedent in deal- ing with Mr. de Cobain. On reference to "Hansard" it will be found that Mr. Sadleir was ordered to attend in lifs place on Thursday, the 24th Ju1y,1856. As this order was not obeyed the Attorney-General for Ireland on the 19th of February in the follow- ing year moved a resolution expelling him from the House. This was carried without debate.

The dinner of Lord Randolph Churchill at the Amphitryon Club on Saturday night was one of the most luxurioue'banquets ever given in London, and would have delighted the heart of a.Roman epicure. It cost somewherP about ten guineas a head, but then an ordinary dinner at the Amphitryon, with good wine, runs up to two and three pounds per head. On Sunday night Lord Randolph was enter- tamed to dinner at the Garrick Club. Among his entertainers was Lord Justice Fitzgibbon, of the Irish Bench.

A candidate in a recent contest, possessing the attributes of a dull, good sort ot man but not of a facile orator, addressed an open-air meeting with some notes concealed in his hat,to which be referred with 811S1DiCi0118 frequency. Not being eminently successful in his observations even under these cir- cumstances, a jeering voice exclaimed. "Speak up, auv'nor, there's more in your 'at than your 'eadr Whereupon the mortified rhetorican replied, "Well Ws all very fine but if you think it's so jolly easy, suppose you come up and try.

Professor Herkomer is a striking-looking man, with a very pale face, and blue-black hair. Though yet in early middle life, he has married his third wife. This lady was a sister of number two wife, of Welsh origin. The first Mrs. llerkomer was a Ger- man; Phe had two children; both are living, a boy and a girl. Professor Herkomer besides being a good winter, is a musician, an actor, and manager of his little theatre at Bushey. Some years ago he was a mesmerist,and used his power for curative purposes. However, he found this so exhausting that he has given up the practice more or less of late years.

The leaders of the Anti-Parnellite party, 'I learn from a trustworthy source, are entering upon the electoral campaign in Ireland in the highest hope of securing an emphatic victory. They adopt the calculation that of the old Irish Parliamentary party 52 are anti-Parnellite and 34 Parnellite, and they calculate that at the general election they will win 26 of the Parnellite seats and lose 3 to 1 Parnellite seats and another 3to 1 Unionists. According to this estimate the Irish representation after the dissolution would he 72 anti-Parnellites, 9 Parnel- lites, and 22 Unionists.

The Americans are much interested in Mrs. Besant, and have given her a cordial welcome. She has been interviewed and ,ilescribed by scores of reporters. The "New York Tribune' ' says that "Mrs. Besant looks like a plump. rosy-cheeked, little Englishwoman. But che is 'lrish, for 'she herself has said it': and she said it twice in her conversation with the reporter. This 'proclamation of her nationality is necessary to one who should judge her by her speech, in which the eve': gentle, sweet and low accents of Cordelia are turned to the clear, liquid, but soft tones which give that charm peculiar torthe voices of educated Englishwomen." The subjects of Mrs. Besant's lectures which she has delivered tolarge audiences in New York, Washing- ton, and Boston are "London: its Wealth and its Poverty," "bangers Menacing Society," "Labor Movements in the Old World," and "Theosophy."

Mr. Henry Clristie. of Sunderland, who won the Draughts'Championship of England recently, is a dark-complexioned young a fellow of twenty-three. He is a shipbuilder by trade,and had the misfortune to lose an eye while at work some two years ago. Mr. Christie has played the game nearly all his life; and showed phenomenal powers on the board while still an infant. At seven years of age he met Mr. Brown, a South Shields player of repute—and beat him. Since then he has studied the game to some purpose. and at the present time has no equal, in this country at least. Unlike most champion draught players, Mr. Christie is nothing-if not original, and while he knows the yalue of playing by "the book," he still more appreciates the confusion into which one of his daring moves may throw an opponent. He is as cool a veteran,aad " Newcassel" accent is rather" thick,!'

div.head: EXAMINER, SATTiRDAY, APRIL 25, 1891. A MAHOMEDAN MARRIAGE IN ENGLAND.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATTiRDAY, APRIL 25, 1891. A MAHOMEDAN MARRIAGE IN ENGLAND.

Dr. Waldstein, the Reader in Classical Archse- olgy at Cambridge, has made a most important and interesting discovery in Bceotia. In the course of excavations conducted by himself he came upon what he believes to be the genuine tomb of Aris- totle. The philosopher died at Chalcis in Eubcea, an island only separated from Bceotia by the narrow strait ot the Euripus. It is curious that this dis- covery should have so closely followed the finding of Atistotle's lost treatise on the Athenian Consti- tution.

Mr. Robert Barrett Browning, his wife, and aunt (sister of the late poet),are leaving Be Vere-gardens ' in tots for Venice,at the end of this month. Between eighty and ninety enormous cases of furniture are on their way to the Palazzo Rezzonico. But the Brownings intend spending a few weeks every year in London either in an hotel or in a flat. They have bought a pretty house at Azolo with a large garden, where they intend spending the summer months, when Venice is too sultry. Mrs. Robert Barrett Browning is an American, with a large fortune. She is comely, stout, and fair; but her health is not good. Mr. Browning suffers from gout. He is 42 years of age, middle height, bald, and good-natured looking. Of late years he has not been able to de- vote much time to his paintings.

The first Mahomedan marriage ever celebrated in England took place last Saturday, at the Moslem Institute, Liverpool, where the followers of the Prophet in that city regularly assemble. The bride was Miss Charlotte Fitch, eldest daughter of Mr. Charles Fitch, J.P., of London; and the bridegroom a Mahomedan barrister practising in London,whose father is revenue secretary to the Nizam of Hydera- bad. There was a preliminary marriage at St. Giles's, Camberwell, on Saturday morning. The Vice-President of the Moslem congregation offici- ated, the condition of fitness for such office being a knowledge of Arabic. The Moulvie, as the official is called, was dressed in a long robe of crimson silk, beneath which was a tight-fitting tithe of embroi- dered black velvet, the whole girdled by a broad gold belt, and wearing a turban of white silk, with streamers which fell over his shoulders. There were two bridesmaids. The bride's responses were in English, the bridegroom's in English and Arabic. The lady repeated after the Moulvie the words of the marriage contract "I stand here in the pre- sence of God and all who are assembled to unite my heart to your heart, and my destiny to your des- tiny, and to be called by your name. Your sorrow shall be my sorrow, your happiness shall be my happiness.' The bridegroom made similar promises, after which the Moulvie delivered an address to the newly-wedded pair, quoting as exemplars Adam and Eve, Mahomet and Khadija, and Fatima and Ali as models of conjugal fidelity. After this the bridegroom placed the ring on the bride's finger. The ceremony ended with the inscribing of the names of the contracting parties and their wit- nesses in the register of the Mosque, one of the witnesses being the Ottoman Consul-General in Liverpool, and another the Minister of Education for the Armenian Provinces, who had journeyed from 'Constantinople to assist in organizing the Moslem congregation in Liverpool.
TAKING THE CENSUS AT WOZZLE.
BY AN ENUMERATOR.

I have been annoyed past bearing by various people consultino, me about their papers., Miss Fipps, our schoolmistress, wasted half of one morn- ing for me. She sent for me and asked to speak to me privately, very privately. I said I was as pri- vate as could possibly be. After remarking that she was too young to remember the last census, she said there was a delicate column, in the return, and she wanted to ask a question before filling it in Then she put some currant wine on the table, but without uncorking it. She knew I was unmarrie4 of course, but was my servant Lilith Ann allowed access to the room in which the papers were kept, when filled up? I assured' her that Liiith Ann, having been educated at a board school, could not ' read writing for the life of her. But had I any female relatives or friends who could take the liberty of going into my room while I was away, and looking over her "return ?" I said I did not think so, unless m 3 Aunt Martha came. who would be sure to take stock of everything I had in the world. This made her downcast; but on learning that my Aunt was at the present moment in the wilds of Australia, in hot pursuit of uncle, she plucked up courage again, and she was fully reas- sured, and would venture to answer that most un- Christian question about her age. She was grateful but forgot to uncork the bottle. Then Mrs. Swizzle, the sea captain's relict, also sent for me, and put port on the table, fully uncorked this time. She also wanted my particular advice. There was a column headed, Condition as to Marriage." It was only proper, of course, she said, that her condition as to marriage should be asked, and it was very thoughtful and kind on the part of the Government ; but she did not exactly know what conditions the authorities required to be stated. Would it do to say simply that he must be under forty,and fair; or was she ex- pected also to state the amount of income she would like him to have, and the maximum number of children that would be agreeable, if a widower? I, of course, cleared up Mrs. Swizzle's mistake, and told her all she had to write in the column was 'Widow," but, although partly relieved, she seemed reluctant to part.with the idea of a prospective marriage by the agency of a paternal Government. I had no sooner done with her than I was sent tor by Mr. J3linson, of the Laurels, who had, a very delicate case of conscience. If truthful, he said, he really must put down his wife as "Imbecile— incurable," and he knew he was liable in £5 if he , made a talse return; but, would I, out of charity, and in memory of the barrel of oysters he sent me last year, excuse him if he did not mention the matter on the return? Now, according to Mrs. J.'s ' account, which all Wozzle hears every week through ' their front sitting-room widow, it is J. who is the imbecile; so I promised to wink at the omission, though the barrel" was really only a flag basket.

div.head: NORTON WATER TOWER.
div.p: THE NORTON WATER TOWER.

A very interesting process is going on just now at Norton in connection with the Liverpool water scheme. The big tower there, has for some time now been practically completed,and this week,•with the object of testing it, those in authority are gradually charging the tank with water, and where- ever there may be thought to be the least suspicion of a leakage measures are taken to secure safety. In due course a report of the experiment will be submitted to the authorities in Liverpool. The engineers and others whose skill and ingenuity have been brought to bear on the erection of the structure were naturally taking much interest in the progress of the test, and amongst those who are taking part in the operations were Mr. A. W. Bright- more, the resident engineer in charge of the section , extending from the Weaver to the Mersey; Mr. W. Atkinson. clerk of the works for the Liverpool Cor- poration; and Mr. William Atherton, of the Pearson and Knowles Dallam Forge, Warrington, under whose watchful care the ponderous ironwork has been wrought and fashioned. In a matter of this kind a little recapitulation may be pardoned, and, it will be as well to take a brief glance at the

div.head: OBJECT AND HISTORY
div.p: OBJECT AND HISTORY

of this tower, the massive and imposing propor- tions of which can be seen from a great distance. The "why and the wherefore" of its existence is nuzzle to many who gaze at it from the windows of trains that run on the three lines of railway from which it is plainly visible, and five times out of six they are left puzzling, unless there happens to be at hand some enlightened citizen of Liverpool who can shed a little information around, as it were. The object of the tower, in a few words, is to reduce the pressure on the pipes laid between it and Liver- pool—to act, as a matter of fact, as a sort of safety 'valve. If the water that flows through the pipes all the way from Vyrnwy has obtained an undue pressure by the time it reaches Norton, a proportion of it finds its way by means of perpendicular piping to an enormous tank, whilst the normal body of water pursues its course to Liverpool. If the tank should at any time become full, provision is made for carrying off surplus water. All this seems simple enough, but to erect the tower has required the expenditure of a great deal of money and a good deal of labour, as well as the exercise of much engineering skill and knowledge.

div.head: DETAILS OF STRUCTURE.
div.p: DETAILS OF STRUCTURE.

The toner is built in the Roman Doric style o architecture, and occupies an elevated position not much more than n stone's throw away from the humdrum country station of Norton. It is railed off and approached by a good carriage road, and alongside has been built a house for the caretaker. The foundations of the tower are of cement con- crete, laid to the depth of ten feet on natural rock. At the top of the tower has been placed an enor- mous tank, which has capacity for holding some 650,000 gallons of water. In height the tower is 100 feet, and the tank ip 115 feet in height, there being 15 feet of ironwork projecting from the top. It is estimated that the iron alone, independent of what water there may on an average be in the tank, will weigh something like 400 tons, and there is room for water in the tank that would approach a weight of 3,000 tons. At the base the diameter of the tower is 94ft., and at the top 82ft., and the tank is slightly less in diameter. .The tank itself is 30ft. 7in. in depth at the centre. The bottom is an ad- verted dome, which " dips" 15ft. 7in., and the re- maining portion of 15 feet projectsat the top. Some enormous blocks of stone have been used in the masonry, and it is said that there are about 250 that will each weigh as much as seven tons. It has been computed that the weight of the whole concern, including the ironwork, when the tank is charged with water, will be about 60,000 tons. Most of the masonry was obtained at Run- corn, at Helsby, and at Norton itself. This part Of the work, between three and four years ago, was started by Messrs. Rathbone. Bros., of Northwich, but has been completed by Messrs. Nelson and Co., of York. The ironwork, as before mentioned, has been carried out by the Pearson and Knowles Com- pany, Warrington. The Latin inscription that has been carved on the bridge round the top of the building, by Mr. M'Cullough, of London, will bear repetition. It reads :—" This water,derived from the fountains of the Severn, is led 80 miles through the hills and valleys of Wales and intermediate country to the city of Liverpool,at the expense of the muni- cipality. In the year of our Saviour 1890." It is only natural to assume that a good many Liverpool citizens, who, as in duty bound, take an interest in the affairs of the city,among winch its water supply has a prominent, place, will find their way to Nor- ton to see it. Norton is not exactly the place for the typical Bank Holiday tripper to devastate ; but I the quiet man in search of a change,might do worse than have a trip of inspection to the tower, though to some he might seem to be taking his pleasure sadly. interest seen the tower there is nothing fur- ther of to study about the village itself,but within a radius of half a dozen miles or so there are
SEVERAL PLACES WORTH A VISIT.

For those of an antiquarian turn there is the little village of Halton, less than a couple of miles dis- tant from Runcorn, and somewhere about the same distance from Norton. It .was formerly a place of some importance, having its .markets, its fairs, its prison, and its castle, but its importance, except to the historian, is a thing of the past, long since for- gotten. The castle, however, remains as a remin- der of the far-away times. Those who go to look at it may be interested to know that it was erected soon after the Norman Conquest, on the brow of a hill that commands a charming view of a great part of Cheshire and Lancashire. It was once a favourite residence of John o' Gaunt, Duke .of Lancaster, was garrisoned for King Charles in 1643. and for the Parliament in the following year. ' Three and half miles or so from the water tower lies Frodsham, where on a clear day a view can be had from the hills that is well worth a railway journey to obtain. From a steep hill in this neighbourhood seven counties can be seen, and on a clear day, so it is said, the " Cat and Fiddle," at Buxton, can be observed. You can't exactly see the cat, nor for the matter of that can you see the fiddle, but the black speck away yonder in the distance is the two com- bined. Midway between Warrington and Norton. the Ship Canal works can be tapped by dropping off at Daresbury Station, which is within a short dis- tance of the Moore section. From Liverpool the traveller can have the choice of two routes. One is to take the train to Warrington and thence to Norton, and the other is to travel to Runcorn, which is within about three miles of Norton. At Runcorn, of course, there is

div.head: FAMOUS BRIDGE
div.p: THE FAMOUS BRIDGE

connecting that little Mersey port with commercial Widnes. • Nearly everybody in this part of the country, it may be Considered; has either seen or heard of that structure, but everybody may not know its dimensions. At a time like the present, when several great engineering enterprises are be- ing watched with so much interest, it may not be out of place to mention them. The total length of the bridge proper is 1800 feet. There are three river openings of 305 feet each. The total number of arches, including approaches to the bridge and the viaduct on Litton Marsh, is 101. The width be- tween the girders for the railway is 25 feet. The height of the girders, above high-water mark, is 75 feet, and the tops of the towers are 128 feet above high-water mark. The ironwork in the bridge weighs 5,100 tons, and the contractors were Messrs. Brassey and Ogilvie. Altogether there is a good deal to be seen in these parts for those who care about such things. Norton will no doubt have its visitors coming now and again for a country ramble, but it is scarcely necessaay to 'say that New Brigh- ton has no cause to be jealous.

div.head: WYCLIFFE SUNDAY SCHOOL. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.
div.p: WYCLIFFE SUNDAY SCHOOL. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.

The anniversary services in connection with Wycliffe Sunday School, were held on Sunday last and must be regarded as among the most enjoyable and successful of recent years. The congregations were good, that in the evening being very large indeed. The musical arrangements were in the hands of Mr. G. Wallington as choir leader, and Mr. W. H. Payton, organist, whose manipulation of the organ at all the services was exceedingly able mid effective. Mr. Payton shows himself to be a sym- pathetic leader and accompanist of Psalmody and sacred music. conbining with this very admirable quality considerable power and brilliance as a player. The hymns and anthems were well chosen, and the choir, which has many new voices in it, very credit- ably rendered them. In the morning anthem, Mrs. Pearson admirably rendered the solo part of "As pants the hart." (Spohr) ; and in the evening anthem, Mrs. Pearson and Miss Roberts were very effective ,in the duet " I waited for the Lord," (Mende's- solin). The second anthem in the evening service "It is high time to awake out of sleep," (Barnby), was given with much effect, although perhaps, a little lacking in precision and emphasis. The chants and hymns were set to good music, and well sus- tained both by choir and congregation. In the after-, noon a musical service, entitled "Tie Prodigal Son,' was iziven by the scholars, and was really nicely carried through, which is highly creditable to the pains and skill of the leader Mr. G. Wallington. The solo parts were rendered by Messrs. W. H. Walling- ton, G. H. Yonge, and Miss F. Booth. The readings were impressively given by Mr. Thomas Wallington, and several scholars also took part; a new feature, and one capable of considerable development. The lads did well, and seemed to enjoy themselves. The preacher at the morning and evening services was the:pastor, the Rev. J. Yonge, who spoke in the morning on "The Teacher's Reward" taking as his text Daniel xii. 3. The evening subject was " Who is on the Lord's side? a challenge for the Times." (Exodus xxxii. 26.) After des- cribing the incident of the Golden Calf, which provoked this challenge :from Moses to the tribes of Israel, ' the preacher went on to say that the words presented a call very timely now, as much need existed for Christian people rallying on the Lord's side, to contend against many evils in society that were subversive of morality and pros- perity. More clear and unmistakeable Christianity is needed in Christian people, in personal, business, social, and political life. Christian people should not indulge in amusements that are doubtful in their tone and tendency, and in none at too great and exclusive an expenditure of time and money. , Christian work was lacking workers, and also re- sources. Might not this be accounted for by the excessive outlay of leisure and means upon self- indulgence and enjoyment? These days, also, are bristling with problems and difficulties with which Christian, faith and energy should deal. Drink and gamblin..; were two prolific sources of sin and crime that need to be dealt with with increasing earnest- ness. Princes and peers need to be faced with a vigorous Christian public opinion, and to be com- pelled to see that they could not sin against God and the people with impunity. Christians should protest against gambling in all forms, whether in hazardous speculation in shares and stocks, in pleasurable philanthropic raffling at bazaars, or in friendly games of cards. If the Church chose to unite they could put down drink and gambling speedily! The times need a declared and manifested Christianity. Much had been said of .late, sneer- ingly, in the Tinblic Press about "the Nonconformist conscience." hi reply to such sneers, the preacher said. "May it ever be true that the Nonconformists of this country are narrow enough to cling to right- eousness, and bigoted enotigh to protest against every form of wrong. On these issues, let them be- come more narrow and more bigoted than ever! The collections amounted to £45. -Os

div.head: rERCIVAL GORDO N ; OR,
div.p: rERCIVAL GORDO N ; OR,
THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT.
BY SYLVANITS COBB.
CHAPTER VIII.

MAR v ELLOUS NEWS FOR SIR RICHARD. With the breaking of day three of the women belonging in the cavern were found who were ready and willing to help in the preparation of breakfast. Provisions in abundance were at hand, and a substantial meal was in due time provided. The very best wine of the country was to be had, who wished for it, and one of the women, of her own accord, brewed a caldron of hot spiced rum- punch. Taken as a whole, the meal was the best the hussars had enjoyed for a long time. When the meal was at an end the brigand chief asked that he might be permitted to confer with the English commander. " What !" he cried, as his late prisoner presented

himself. "Are you the Man ?" "They were my own children who set me free," Maxwell answered. "Will you tell me how, your soldiers found this place ?" "With pleasure." And he told him, in brief, the whole story. Don Lopez swore roundly at his own stupidity, and acknowledged that he had no one to blame but himself. And then be made known his chief reason for having asked for the Meeting. He was anxious to know what they purposed to do with

him. Said he: "It will be of no earthly use for you to deliver me up to the authorities, for I can assure you that no court in the land will convict me. If you burden yourself with me, it will only be to see me set free by the first tribunal that passes upon my case." "Very well," said Maxwell, with a polite bow, "then the odium of the transaction will rest with another, and not with me. Considering the man- ner in which my liberty was to have been gained at your good will, you cannot ask me to consider your case tenderly. Do not forget, sir, that you told me how you were bound by your brigand laws, even to the penalty of death. Allow me to remind you in turn that I am bound both by the laws of God and man. Calling to mind the cold- blooded, useless murders your hands have wrought, I should deem myself equally guilty with your- self should I suffer you to go unpunished through any fault or failure of my own. So, my good sir, you will hold yourself in readiness to depart with me." The brigand bowed his head, and from that time his bearing was not that of a man who expected a tribunal of his country's judges to set him free. Three of the women, who, the brigands all ac- knowledged, had had no hand in their robberies, at their own request, were suffered to remain in the cavern, free. The others—five of them—chose to go with their husbands—or four of them with their husbands. The gipsy woman declared that she would go with the troop, and find another husband among them when they had regained their liberty, which tfiey were sure to do. Horses were found for all, with several excellent animals to spare for sumpter service and for relief. The wounded were comfortably provided for, our invalid sergeants being so far recovered that they could ride without difficulty. The brigands, thirty- four in number, were secured to their saddles, with only one arm at liberty, and behind each one rode a watchful hussar with a loaded pistol ready

for use. At Maxwell's suggestion, a saddle was so ar- ranged, by the harness-maker of the regiment, who chanced to he one of the squadron, that •Per- cival and Caroline could ride upon it in company. and with entire ease and safety. It was placed upon the back of one o the strongest and gentlest of the horses, and thus Sir Richard's cherub was made infinitely happy; and Sir Richard himself did not object. in fact, he was rather pleased than otherwise, for the arrangement left him to his own comfort. The thought of a serious love passage between two children Hie them would have appeared to him simply ridiculous had it been hinted to him. In his own mind he never could have conceived it. And thus the cavalcade set forth, and fortune was favourable at every step. They made over thirty miles on the first day, and little more than forty on the second. On the evening of the third day the troop entered the old Moorish city of Al- cantara, on the Tagus, and only a few thiles from the Portugueie frontier. Here Maxwell made inquiries concerning the judicial establishment, and was much pleased to learn that one of the highest courts of justice in Estremadura was at that very time in session—a court, too, from the superior judges of which had gone forth an offer of heavy reward for the appre- hension and delivery to justice of the noted brigand. Further, the colonel was credibly informed that the chief justice—Don John de Castro—though a humane man generally, would have no unwise mercy upon such criminals as De Miranda and his band had proved themselves to be. So to the authorities of Alcantara our colonel made his appearance; and when he had succeeded in convincing them that Don Lopez and his whole gang were at their disposal, their joy and satisfac- tion were beyond utterance. And there the brigand prisoners were delivered up, much to the relief of Maxwell and his com- mand, and to the great joy of everybody, saving only the brigands themselves. And we may here say, that, after due trial, the robber chief, together with four of his principal officers, was condemned, and promptly executed, the rest of the gang being ordered into the military service, to be transported to the Spanish posses- sions in America. During the march, by day, as we have seen, Percival and Carolinf; were together occupying the same saxldle, and the reader needs not to be told that the boy.put forth every effort of his skill and ingenuity towards making his gentle companion's ride easy and pleasant. She had looked upon him as her champion and hero from the first, but with the lapse of time he had become more than that. She had come, in fact, to look upon him as especially belonging to her—as one upon whom she might of right rely, and whose faith, and love, and good-will must be hers, first, and last, and for all time.

In the evening, when the troop had found com- fortable quarters for the night, Sir Richard spent the hours between halting and sleeping with the genial, gentlemanly officers, leaving his cherub to the care of the faithful nurse; and the faithful nurse was glad to see the two beautiful children enjoying themselves. At the end of a full week, Col. Maxwell found the commander-in-chief at Salvaterra de Magos, a considerable town of Portugal, not more than five- and-thirty miles from Lisbon. In his visit to Sir Arthur he took with him Lieut. Col. St. Vincent, Percival Gordon, and Sir Richard Archer; and St. Vincent, being the officer who had been com- missioned for the expedition, first reported. Wel- leaky complimented him highly upon the efficient conduct of the mission, and directed his private secretary to make a minute for special reference. While the rescue of Col. Maxwell, and his brave companions gave him the keenest satisfaction, he was sincerely rejoiced that' the notorious brigand had been captured and delivered up to justice, and his band broken up. To Maxwell's story Sir Arthur listened with absorbing interest, and at its conclusion he took Percival upon his knee and blessed him with paternal love and goodwill. He asked the boy many questions, the answers to which both pleased and surprised him. Said he, with his arm thrown around the little fellow, who now stood by his side: "I have often wondered if the boy's heroic con- duct on board the transport, in the matter of the mad gunner's mate and the magazine, had not been somewhat highly coloured; but I can now well understand it." After this he turned to the baronet, his manner clearly betraying that he had something of more than passing moment upon his mind. "Sir Richard Archer, I am glad to meet you; and especially thankful that you have been rescued from impending death by officers of mine. Perhaps, after all," he added, with a warm and happy smile, as he observed a suggestive movement on the part of Col. Maxwell, "we ought to give the credit of your rescue to this gallant boy ; for he certainly was the guiding spirit of the whole thing." "0, no, sir l" Percival interposed, tremulously but earnestly. "if you could have seen how Col. St. Vincent led his men up the mountain, and how de entered the cavern, and how he fought-0, he should have the credit, sir !" " Aye ; but who led me up the mountain? and who entered the cavern by my side, and pointed out to me the work in hand ? ' said the lieutenant- colonel, nodding pleasantly towards the boy. "Anti who, in the end, saved not only the life of Sir Richard's little daughter, but, very likely, ' the lives of himself and mess well ?—for, had those Istrong men not been foiled our deaths might have resulted; and, certainly, you, my boy, and you I alone, detected the impending evil, and was Quick ' and nromnt to avert it."

So—SpOEe Col. Alar Well, and when he had con- cluded, the little hero shrank away like one frightened. The flattery really distressed Mgt. But a few assuring words from Sir Arthur soon placed him at his ease, after which the chief turned again to the baronet. "Sir Richard, I have news for you that may surprise you, though / think not unpleasantly. Your younger brother has more cause than you dream of for not caring again to see you in the flesh. You have corresponded with him regularly,
I suppose?" "I have kept him informed of my movements, sir," replied Archer. "And he has written to you?" " Yes, sir." "At how late a date have. you assurance that he

received a letter from you ?" - "The last letter I zeceived from him came to me at Malaga, by the way of Gibraltar; so I know he must have received the last letter I sent from Rome, previous to leaving Italy, for in that I gave him the directions for addressing me on Spanish

soil." "Ha!" exclaimed 'Wellesley, brightening. "Then we may know that he has been deceiving the people at home. Your solicitors know nothing of your having left Italy, and they have sent a messenger ' to Rome to rack you. But I will explain." At this point tifb chief drew forth a large pocket-book, from which he selected a worn and crumpled letter. "This missive," he resumed, "I received, only three days ago, from the chief secretary of the Lord High Chancellor of England, and in it I am earnestly requested to make such inquiries as I conveniently can after the whereabouts of Sir Richard Archer, of Dorset. I little dreamed, when I had read it, how conveniently the means of answering were to be vouchsafed. Tell me, my dear sir, were you ever personally acquainted with a certain Benjamin Archer ?" "Benjamin Archer is the family name of the Earl of Elmdale," retuned the baronet, wonder- ingly. "I do not know that I ever saw him." "Was he not related to you by blood ?" "Distantly, Sir Arthur, but he was very wealthy and very proud; and I was not poor enough to care for either his assistance or his friendship. He was a crotchety old man, wishing that he might be able to prevent his relations from stepping into his shoes. I think my father and he were cousins, at least twice removed." "And yet," said the general, seriously, "your distant cousinship proves to be a strong bond between yourself and the earldom. Benjamin Archer did four mouths ago, without issue, and he had been an only child. In looking ,up the ' succession they found no living representative until they had gone back three generations, at which point they found children of a younger brother who had died during the lifetime, of the then reigning lord of the manor. That brother's issue has been critically followed, and the records all found in due and ample form; and, my dear sir, it has appeared, beyond the reach of doubt or question, that a certain Richard Archer, baronet, of Dorohester, in Dorsetshire, is the true and legiti- mate earl. Here is the record. It is not private, though confidential to me. You can examine it."

Sir Richard had flushed and paled by turns during this recital, and now that the climax had been reached he was completely overcome. Though already wealthy and a baronet, this sudden and undreamed-of step to the peerage and to one of the longest rent-rolls of the realm wrought upon his emotions most deeply and powerfully, and, after a little time, he asked that he might be permitted to take the letter and go away by himself. He hardly knew what to make o it. He could not realise it. With a few kind words, Sir Arthur gave him the missive, and bade him keep it as long as he wished. "And," he added, "when you shall have made up your mind upon the matter of your return to England, I will give you such assistance as I can command. And, further, I shall probably employ you officially, by giving into your care dispatches to the War Office." The baronet took the letter, and having thanked the chief for his great kindness, left the room. "He will grace the pterage, I am sure," said Sir Arthur, after Archer had gone. "Such a man as that, with such magnificent physique, ought to have been a soldier." "He is not exactly of the moral stuff of which soldiers are made," ventured Maxwell, "but I agree with you he will grace the peerage. At all events, he will be proud enough.' Thus speaking, the colonel glanced towards our hero, who sat in a far corner, engaged in looking over a military map, which he had found on a camp-stool by his side, and the words that fol- lowed were spoken rather as though he thought aloud, than as a speech adreased to another: " If this ancestral windfall could have alighted upon our brave little hussar yonder, there would have been same sense in it I" Then he called, in a different key: "Say, Percival, how would you like to be an earl ?" "I would rather be a colonel of hussars," was the quick, emphatic answer. "My dear boy," cried Sir Arthur, to whom a lofty peerage was even then assigned, though he knew it not, "do you rest easy. If you and I both live, you shall wear a colonel's epaulet, or I am a false prophet." Two large, bright tears trembled for an instant upon the lids of the large grey eyes, and then rolled down the brown dimpled cheeks of. the boy, as he feelingly replied : "Indeed, sir, I will do all I can." "All right. Stick to that, my boy, and hope for the rest." Afterwards the chief said to Harry Maxwell: "I did not promise wildly. The boy comes from good blood. Two of his ancestors were baronets, and in pushing his claim, should the opportunity ever arise, I have the record of Archy Gordon to which to refer. We must look to it that the little fellow has every possible advantage for a good and I substantial education." And Col. Maxwell gave his pledge that he would make the boy's education his special charge. During the three weeks that followed the arrival of Maxwell at the English camp Sir Richard Archer, now Earl of Elmdale' allowed Percival Gordon to be an inmate of the house he occupied. He had satisfied himself that his little daughter would sigh her life away if kept from her hero while he was so near, so he made a virtue of neces- sity, and permitted the companionship, but upon the promise of Nancy that she would keep them always within sight; and as this was her sole duty and occupation she could not fail in its proper f fillment. As for any danger of undue affection, though the thought had presented itself, in view of the wonderful precocity of both the children, he did not borrow trouble. They would be separated by the inevitable very soon, never, in all probability. to meet again. And we may be sure that the children were happy. The Colonel relieved Percival from all duty, bidding him entertain the bright-eyed Caroline, and take good care of her. Hand in hand the twain went through the camp, made cheerfully welcome wherever they came, petted by koth officers and men, beloved by all who knew them, and made the recipients of every possible favour. Sometimes, when in the shady orange or lemon groves, or elsewhere by themselves, with only good old Nancy to see, the boy's arm would find its way around his compnion's shoulders, while she would fondly cling to him with an arm around his waist. And so they walked, and talked, and were happy. "Aim, dear Caroline," he said one day, as they cat in A vine-clad arbour in the garden of the house in which they resided, while Nancy napped on a seat close at hand, f' what shall I do when you are gone? I shall be very sad; and I know I shall be unhappy," The gill looked up, with a startled light in her deep, blue eyes, and turned pale. She caught her companion with a convulsive grasp upon the arm, and rolieklv eriP(l. "No, no! You will go with us! 0, you won't stay here. Colonel Maxwell will let you go, I know. I will ask him." Percival shook his head sadly, and for a brief space it was upon his tongue to bemoan the hard fate which he knew must very soon come; but he restrained himself in time, and when he finally spoke there was a warm smile upon his handsome face. He bent and kissed the tear-wet cheek, and tendetly said: "Dear Carrie, we must learn to wait and pray. I am going to be a soldier, and Sir Arthur has promised that I shall be a colonel, if I live, and if he lives, too. But I shall not wait for that. When I alit a captain I will come and claim you for my own. You will wait for ma, lam sure.' "I will wait for you while I live," she fervently answered, returning his kiss and putting aw)y her tearful look. The thought of that grand time in the future when her hero, grown to man's estate, still true and loyal,, should come to claim her for his own and for all time, filled her with wondrous delight, and the thought of parting was for the time forgotten. Meantime_ ak Billiard was busily engaged in

matters of business thrust upon 111111 by Ins ooex- peeled elevation of station. He had assured him- self beyond the possibility of a shadow of doubt that he was truly and legally Earl of Elmdale, a peer of England, and owner of Eundale Manor and all its belongings. On Monday, the fourth day of September, an English ship was to sail from Lisbon for London, and by that, ship the new earl had entoged pas- sage. On the morning of the previous Saturday •he was ready to set out from the camp, Colonel Maxwell proposing, with a good escort, to accom- pany him. While preparations for the start were being concluded little Caroline crept to the colonel's side, and asked him to let Percival go with them.

And the kind-hearted colonel, as though of his own accord, asked the boy if he would like to see Lisbon. The answer can be readily imagined. So at Lisbon the separation took place. Nancy saw that her two pets were deeply affected, and she contrived that they should be alone together during the last half hour. Had they been man and woman, the loving twain could not have planned more solemnly for the future; and when, in the last moment, they were twined in a fond embrace, they turned their thoughts heavenward with a faith sublime—a faith such as the pure in heart, who lean with simple trust upon the Heavenly Father, alone can feel.
(To be continued. )

div.head: RHYMES IN DIALECT.
div.p: RHYMES IN DIALECT.
TIP OWD PUMP.

Th' owd pump stan's yon th' nook o' t' fowd. 11l pown, an' eawt o' gear; Id hesn'd bin mitch use, aw know, This five an twenty year. Aw cut mi name on't when a lad— Time hesn'd scrat id eawt ; An' hey! wod sups aw used to hey Fro' th' hoyle o' top th' speawt. Afooar aw'd lamed to toddle reight, Aw'd crawl to wheer id wor ; An' hey! wed brats aw used to deet VVi' scamtnerin' so for. Aveve swung o' th' handle scooars o' times, An' getten ixonv a bump, Thro' foin' off thaa throne o' mine, 'Peearkt up atop o' th' pump.

Mi mates an' me, wod gam we hed, Aside on't, in eawr youth; When life wur sweet, an' hearts wur blythe, An' tongues wur tipt wi' truth. But deawn i th' village churchyard yon, The's mony a grassy clump, 'At serves to show th' last restin' place, 0' some who played hi th' pump. Th' owd pump looks like a monument To joys 'at's passed away: An' t' thcwts' at fill this brain o' mine
Mi tongue con never say. For tho' id handle's maskerd off, An' th' woodwark's rottin' fast, Aw like id wed, becose id brings Glad memories o' th' past. Owd Keither--7th'_farmer, used to co,—
Fie doesn'd do id neaw,— An' mek th' owd pump giP fost-rate milk; _ . . .
We coed id lies'ther;S lieaw One day th' lads dropt a mongrel pup Inside his big milk-tin; Ile drooave off, fun eawt tlf nasty trick, An' shunned tie pump ever sin.

One fleet aw' geet inside o' th' pump, When Nan an' Turn o' Kits Wur cooartin' theer ; aw give a grooan,— They welly lost ther wits. An' mony a tale abeawt owd Scrat l'th' pump's bin fairly towd ; Well, o'er that marlock aw'll say nowt, For aw wur th' ghost o't' fowd.

Hey me, wod creawding memories Rush, TAB mell, thn' mi brain; Some notions mek me sorrowful, An' others mek me fain. But th' sweetest memory ov o t' lot, Fair meksmi heart go bump; Aw won th' lwd lass beside id, an' Thro' thad aw like th' owd pump!
JACK 0' ANN'S.
WHAT EATS UP WORKMEN'S WAGES?

It is estimated that every workman in England and Wales averages tendays' loss of time every year, and, of course, loses wages 'n proportion. The total amount of wages annually lost in this way is something over £14,000,000 in this country alone ; and in France it is

almost as much. If ;his loss were equally divided among the workmen, it woud not be heavy on each one, but it is very unequally diviled. Whereas many men do not lose a day from illness 'or years in succession, others lose weeks or months. Now, illness is expensive in two ways: first, on account of wages that cannot be earned, and, second, on account of extra costs that must be met some- how—doctor's bills, rnedine, and little luxuries needed at such times. To meet these expenses how many things go to the pawnshop? Ad what poverty and sorrow follow, millions of men and women in England know. If only two lines each were devoted to all the cases of this kind now in the country, the biggest news- paper published in London would not contain alb half of , them.

A steamship fireman, named Richard Wade, living in Glasgow, was confined in a hospital in Halifax for nearly a year, of course losing all his wages for the whole time and going through foarful suffering besides. The doctors there gave him up to die, but he finally got well, and came back to Scotland and resumed his work.

Joseph Robinson, now living at 14, Ainsworth-street, Ardwick, Manchester, a few years ago, had an awful time. You may wager he won't forget it in a hurry. He was a young man then, about forty, had always been sound as a nut, and couldn't imagine what on earth was the matter with him. In fact, there didn't appear to be much wrong with him at first; he felt tired and weary (without any overwork to cause it), was " always yawn- ing," and had a bad taste in the mouth. The result was that he went from one medical institution to another, and was off his work for weeks and weeks, and came near having to lose his leg, by reason of a disease caused by bad blood. He also got well, but not because of what any of the physicians were able to do for him. Mr. Robinson has been for forty-four years in the employ of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway. Another employe of the same railway, alluding to an experience of his which took place in 1887 and 1888, says :—" I was'obliged to draw money from my club all the time to help support my family." It is fortunate for working men that they can get help from their clubs in such emergencies, yet we must not forget that the money comes out of the pockets of other working men. It is merely mutual insurance; the loss falls on many instead of on one only, but it is a loss all the same. Well this young man, Edward Perrin, was so ill the doctors said he was fast breaking up with consumption. He had chills, night sweats, and a hollow cough, that sounded like a muffled drum, sure enough. After they had booked him second class for the graveyard, the good physicians

turned their attention to more hopeful cases. Yet he is all right to-day, and has as fair a prospect for a long and healthy life as anybody in this island. Yet, while he was creeping about looking for smething to cure him, lie was, of course, doing no work and earning no wages.

We could go on giving cases like these till we filled this paper full of them, but what is the use? Every- body knows the country is full of thorn, and can judge what they signify to people who can just scrape along when the breadwinners are strong and hearty,and there- fore what a calamity it is when some disease keeps them off their work for Heaven knows how long. No sensible person needs to be told that all the sicic persons in England are not afflicted with the same ail- ment, but nine out of ten are—namely, indigestion and 'dyspepsia and its consequences, and these include nearly the whole list of ailments. The men mentioned in t'ais article had it,and after a lot of trouble and expense,were finally cured by Mother Seig,el's Curative Syrup. It would have been pounds in their pockets if they had used the Syrup in the first place. But they will know next time, and the best kind of wisdom is the kind that comes by

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

- - - HOUSE OF LORDS.—MOAT. The Lord CHANCELLOR took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four. THE ARMY Sesoms BILL.—Lord Bnowxtow moved the second reading of this Bill, which came up from the House of Commons. The Bill was read a second time. Buts ADVANCED.—The Public Bodies (Provisional Orders) Bill passed through Committee. The Middlesex Registry Bill was read a third time and passed. The Elec- toral Disabilities Removal Bill passed through the Coen- mittee without amendment. The House adjourned at 25 minutes to 5. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. MERSEY DOCKS BILL.—The Mersey Docks and Harbour Board Bill was read a third time and passed. THE CHARGES AGAINST MR. DE COBAlN.—Replying to Col. Saunderson, Mr. W. H. SMITH said that if Mr. De Cobain continued to remain outside the jurisdiction of of this country, it would have to be considered whether the same proceedings should not be followed as in the Sadleir case. The right hon. gentleman informed Mr. T. Healy he had no information as to whether any of the accessories of the crime were to be put on their trial. MR. DAVITT .AND THE LABOUR COMMISSION.—Answer- ing Mr. Norris and Mr. Cobb, Mr. SMITH said that, al- though no representative of the dock companies has a place on the Labour Commission, their iitterests would be fully looked after. After the evidence given by Mr. Davitt before a Special Commission, the Government did not think he was qualified for an appointment on the Commisssion. THE CLITHEROE CASE.—Sir R. WEBSTER, answering Mr. Cobb, said the recent decision in the Clitheroe case had simply declared and had not altered the law. The Government saw no necessity for a change in the law of divorce. THE ALIEN ACT.—Sir M. HICKS-BEACH told Mr. Howard Vincent that the Alien Act would continue to be enforced at the 23 ports frequented by poor foreign immi- grants. . THE LAND BILL—The House having gone into Com- mittee on the Irish Land Bill, Mr. LABOUCHERE moved to leave out the whole of Clause 1. During the course of the hod, gentleman's remarks he was more than once called to order for irrelevancy. The amendment was ultimately defeated, and' the clause ordered to stand part of the Bill. On Clause 2, which provides for the establishment of a land purchase account, Mr. SEXTON • moved an amendment preventing the county percentage being carried to the guarantee.—Mr. BALFOUR opposed the amendment, which was afterwards withdrawn.— Colonel Nolan's amendment to the sub-seetion of the Clause fixing the county percentage at one shilling for all holdings paying a purchase annuity under £l5 was negatived by 292 to 5, the result being received with loud laughter from all parts of the House, The House adjourned at 12.30. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The hord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at half-past five. TIER MERCHANDISE MARKS BILL.—Lord BALFOUR, in Moving the second reading of this Pill, said its objects were simply to remedy two defects in the existing Act. The Bill only consisted of two clauses, namely, to enable the evidence of the entries at the Custom. House with re- ference to goods improperly marked and fraudulently marked to be sufficient. This referred principally to Cases of perishable goods. The second clause enabled the Board of Trade to prosecute in cases where the interests of any considerable section of the public were concerned. The neble lord stated that the Bill had passed through the House of Commons with its unanimous approval. The Bill was then read a second time. BILLS ADVANCED. The Army School Bill passed through Committee. The Electoral Disabilities Removal Bill was read a third time. The Sale of Goods Bill passed , through the Committee without amendment. The Chari- ties (Recovery) Bill was read a second time on the motion of Lord Herschell. FIRST READINGS.—The Law of Evidence (Scotland) Bill and the Drainage Improvement of Land (Ireland) Bill were read a first time. The House adjourned at six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.,—TurssnAy.

The Speaker took the chair at two o'clock. MR. DE CODAIN.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND told Mr. T. Healy that the warrant against Mr. de Cobain Was issued for the offence of inciting to the commission of a felony. There was no evidence that any other per- son had committed the offence.

IRISH LAND BILL.—In Committee on the Irish Land Bill, the discussion was resumed on Mr. S. Keay's amend- ment proposing to omit from Clause 2 words providing that where a sum 'is applicable out of the guarantee de- posit for the discharge or reduction of an irrecoverable debt, only one-half the amount should be paid out of the guarantee deposit to the land purchase account. —Mr. J. Morley thought it most unfair that the landlord's deposit should be relieved at the expense of the taxpayer ; while Mr. BALFOUR areued that it was only reasonable that the liability for theY failure of the tenant should be shared between the locality and the landlord. Mr. T. W. RUSSELL, Colonel SeurmEnsoN,and Mr. GLAnsToNE took part in the debate which followed, and on a division the amendment was negatived by a majority of 47 votes. Mr. Knox's amendment requiring the landlord to bear three-fourthsinstead of one-half of the risk, leaving the remaining one-fourth to the locality, Was also rejected; as was also Mr. M. Kenny's, to the eflect that the landlord's liability should continue during the full term of 49 years. COUNT OUT.-At the evening sitting a count was Moved, and 40 members not being present, the House adjourned.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDNESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDNESDAY.
The Speaker took the chair at a quarter-past twelve 'Clock.

•Port&ic BILLS, &c.—The Bolton Corporation Tramways Bill was considered as amended, and ordered for third reading, as was also the Salford Corporation Bill. Some discussion ensued on a proposal by Mr. Ritchie, with the shiect of relieving the Treasury from the responsibility hitherto undertaken in regard to the introduction and carrying through the House of bills promoted by the London County Council. Nothing definite resulted from the discussion,Mr.Ritchie indicating that he would again bring up the matter on an early date. PLACES OF WORSHIP.—Mr. S. Even moved the second reading of the Places of Worship Enfranchisement Bill, the object of which is to enable the trustees of places of Worship built on leasehold land to acquire the freehold .„011 reasonable terms. Mr. BYRON REED moved that the bill be read a second time that day six months. Colonel Nolan supported and Mr. Ambrose opposed the bill. Mr. 1/4„A'rrriEws said his personal sympathies were in favour °I providing legislative means for the acquisition of Qeclesiastical sites when they could not otherwise be secured, but as a lawyer he did not think that the priit. ciPle of the present bill could be defended. Mr. OSBORNE koacIAN supported the measure on the general principle of justice, and because it dealt with what was a burning cltlestion, especially in Wales. The bill was read a second tune by a majority of 108, the announcement being re- 'Owed with loud Oppositbn cheers. The Ancient Monuments Protection Act, 1882, Amend- bent Bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-THIIRSDAT.

THE PORTITO-U;SE DIFFICULTY.—The Marquis otSAtis- Ryßy, replying to the Earl of Kimberley, said he was afraid there was no doubt that a most unjustifiable attack had been made upon a British expedition by the g'.3rtuguese. The Minister of Portugal had intimated to yn that instructions had been sent to remove every Obstacle to the passage of possible travellers up the _r,ungwe, but the demeanour of Portuguese officials on the East Coast of Africa had on more than one occasion Lisbon so little with the assurances received from I:i.lsbon, that her Majesty's Government had thought it desirable to send three war vessels to the Pungwe as BPeedily as possible. NEWFOUNDLAND DELEGATES.— On the motion of Lord UIINRAVEN, the five Newfoundland delegates were ad- Mitted to the bar of the House, and Sir WILLIAM WHITE- WAY, the Premier, addressed their lordships, specifying the objections of the colony to the Newfoundland ilsheries Bill. At the close of Sir WilliaM Whiteway's ,BPeech, Lord Knutsford suggested the adjournment of the debate, in order that the arguments contained in Lilo speech might be examined. The debate was accord- '"glY adjourned till Monday. BILLS AnvANcEn..—The Betting by Infants Bill and the -l'orrowing (Infants) Bill was referred to a committee, With an instruction authorising their consolidation into 0 rl,e- The Charities (Recovery) Bill passed through Com- w---ittee, and the Taxes (Regulation of Renumeration) Bill as read a second time. The House adjourned at one minute to six o'clock. TI HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TEUR e STMS. RAILWAY SERVANTS.—Sir M. HICKS BEACH informed V'. A new writ was ordered to issue for South Dorset, and Mr. M. H. Morrell took his seat for Mid- Oxford. • THE BUDGET.—FREE EDUCATION. ,t The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER made his annual , financial statement. He said the Government were able to point,to an excess of £1,756,000 over the surplus sug- gested in his Budget speech last year. With a Budget estimate of £87,376,000, there had been an expenditure of £87,732,000, including the supplementary estimate, the figures were :--Total grants, £88,511,000 ; pctual expenditure, £87,733,000, Out of the total increase in the revenue, alcohol chiefly spirits furnished £900,000. The reduction of the tea duty had resulted in a net loss to the revenue of £1,073,000. To- bacco showed an increase of £456,000, another evid- ence of the increased wealth of the working classes. He defended the increase in the alcohol duties, and re- pudiated the idea that there was any pledge on the part of the Government that the increase should not be made if they did not carry their scheme for buying up licenses. As to the question whether one third of it should be re- mitted, representing the amount which it was last year proposed should be spent in buying up licenses,he pointed out that the money had been assigned to the excellent purpose of developing technical education. It would, he said,be a small and doubtful boon to take off a penny per barrel on beer and twopence per gallon on spirits, and therefore he had come to the conclusion to make no re- (Action. Coming to the accounts for next year, he said the total estimated expenditure was £88,319,000, an increase of about £1,000,000 on the past year, part of which was due to Irish relief works. Looking to the increased cost of armaments and the heavy burdens on the home taxpayer, he suggested that there should be a call on the colonies for some increase in their contributions for Imperial defence. With regard to the estimated revenue for the coming financial year, he estimated that would be an increase in revenue of 2 per cent., which would be equal to £1,200,000. He estimated the total revenue at £90,430,000, against £88,440,000 last year, and said he expected to find himself with a surplus of about £2,000,000. Various suggestions had been pressed upon him as to the disposal of this surplus, but the 'government did not intend to depart from the. pledge given in the Queen's speech with respect to ele- mentary education, and if the House seconded him by a resolute determination to get through its busi- ness no administrative delay of a single day would occur and education would be free from the Ist Septem- ber next. This would ultimately absorb quite two millions, the amount of his surplus, but by reason of the necessary delay in bringing free education into force this year he would have £OO,OOO of his surplus remaining. He proposed to devote £500,000 of this to the reconstruc- tion of barracks, which would save tke necessity of borrowing for this purpose, and the remaining £406,000 ,he proposed to devote to the withdrawal of light gcld from circulation. Mr. GLADSTONE said that after Mr. Goschen's long and able statement his impression was that inasmuch as there was no change in taxation no serious demand would have to be made on the time of the House to secure its assent to the financial arrangements of the year. He asked when the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer proposed to go forward with the consideration I of the subject, and Mr. GOSCHEN suggested Monday. Mr. MUNDELLA asked when they might expect to see the Government scheme of free education: Mr. Gosc HEN said that the introduction of the Education Bill would depend on the progress made with the Irish Land Bill, but there would be no delay. Progress was soon after- wards reported on the resolution before the Committee. The second reading of the Summary Jurisdiction (Youthful Offenders) Bill was moved by Mr. MATTHEWS, and after some discussion was carried by 143 to 54.

div.head: NORTHWICH DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION..
div.p: NORTHWICH DIVISION LIBE- RAL ASSOCIATION..

-- IMPORTANT SPEECH BY MR. BRUNNER, M.P. The annual meeting of the Council of the North- wich Division Liberal Association was held on Saturday afternoon, in the Gladstone Club, North- wich, under the presidency of Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P. There was a good attendance,and among those present were Mr. E. Milner, hon. treasurer; Mr. W. Handley, general secretary; Mr. G. E. King, secre- tary of the Gladstone Club, Northwich ; Messrs. Prince, A. Spencer,G. Shaw,W. H. Tolfree,G. Ander- son, Clegg, T. Handley, Millington, J. Burgess, G. Pimlott, B. Golden, E. Williams, J. Nusha, F. W. Hughes, R. Woodier, D. Hughes, J. Capes, J. T. Yearsley, and J. Proudfoot. Letters of apology for non-attendance were read from Mr. E. H. Moss, Mr. Bratt, and Mr. Mclntyre. Mr. Handley submitted his annual report, which re- ferred in detail to the work of the year, and gave the following as a ,summarized result of the registreion work,as compiled from the returns of the district agents: owners' claims sustained by Liberals; 81 • Tories, 27; occupiers, 183 Liberals and 84 Tories ; 'Odgers, 86 and 103; ownership objections, 5 and 10; occupiers, 34 and 13; and lodgers, 2 and 0 ; total 391 Liberals, and 237 Tories ; or a gain of 154 as the net result of our work in the revision courts. The growth of the regist?.r since the enactment of the Franchise and Redistribution Acts of 1884-5 was noted. The Parliamentary register of 1885 contained a total number of 10,577; that of 1891 contains 12,328, an increase of 1,751. or over 16 per cent. The County Electors Act of 1888 added to the register, for County Council purposes, a new portion, named division 3—being mostly the names of men—containing some 800 additional electors, so that the registration work taken cognizance of by the district agents comprises a total of over 13,000. Qn the motion of Mr. King, seconded by Mr. Taylor, the report was adopted. STATEMENT OF ACCOUNTS. Mr. Milner submitted the statement of receipts and expendiSure for the year ending December 31st last. It showed the receipts, with a balance in hand of £lB 19s. 2d., to have been £209 2s. 7d. The payments, includ- ing £152 for salaries. reached £173 9s. 9d., leaving a balance in hand of £35 12s. 10d. Mr. Milner explained that from the date when their accounts were made up, it must of necessity appear that they had a balance in hand. They did not get the subscriptions for 1890 until the present year, nor were they able to pay the accounts through their not being all in on or before December 31st. That day they were really in debt, as would be seen by the bank book. It was 'decided that Mr. Picker- ng and Mr. Tolfree should audit the accounts for 1890. ELECTION OF OFFICERS. The following officials were selected : president, Mr. E. E. Moss, Ravenscroft Hall, Middlewich ; chairman of council, M. IlEnry Deakin; chairman of executive, Mr. Henry Bratt ; treasurer, Mr. E. Milner ; and hon. sec., Mr. A. Fletcher. The following gentlemen were elected co-opta-ive members of the General Council : Messrs. Bunn, Taylor, Woodbine (Middlewich), H. Lockhead, A. M. Fell, J. Sidiorn (Winsford), W. Topham (Northwich), Thomas Rigby (Sutton), James Pritchard, W. R. Earp (Runcorn), T. Hewitt (Wincham), and E. Ravenscroft (Moulton). The election of 13 representatives on the Council of the National Liberal Federation resulted as follows :—Messrs. E. H. Moss, J.P., G. H. Deakin, James Handley, J.P., P. Speakman, C.C., A.Fletcher. H. Bratt, C.C. E. Milner. C.C., H. Capes, T. Handley, Joseph Mil- lingeon, A. M. Fell, and W. Handley, and the Rev. F. Carter. For the Cheshire Federation Council the repre- sentatives appointed were—Messrs. E. H. Moss, A. Fletcher, E. Milner, and W. Handley. CONFIDENCE IN ME. BEUNNER. Mr. Aaron Spencer kßarnton) proposed in suitable terms. "That this Council of the Northwich Division Liberal Association hereby expresses its great obligation to J. T. Brunner. Esq., for his valuable services as member for the division—(applause)—and the support he has uniformly given to all questions, both in and out of the House of Commons having as their object the moral, social, and intellectual progress of the people; and hopes the time may soon arrive when the electors of this constituency will have the opportunity of expressing, at the ballot box, their continued confidence in him as their representative—(hear, hear)—and also as a sup- porter of our revered leader, the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone." (Applause.) Mr. Clegg (nuncorn) seconded the propositioniremark. ing that Mr. Brunner had loyally fulfilled his duties in the House, which showed that he loved his work. By his recent action in connection with the Subsidence Bill, he had demonstrated his wishes for the interests and welfare of his constituents in the salt district. (Ap- plause.) If there was a wrong to be redressed,. Mr. Brunner was there, and did not hesitate to speak out about it. He had gained the sympathy of the People of Runcorn most thoroughly, a circumstance illustrated in a marked manner when he sustained a severe bereavement. The sympathy shown by every class on that occasion was something marvellous. In Mr. Brunner they had a member whose moral and social character was of the highest order; and on all those and many other accounts they had a gentleman of whom they could not be too proud. (Applause.)—The motion was carried by loud acclamation. *MORAL, SOCIAL. AND INTELLECTUAL PEOGRESS. Mr. Brunner said he was much obliged to them for the very kind expression of confidence in him as their member. They knew it was an 91d and very trite say- ing that the thanks of a constituency were the only wages a member of Parliament got. They were to a man likehimself, who did not want money, the very highest wages a man could get in this world. The resolution spoke of his devotion to matters having for their object the moral, social, and intellectual progress of the people. To his mind those questions were far more important than any others. Many questions, excepting so far as they attained that purpose, were of very small import- ance. Whether they paid a little more or a little less in- come tax; whether they paid a little more or a little less for their tobacco or tea, were matters et comparatively small coasequence conned wttiv then measures hav-
