div.p: THE EXAM INER, SATURIAY, APRIL.2S, 1891.

hag an effect upon the moral, social, and intellectual progress of the people. He took it that by expressions of that sort they were thinking of the great question of, education, of licensing legislation, and of the many sub- jects that went by the general name of the labour ques- tion. Mr. Handley, in his report, touched with eloquent and graphic strokes upon the great work done by, his friend, Mr. Arthur Acland, the member for Rotherham, through whose intervention it was mainly due that the 3d. per gallon upon beer, and the 6d. per gallon upon spirits, were devoted to TECHNICAL AND SCIENTIFIC INSTRUCTION. No piece of more important work had been done since 1870 than that little performance on the part of Mr. Aeltrid. Mr. Handley had said that the technical in- struction which was now obtainable at the hands of the wC oaus ntthye eChoeu tnhciihl and etdhfeu IS Soh he eßaehnl sei nt hg et o n B rSi ct ihsoho laorft zAarht and farmer to complete more satisfactorily with those on the ccntinent of Europe. He had all his life been convinced that if there was anything in other coun- tries that was better than what they possessed in Enly,land, they should get it for themselves. If they took right lines on the question of education they would give to all their children, not only assisted education, as they did in their elementary schools to the extent of three- fourths, but they would have free schools. if they ob- tained free schools and good schools; if they gave to all the children of the nation an equal chance at the starting point, they would have done more than anything else by that action to abolish all the troubles that they now knew as social difficulties, than by any other means of which he was cognizant. The rich people of this country had never been ashamed, and he doubted whether they ever would be ashamed—(la.ughter)—to take the money that was left by benevolent donors, in past days, not for rich people; but for poor scholars. The rich people of this country had never been ashamed to take advantage of those charities aud he trusted that, following their example,they would never be ashamed of it. (Applause.) Referring to Trades Unions, he said he Pelieved that they were a great education for the work- ing:men of this country, and he believed that Trades Unions would not do any harm, either to the employers or to the employed. (Applause.) He had lately had a good deal of work to do on the Standing Committee on Trade. He had been a member of one of the two so- called Grand Committees on Trade ever since he first had the honour of being elected a member of Parliament by them. He had to tell theinjthat it was a matter of the ut- most moment, deserving their most serious consideration, that the leaders of the workingmen and the leaders of the great political parties in this country were taking what to him seemed to be a most dangerous line. Year after year the Houses of Parliament were asked to give more protection, more regulation, and more restriction to workingmen and to other classes is the country. Every set of men and women seemed to desire at the hands of the State some protection in order to make their profes- sion a close corporation. Theaccountants went to them a few years ago, and they now called themselves Chartered Accountants; the architects came beford.them this year asking that no men might be allowed to call themselves architects without the permission of an elected body. The miners had come to them asking for protection that they might not be allowed to work more than eight hours; the midwives had come to them —(laughter)—the nurses had come to them, and the sweeps had come to them (laughter) all ask- ing for protection for themselves and for pre- venting anybody else going ilia their trades. That was the most dangerous line the English people could take, and he warned them of it, aria he urged them amongst their fellows and, all over the country to maintain that freedom and independence of character ' which had been the characteristic of the English people; and to manage their own affairs and not have them managed by Government officials. It seemed to him that the system he had described was doing a great deal of mischief year after year. They had it from all parts of the country; the fac- tory owners and the representatives of the 'working- men were meeting together and agreeing to the ap- pointment of more officials, and every time they met they agreed that it would be very well to have working- men appointed as officials and as inspectors. He asked them not to be tempted by that prospect of what mig,l4 be looked upon as promotion. They had just had a dis- cussion in the Grand Committee as to whether working women should be allowed to work up to ten o'clock at night. Hitherto the hours which they had been per- mitted to work had extended from six in the morning till nine at night. They were not allowed to work more than twelve hours a day. The Home Secretary, Mr. Matthews, brought in a bill, one clause of which per- mitted women, if they pleased, to work till ten o'clock. One after another of these goody-goody gentlemen got up to say that it was not well for the health of women that they should be out after nine o'clock at night. (Laughter.) He thought he put a stop to that nonsense by telling them that they never objected to allowing their daughters and wives to go out at 10 o'clock at night, and to stay out four hours at a ball; and if it were right and good for the health of their wives and daughters, he del not see why they should interfere with the rights of women who stayed out at work till ten o'clock. (Applause.) He believed in men and women obtaining freedom for themselves; but when they came to the young it was different. He would not declare his opinion on the question coming before the Committee next week; bdt he maintained that just as they ought to stand up for the freedom of men and women, so they ought to protect children against themselves, against the cupidity of masters, and the thoughtlessness and ignor- ance of parents. (Applause) Something had been 'said, in very kind terms, by Mr. Spencer about the recent piece of worlc done by him at Knutsford. It seemed to him i that the change n the management of

THE 'OREAT LIQUOR TRADE was one that concerned them all. He was, as they knew, not a total abstainer. He was not at all wishful to abolish public-houses; but he did want that those pub- lic-houses, which were a nuisance to them, should be, in Jahn Morley's wOrds, " either ended or mended." Until they had an opportunity of offering to them the manage- ment of that matter of liceosing,in the localities in which they lived, it remained the duty as it was the privilege of the magistrates to regulate it for themselves. It was well known to those gentlemen what he wanted was not a forcible interference with the freedom of his neigh- bours, but only that the magistrates should consider, in addition to the vested money,interests of the publicans, the vested interests in order and decency which belonged to everybody who lived in Cheshire. His resolution was carried in the proportion of 58 to two. He thought when they found 58 magistrates of the county of Chester on one side, and two upon the other, the probability was that they would have a change for the better before long. (Applause.) He had been so very much occupied with the question of subsidence that he was, very glad indeed to have done with it for a bit. With their permission, he did not mean to Say anything on the subject. They had not yet finished the Bill, and he would have a ffreat deal to think about it during the next week. He had to thank them again, as he had thanked them many times, and it would probably be his lot to thank them again, for that kind expression of their confidence, and he could assure them that nothing in the world could give him greater pleasure than to go on in his wprk in their service. (Applause.)
NOT A MODERATE LIBERAL.

On the proposition of Mr. Prince, of Winsford, seconded by Mr. G. King, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Brunner for his presence and address. Mr. Brunner, in responding, said he was not going to be a moderate Liberal; lie did not intend to sink into

that rank. He hoped he would never slacken his efforts until every family in the country had available the com- forts and refinements of life which were now to be had for £2OO a year. If he could bring about that during his life, and help to bring about as much as that, he should begin to think about becoming a moderate Liberal. (Applause.) There was danger in that position; when a man had been a member for one constituency for a considerable time, there was a temptation before him to earn the good-will and support of the moderate people and the Conservatives. He did not want to give way to it. What he wanted was for them to be always in the car, a•lways moving ahead, and never to join with the party of the stick-in-the-muds. (Laughter and ap- plause.) The meeting then terminated.

MR. GLADSTONE ON THE IMPENDING ELECTIONS. Mr. Gladstone has addressed to Mr. Benson, the Liberal candidate for Mid-Oxfordshire, a letter commending and supporting his candidature, and conveying the expres- sion of similar sentiments to those who are now " figh t in- terests" similar battles in defence of the highest national at Whitehaven, the Harborough Division of Leicestershire,the Stowmarket Division of Suffolk,and in South Dorset. Mr. Gladstone points to the " remarkable progress in public opinion in and since 1887, which has given over to the Liberal party on the by-elections occurr- ing from time to time a balance of no less than 16 seats and has thereby afforded a prophetic indication of what is likely to happen when the whole of the constituencies are invited at the coming dissolution to pass judgment on their present representatives." He shows that the course of recent events has continued to bring home to the mind of the country that practically and in the main Irelavd stops the way to legislation on questions of importance and urgency; that Parliament is now " deal- ing with a Land Purchase Bill for Ireland, which, in defiance of the sense of the country expressed in 1886, creates an Imperial liability to facilitate the purchase of Irish estates, constitutes the Exchequer the direct creditor a the Irish occupiers indiviau- ally, leaves us to meet 'default by evic- tions, and provides by way of security, an ultimate charge on funds properly and strictly Irish, without any consent or control of any local authority in Ireland, or of her representatives in Parliament." The pledges of 1888 to supply Ireland with a large system of local self-government remain unredeemed; and in "the other departments of administration there prevails a similar disposition to prolong or revive that sentiment of hostility between the nations which the Liberals be- lieve that the people of Great Britain have entirely for- sworn." In concluding, Mr. Gladstone says :—" All we have W desire is that each man in each of those consti- tuencies may justly remember that with him rests the ultimate power in these great matters, and that where the power lies, there lies also the responsibility." Mr. Gla4tone has written a letter to Mr. Shee, the Liberal candidate for Whitehaven, in which he says that Mr. Shee's personal position as a Roman Cath4ic de- mands special notice,because recent circumstances bring it again into question whether religious opinions are or are not to be a disqualification for political offices. Mr. Gladstone points out that the offices of Viceroy of Ireland and of Lord Chancellor of Great Britain may be held by a Unitarian or a Jew, by a Mohammedan or a Buddhist, by an Agnostic or an Atheist,but not by a Rom an Catho- lic, who, however. may be Prime Minister. Mr. Glad- stone hopes that the constituency of Whitehaven, by re- turning Mr. Shee, will pointedly condemn a state of law uniting in a singular degree gross injustice with gross absurdity. MR.. BALFOUR REPLIES. Mr. Balfour, writing to a correspondent in criticism of Mr. Gladstone's recent letter to Mr. Benson, Liberal can- didate for Woodstock, says the policy embodied in the Crimes Act of the present Government has reduced crime to a lower level than at any period since (now more than ten years ago) a Conservative Government last had any lenthened tenure of office. In any case, Mr. Bal- four continues, the last man to criticise it is one who, like Mr. Gladstone, has the unique distinction of having as Prime Minister, passed and administered no less than three Coercion Acts, all from his present point of view more open to criticism and objection than the one now in force,

div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
--- TIMESDA.Y.—Before His Honour Judge Ffoulkes. rHE CAUSE LIST comprised 6 adjourned plaints, 149 original plaints, 4 default summonses, and 29 original

judgment summonses. STICKING TO A BARGAIN.—A barman, named Joseph Henry James, sued William Limeocks, of 165, Orford- lane, for 93. the value of a carpet sold to defendant. It appeared from the evidence that the plaintiff formerly lived at 165, Orford-lane, and the defendant succeeding him in the occupation of the house agreed to take the carpet of the kitchen and to pay 93. for it. Defendant finding the carpet not so good as he had expected, refused to pay for it, and wanted plaintiff to take it back but the latter refused to do s.) on the ground that" a bargain's a bargain." .A verdict was given for the plain- tiff. AN UNSIISTAINED CLAlM.—Samuel Claffe, furniture dealer, Sankey-st., sued William Watson, of Winvick, for 17s. 6d., balance of an account alleged to have been owing for a basinette and rue; sold to defendant. The articles named, it was stated, were sold for £2 17s. 6d., the basinette for a 10s. & the rug for 7s. 6d. Defendant had paid £2 but refused to pay the rest. In defence Mrs. Watson and her daughter said that the basinette I was a second-hand one and was sold to them for 305., and the rug for 7s. 6d. They paid 15s. on account and then the price of the basinette was raised to £2 103. They had, in fact, by mistake paid 25.6 d. over the amount they had agreed to pay. A verdict for the defendant was given. A COLLISION BETWEEN VEHICLES.—THE JUDGE

- - ON PERJURY BY WITNESSES. In this case, WilliAm Holland, carter. of Newton-le- Willows, and his wife, Elizabeth, claimed £5O for per- sonal injuries sustained by the female plaintiff, and for damages to a trap owned by Mr. Holland, owing to the negligence of a person in the employ of the defendant, William Naylor. cart owner and beerhouse-keeper, 18, Cross-st., St. Helens. Mr. Mulholland, barrister (in- structed by Mr.H.J.Longton) appeared for the plaintiffs. and Mr.Swift,barrister (instructed by:Messrs.Ansdell and 'Eccles, of St. Helens) was for the defence. In his open- ing statement Mr.Mulholland said that Mrs Holland was proceeding in her husband's trap or dog cart, from New- ton-le-Willows to St. Helens, on Saturday afternoon, the 14th February. The son, Daniel Holland, was driving, and when they had gone a certain distance they met the defendant's wagon. The road at the point was paved to a width of 18 feet, and the other part, which had a width of about six feet, was without paving. When the wagon got within thirty yards of the trap it turned on the centre of the road. Holland drew his trap to the • left side of the road, the trap's left wheel being a foot on the soft ground. The wagon, however, came on at a trot, and one of its wheels struck the wheel of the trap. The trap was thrown up and Mrs. Holland was pitched out, and when picked up was un- conscious. She was taken home, and Dr. Moun- sey was called in. He found that she had had two of her left ribs broken and a third staved in. One of the ribs had not yet united and would probably be a permanent injury. Mrs. Holland was confined to bed for three weeks and had to be attended' by the doctor for a month. Thomas Robinson, turner, of Earlestown, spoke to having seen the trap and wagon approach one another. The wagon was driven by a youth, who was lying down in the wagon with a horsecloth partly over him. Another youth was sitting on the side of the wagon, but he had no control over the horses. He corroborated the state- ment of Mr. Mulholland as to the collision, and added that the youth in the wagon did not stop, and Daniel Holland had to run after him. Daniel Holland gave corroborative eyidence,and stated that as soon as he recovered himself after the collision, he jumped down and ran after the wagon, which was going away at a trot. The horsecloth was over the name on the front of the wagon, and when witness lifted it up the youth in charge, a son of the defendant, tried to kick his hand.' He was sure that two horses were attached to the wagon. Mrs. Holland corroborated the statements with respect to the accident. After she regained consciousness she was at home. Her ribs were injured and she had since been unable to do any work,and had to employ a woman for nine weeks at 34. 61. a week. Her husband had attended her at nights and consequently had lost nine days work. Dr. Mouncey, of Newton, said that he was called to see Mrs. Holland on the evening of the 14th February. She complained of pains in the head and left side, and of a difficulty in breathing. He found the skin stripped off part of the leg and thigh, and the Bth and 9th ribs were broken, the 10th being staved in. She was perfectly helpless and had even to be turned over in bed. The eighth rib had not yet set, and the consequence was that it had caused a muscular swelling en the left shoulder. Mrs. Holland was 59 years of age and it was unlikely that tile rib would unite. The very act of breathing, to some extent, prevented the rib uniting. Edward Naylor then described the injury that had been done to the trap Witnesses for the defence were next called. Edward Naylor, 18 years of age, the son of the defend- ant, said he was a carter for his father, and was driving the wagon at the time in question. He denied that he had been asleep when in charge of the vehicle and was not even lying down on the wagon. He was on his own side of the road, and there was, he said, plenty of room for the trap to pass. Joseph Halsall, a lad who had been in the company of the last witness, at the time of the collsion, and Wm. Naylor, the defendant, also gave evidence for the defence. His Honour, in giving his verdict, remarked that the evidence gave another illustration of the sadly increas- ing offence of perjury, an offence which had been corn- . mented upon by a great many judges both in the high courts and in county courts. He then commented severely upon the evidence of Edward Naylor and Joseph flaisall. The story, he said, had evidently been made up between these two boys, which was a shacking thine, to do, and Naylor had not improved his position by the flippant manner in which he had answered questions in the box. A verdict was given for the plaintiffs, Mrs. Holland being awarded '£4o damages, and this together with 6•two or three smaller items, made a verdict for £45 85. 6d. against the defendant. I

MID-OXFORD ELECTION. The result of Tuesday's polling in the Woodstock Division was declared on Wednesday as follows G. H. Morrell (C) G. R. Benson (L)

Majority 6BB After the declaration of the 'poll, which was received with cheers and groans by an immense crowd, Mr. Morrell proceded to the Conservative Club where he ad- dressed the crowd from a window, thanking the electors for the proud position in which he had been placed, and acknowledging the services he had received from the Liberal Uaionist. Mr. Benson spoke at the Liberal Hall, and expressed his readiness to Belt the seat at the next election. The population of the division ia given at 49,800, and the registered electors' number 9,725. In 1886 Mr. Francis William Maclean, Q.C., was re- turned unopposed as a Liberal Unionist. In 1885 there was a contest, the- voting being as follows :—F. W. Mclean (L), 4,327; Viscount Valentia (C), 4,138 ; majority. 189. The following telegram from Lord Salisbury was received by Mr. Morrell on Wednesday night :—" Pray accept hearty congratulations on your magnificent victory. STOWMARKET.

There is no abatement of political activity in the Stow- market Division of North-West Suffolk. Mr. Greene, Conservative can3idate, is sending the electors a card containing his portrait and the words "A Suffolk man for Suffolk." Mr. Stern, the Gladstonian, has been can- vassing the freeholders of Bury St. Edmunds with some success. A large number of volunteer workers are en- gaged on both sides. SOUTH DORSET._

A Conservative demonstration was held at Dorchester on Thursday night, and was addressed by Mr. Parker Smith, M.P., and others. The Gladstonians met at Wey- mouth, Lord Cavan, Sir A. Hayter, and Hon. B. Cole- ridge being present. HARBOROUGH DIVISION.

Both parties in the Harborough Division of Leicester- shire were occupied on Thursday in canvassing. Mr. Logan, the Gladstonian candidate, spoke at Wigston and South Wigston on Thursday night, and was supported by Mr. Broadhurst and Mr. Phillips, M.P.'s. Mr. Hardy, the Conservative candidate, spent the day at Lutterworth, where he addressed two meetings, being assisted by Mr. Muntz and Lord Feuding.

div.head: WHfrEHAVEN.
div.p: WHfrEHAVEN.

Mr. G. H. Shee wa(;171-in-d—ainoininated as the Glad- stonian candidate for Whitehaven. Sir James Bain is the Conservative nominee. The closing meetings in this campaign were held on Thursday night. Mr. Shee held a meeting in the Circus, Sir Joseph Pease add Mr. Dun- can, M.P., being the principal speakers.

div.head: MR. PARNELL AND MRS. O'SHEA..
div.p: MR. PARNELL AND MRS. O'SHEA..

A London morning journal has reason to believe that a marriage between Mr. Parnell and Mrs. O'Shea will take place before long, and that the date has already been fixed. After the 17th of next month the parties will be legally at liberty to marry.

div.head: SHOCKING DOMESTIC TRAGEDY.
div.p: SHOCKING DOMESTIC TRAGEDY.

HALLE, TUESDAY.—A shocking domestic tragedy oc- curred to-day at the little village of Atbrecktsham, near Leipsic. A market gardener named Damon murdered his wife and four childran with a hatchet, and then hanged himself in an outhouse. Financial worries are suppcsed to have led to the crime.

A Stay from
LANCASHIRE, DERBYSHIRE, & EAST COAST RAILWAY BILL.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.

The consideration of this Bill, which authorizes the construction of a trunk line across England from War- rington on the west to Sutton-on-Sea on the east, was continued on Monday, before the Select Committee of the House of Commons, presided over by Mr. Walter James. Mr. George Woods, managing director of the Longford Wire and Steel Company, carrying on business at War- rington3was the scat of the wire industry in England, there being five factories there. His company employed about 150 hands, and two others employed between 500 and 600 each. His company made about 100 tons a week, but when trade was brisk, the output was more than 140 tons. About . 70,000 tons per annum of wire rods were also made, and the amount of wire would be 50,000 tons per annum. There was one company in the iron business with a paid up capital of £BOO,OOO, which con- sumed 160,000 tons of coal per annum, and he thought they made about 100,000 tons of bars and sheets. War- rington produced altogether about 150,000 tons of bars and sheets, the amount of pig iron consumed being about 170,000. The number of hands employed in the iron in- dustries of Warrington must be between 5,000 and 6,000. The total consumption of coal there would be about 450,000 tons. Asked whether he lzd thought of the benefits of access to the Derbyshire coMifields, the witness said that as a matter of fact he did not think the Derby- shire coalfields would be able to compete in ordinary times with the coalfields of South Lancashire, which were only a short distance from Warrington, but it would be a great convenience when the necessity arose to be able to obtain another source of supply. In his opinion the proposed line would be of considerable value to the industries of Warrington. Amongst those industries were cotton, tanning, and soap, which would be greatly benefitted by improved and additional railway facilities. Cross-examined by Mr. Littler Q.C. (for the London and North-Western Railway Company), the witness admitted that at present Warrington was exceptionally favoured as regarded railway communication. He was, however, in favour of the proposed line, which would shorten the distances to several places and open up new markets.— Mr. Bidder, Q.C. (for the Midland Railway Company), cross-examined the witness with the object of showing that Warrington would not derive much advantage from being in direct communication with Sutton-on-Sea. —ln reply to a question from Mr. Littler, he admitted that Grimsby and Goole were a little nearer Warrington than the proposed new port at Sutton. Mr. Naylor, timber merchant, carrying on business at Warrington, said that the proposed line would be of considerable advantage to his business. Wimber was getting scamp around Warrington, and a good deal had to be brought from Wales and Ireland. By this time, however, the district of "The Dukeries " and Sherwood Forest would be opened up, and timber could then be quickly and economically transported to Warrington. Mr. Charles Muirhead, fish salesman, of Manchester, supported the scheme as one likely to considerably im- prove the fish supply of Manchester. Mr. Needham, mining engineer, residing near Maccles- field, said that the consumption of coal in Macclesfield was something over 100,000 tons per annum. Mr. Francis Rathbone Thompson, corn miller, near Macclesfield, said he purchased about 6.000 tons of grain a year from Lincolnshire, and about 11,000 tons from Liverpool. At present the grain from Lincoln came by way of Nottingham and Uttoxeter to Macclesfield. The proposed line would, he believed, shorten the journey by about twenty miles. Dr. Hewett, managing directoAf Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, of Northwich, gave evidence as to the increased facilities the line would afford.—Cross-exam- hied by Mr. Bidder, Q.C., he said it was correct that his company were erecting extensive chemical works near London, but they did not intend to leave Northwich. The new works would be additional. The Committee adjourned.

div.head: TUESDitY.
div.p: TUESDitY.
The Select Committee of the House of Commons, pre- sided over by Mr. Walter James, sat again on Toe- day, and heard further evidence in support of this Bill.

The Chairman, addressing counsel for the promoters, said it was obvious that it woul,l be to the interest of landowners, traders, and the community at large if a new railway were made. That was patent, and the Committee, therefore, did not want a repetition of evi- dence in that direction.

Mr. Pembroke Stephens, Q.C., (for the promoters). said that the difficulty they had got to contend with was that the three railways opposing would say that the existing accommodation was sufficient, and therefore it was only by showing from the local circumstances of each district that the people were not satisfied with the railway accommodation that the promoters could make out their case. Although that course might appear to entail a good deal of evidence, yet it must be remem- bered that the line was one running right across Eng- land.

The Chairman: That is a perfectly legitimate conten- tion on your part, but kindly let us have it as short as possible. Mr. W. Walker, a member of the firm of Peter Walker and Co., Limited, brewers, of Warrington and Liverpool, was then called. He said that the Company's principal breweries were at Warrington, and for the purposes of their business they used large quantities of malt, which came from the Lincoln, Newark? and Chesterfield dis- trict. At present the means of comrnunicatiqn, were not satisfactory, the route being indirect. It would be a great advantage to their business if the proposed line were constructed, and would open up the district between Warrington and Macclesfield, which, under existing circumstances, was difficult to reach. The company would then be able to dispose of a con- siderable quantity of grains to the dairy farmers in that region. Mr. Thomas William Britten, coal merchant, carrying on business at Buxton, said that he drew his sunplies from East Derbyshire by the Midland Railway Company. The service was not satisfactory; nothing could be worse. At present the distance from Chesterfield to Buxton was 30 miles, but by the new route it would be 21 miles. Witness, complaining of the great delay in the carriage of coal, caused some amusement by handing to all the counsel engaged in the case a reprint of a letter he had written to the newspapers instancing the cases of delay. The time occupied in transit in some of the cases varied from 34 days to eleven days. In one truck of coal on its arriving at Buxton, he found a bird's nest contain- ing five eggs—(laughter)—and lie suggested that so long had the truck been on the journey that the bird had had time to build the nest and deposit in it the contents. (Renewed laughter.) Cress-examined: What kind of bird was it that laid the eggs? I was not there when the eggs were laid. (Laughter.)—Can you tell me when it was that this bird took a fancy to the truck? No, I don't know. (Renewed laughter.) Witnesses from Derbyshire and Lincolnshire having been examined, the Committee adjourned. WEDNESDAY.—WARRINGTON DOCKS. Mr. Ward, a farmer, near Alford, East Lincolnshire, gave evidence as to the benefits he would receive from the proposed line, if constructed. • The Chairman after some conversation said the Com- mittee did not wish to hear further evidence from land- owners, traders, and coalowners or occupiers along the proposed line of route. Mr. Bidder, Q.C., said the other day he used some words which were capable of the interpretation that the Manchester Ship Canal was bankrupt. He wished to sly that that expression was not intended to mean that the concern was bankrupt in the sense of being unable to pay its debts, but that it was in the position of being unable to complete without further money. which it was seeking to borrow from the Manchester Corporation. Mr. Marshall Stevens, one of the executive, officers of the Manchester Ship Canal, wo then called by Mr. Pem- broke Stephens, Q.C., to expltin the circumstances of the dock at Warrington.—He said that the Manchester Ship Canal had never in any way retreated from their undertaking for the completion of the Warrington dock. Over £lOO,OOO had already been expended upon the dock. Two-thirds of the Canal was completed.—Cross-exam- ined by Mr. Bidder Q.C. (for the Midland) : The Ship Canal Company had not expended all its money, but was carrying on full work in the direction of construction. They had not, however, enough money to carry them over the next session of Parliament, and accordingly were now seeking powers to authorize the borrowing from the Corporation of about £3,000,000. The last call on the shares had not yet been made, and it was absolute- ly wrong to say that the calls when made were not paid. —Cross-exaeiined by Mr. Littler, Q.C. (for the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire): Are you aware that the Warrington end of thi lines comes on to your dock on the opposite side to the London and Noith- Western ? Oh, yes.—Do you know that in order to get at your dock it has to cross two public roads? No, Ido not know that.—That is a little awkward? No, I don't think so. After hearing other witnesses, the Committee ad journed.

THURSDAY. Mr. A. Giles, M.P., civil engineer, gave evidence as to the capabilities of Sutton as a harbour. Mr. Cooper, engineer for the. scheme described the different sections of the proposed line. ?The Ship Canal Company had consulted him with a view to constructing their Warrington docks so as to accommodate the coal traffic the line would bring. The viaduct over the Mid- land Railway at Monsall Dale would be 543 yards long, and the greatest height would be 270 feet, being the highest in England, but nothing unusual in other coun- tries. The estimated cost of construction was £4,227,522. I He emphatically denied that there was any agreement between the promoters and the Great Northern Railway Company. The Committee again adjourned. THE ACTRESS'S BREACH OF PROMISE
CASE. SCENE IN COURT.

1 Mr. Justice Cave resumed his summing up in the Hurlburt breach of promise action on Monday. His Lordship was proceeding with his summing up when a dramatic incident occurred. A lady, twlieved to be Mrs. Hurlburt, came up through one of the doors under the Bench, and after having listened tor a few seconds to tho judge's summing up, she shouted out in an excited manner—" My lord, I claim a hearing. I cannot stand still and hear such a parcel of lies.' There was great sensation in court. Mr. Hurlburt motioned to the lady to be silent, and Mr. Ernest Beckett rose from his seat and led the lady out of court. Mr. Justice Cave pro- ceeded quietly with his summing up, telling the jury that they must say whether they believed the evidence of the plaintiff or the evidence of the defendant. If they believed the plaintiff, the fact that the defendant was a married man made no difference. If he had promised to marry her, he was liable in damages. If they came to the conclusion that Mr. -Efurlburt did not write these letters, there was an end of the plaintiff's case. The plaintiff had to satisfy the jury (1) that the defendant did write these letters; (2) that he had promised her marriage, and that she bona fide believed that he meant to marry her. If she had proved both these points to their satisfaction they must find a verdict for the plain- tiff. If she had not proved both these points they must find a verdict for the defendant. If they found for the plaintiff they must give her damages. The amount of damages must depend very much on tha general view they took a the circumstances of the case. The jury retired to 'consider their verdict at one o'clock. At 2.38 the jury returned into court. The foreman said they found that there was no promise of marriage. His Lord- ship said: That is a verdict and judgment for the defen- dant. There were some symptoms of applause at this judgment, but they were instantly suppressed PLAINTIFF A MANCHESTER CLERGYMAN'S DAUGHTER.

NEW YORK, TUESDAY.-Mr. W. P. Lockin,gton, whose name was mentioned in the recent trial of Evelyn v. Huebert writes to the " Philadelphia Inquirer," saying that plaintiff is his sister-in-law, and the boy Walter is. his son. The plaintiff is a daughter of the late Rev, Charles E. Ellis, who was a highly respected and gifted clergyman of Manchester, England. Mr. Lockington states that his sister-in-law at her own request took charge of the education of his boy, but he knows nothing of her gambling or of her love affairs.

div.head: Ht7III.i3ERTISM AND THE "TIMES."
div.p: Ht7III.i3ERTISM AND THE "TIMES."

In an article on the way in which the "Times," at great length, puffed Mr. Hurlbert's book on Ireland, the "Pall Mall Gazette" says : Everybody who has read the proceedings in the case of "Evelyn v. Hurlbert" will agrae that if Mr. Hurlbert's story is true, then "Wilfred Murray" is about the most atrocious scamp who ever trod this earth. We wonder how the "Times" lilies the thought that this is the creature who (on Mr. Hurlbert's showing) is responsible for those "unimpeachable facts " which it insolently declared were worth thrice the contents of Mr. Morleycs brains! Of course we are aware that there is another alternative. Mr. Justice Cave thought that such forgeries as Mr. Hurlbert attributed to his " secretary" were "in- credible." It may be so. It may be that Mr. Hurlbert himself is Wilfred Murray. We are not concerned here to affirm or deny it. Either alternative is quite enough to cover " Hurlbertism and the Times" with the dis- gusted contempt it deserves. Either the "unimpeach- able" Unionist oracle is himself a liar and a scoundrel, or he employed a "ghost" who is. In either case the " Times " pledges itself to the words of the liar, which- ever it be, as gospel. We leave it to our contemporary to decide on which horn of the dilemma it prefers to be impaled.

div.head: CLITBEROE QASE,
div.p: THE CLITBEROE QASE,

Mrs, Jackson continuing her vindicatory hOrtative lii the "Lancashire Evening Post," says the letter she received from her husband asking for money to bring him home was a terrible shock to her. She quotes correspon- dence which passed between them containing a good deal of recrimination on both sides. In one passage Mrs. Jackson says she had found out that Mr. Jackson did not marry her for herself. She aceu.-.es Mr. Jacksoa of using very 'shocking language to her brother-in-law and sister on his return from New Zealand. As to his means, she says she ascertained that he had £lOO to take him to New Zealand, and £1 per week afterwards, but no capital to start farming with. _ _ _

Mrs. Jackson, continu7ng her statement on Wednesday says she felt sore all over for several days after her forcible seizure, owing to the rough treatment she received. She added that ,her husband and his sister applied humiliating epithets to hr while she was an inmate of their house, and that the former threatened to screw her neck if she rose from the sofa upon which he had pushed her. ___ _

div.head: MR. JACKSON'S REPLY.
div.p: MR. JACKSON'S REPLY.

A Blackburn correspondent says :—For some time past Mr. Jackson has anticipated the course his wife has taken, and accordingly has been collt.ting material for a reply. He is now busily preparin :t• a statement which he will make public as soon as the publication of his wife's "vindication" has been com- pleted. The latter, he says, contains statements which are not true. It is his intention to contradict these, and to put evidence before the public which he hopes will completely refute the charges that Mrs. Jackson is now making against .him. Among other things, he will publish his wife's lore letters.

div.head: PORTUGUESE ATTACK ON BRITISH STEAMERS.
div.p: PORTUGUESE ATTACK ON BRITISH STEAMERS.
CREWS IMPRISONED.

A Cape Town telegram of Monday's date reports the arrival of Sir John Willoughby at Delava Bay. Sir John Willoughby states that the two steamers in which the expedition under his command were proceeding up the Piung,we River to Mashonaland were fired upon by the Portuguese, who afterwards seized them. and imprisoned the crews. Sir John Willo.whby had offered to pay duty on the stores being carried, but receiving no reply within forty-eight hours, st-irted up the river.

div.head: -THE BRITISH DEMAND
div.p: -THE BRITISH DEMAND

Lord Salisbury has given instructions tg the British Minister in Lisbon to demand immediate explanations from Portugal regarding the alleged outrage on British steamers in South Africa. The Portuguese Minis- ter in Paris has forwarded to the newspapers a statement in which he says that the British steamers which at- tempted to ascend the Pungwe River without permission from the Customs authorities were seized for smu gang and infringement of th.- regulation;. Re (.Iles that anyone on board was badly treated. It is added that there is no intention to interfere with transit up the river. •
THE M.P.'S IN TROUBLE.
THE PARIS RUMOURS

Happily the report that two Ene.lish M.P.'s had been arrested in Paris on a disgraceful charge was contra- dicted on Tuesday eveeing. Unfortunat* names had been mentioned privately, but the contradiction has set many minds at rest.

div.head: MR. DE COBAIN
div.p: MR. DE COBAIN

It is stated that Mr. de Co-bain, M.P., has not given up his intention of returning at the earliest possible mom- ent to meet the charges against him, but at present his nervous temperament is so strained and his health so indifferent that it would not be wise to undergo the torture of a public trial. He stoutly asserts his inno- cence.

CAPTAIN VERNEY, M.P., Who returned to England to meet a charge that has been preferred against him by the London police, was arrested on Saturday and taken.before Sir John Bridge at Bow- street. Miss Baskett, the principal witness, identified the prisoner as the "Mr. Wilson" who had, as her evidence went to show, conspired with a Frenchwoman named Florent to commit the offence alleged. The hear- ing was adjourned, the prisoner being liberated on bail.

div.head: AIIIIANZA.I EXPEDITION.
div.p: THE AIIIIANZA.I EXPEDITION.
150 NATIVES KILLED.

SIMLA, TUESDAY.—lntelligence from Sir William Lock- hart's Column states that the enemy kept up a desultory fire upon the camp throughout the night of the 19th. Yesterday morning the troops moved out, and drove them back down the Khenki Valley, with the has of 150 On the British side one man of the King's Royal Rifle Corps was killed and four wounded. The troops subse- quently destroyed two native villages. SEVERE FIGHTING. THE ENEMY ROUTED: 300 KILLED. MinalatA, TlWRSDAY.—lntelligence brought by a spy confirms the report of the comple, e rout of the Orakzais on the 20th inst.,with 300 killed and woundei. The fact that the enemy 4,bandoned their dead is confirmatory of this news. The Orakzais opposed the British force un- aided. Two other tribes who were awaiting the result of events hastily retreated when the defeat of the Orak - zais was apparent. The enemy was corn; letely sur- prised by the King's royal corps and the Gho, rkas.

div.p: THE ADVA.Nek: ON MANIPUR-

Kohima column, about 1,000 men and three guns, was to have advanced 20th. Silchar column, 1,600 rifles and two guns, was at Barak 19th. Tammu column pushing up, Approximate strength, 320 British, 750 Native troop 3.

I• Gladstone BOTH the leaders of the two (Treat and political parties have, during the past week, addressed their sup porters in the country—Mr. GLADSTONE by means of letters to Liberal candidates at the by-elections, and Lord SALISBURY by means of a speech as Grand Master of the Primrose League. A com- parison of thestatements of the two ought to be sufficient to convince the undecided e lector, who wishes to see progress made and justice done, that he has nothing to gain by throwing in his lot with the Tories. Going no further back than the pre- sent year, the leader of the Liberal party earl point to " efforts to improve the law with regard to registration, and the principle of one man one vote,' the law of conspiracy affecting combinations among workmen, and to Self-government in rural parishes " ; while the Tories on the other hand have displayed their Toryism in resisting everything that was in the direction of putting full power in the hands of the people. It is true they are busy with an Irish Land Bill, "commencing with thirty, and terminating probably with one hundred, millions sterling." But the worst feature of the scheme LS that it constitutes the Exchequer the direct creditor of the Irish ocuipiera ; and thus sows the seed of mischief for the future itt dealing. with Ireland. There is this to be said for the measure from the Tory point of view, namely, that it will put money into the pockets of Irish landlords upon terms which are very much to their liking ; but we have Yet to learn that this peculiarity will be likely to prove gratifying to the taxpayers. If there was one thing made clearer than another, at the last General Election, it was that the Tory Part)! had no mandate whatever for dealing with thelrish land question. On the contrary, it was to a large extent because they denounced all schemes of land purchase that they secured a majority. They broken faith with the nation in this matt.er—eve" local as they have broken faith in failing to give done thou self- government to Ireland. They have haves

things which they ought not to have done, and they have left undone things which they ought to have done, and there is no health in them. That this is so is, happily, being recognised by the electors, and that ia why, as Mr. GLADSTONE puts -it, we have witnessed "that remarkable progress in public opinion, since 188 Z, which has given over to the Liberal party on the by-elections occurring from time to time a balance of no less than sixteen seats."

But it is in relation to the treatment of Roman Catholics that the most instructive contrast is afforded between the Liberal leader and the Tory leader. The "No Popery" cry has not been speci- fically raised as in the old bad time before the Period of Catholic Emancipation; but an anti- tatholic feeling is being stirred, and the Tories are trading upon it. It is only a few months since they threw out Mr. GLADSTONE'S bill for placing "all persons upon an equal footing with respect to the holding of the Viceroyalty of Irelan.d, and to the discharge of the civil duties of the Lord CHAN- CELLOR of Great Britain." The Catholics are shut out, and so far as the present Ministry is concerned they are to remain shut out; they are denied a qualification to hold either of these offices which is not refused to Jews, Mahomedans, Buddhists, or Atheists. The flame of religious animosity has been kindled; and, on Tuesday, Lord SALISBURY WaS craftily employed in fanning the flame. Refer- 11g to the action which the Catholic clergy of Ire- land have taken in opposing Mr. PARNELL he said :

Now, I think it is a matter of no small congratula- tion that this has been brought home, or is being brought home, to the electorate of t nglakid. What they are asked to do is to place Ireland under this hybrid secular-ecclesiastical power; and in placing Ireland tley will place those of our brethren in the North of Ireland, who undoubtedlx will receive no mercy and no consideration from this novel and monstrous power. _ . - - -

Coupled with this declaration, the Tory chief would have us believe that if the same thing hap- pened to the Church to which he belongs he should be equally keen to denounce it. But he does not surely expect that anybody will accept that as anything more than "a Salis- bury." It is coming it a little too strong, when it is yet remembeied that, during the Irish Church agitation, the "hybrid Secular-ecclesiastical power" :of the Church of England was exercised to tie fullest extent to thwart Mr. GLA.DSTONeS measure of disestablishment in Ireland. Was Lord SAMS- ICORY keen to denounce the clergymen who lectured and preached themselves hoarse on the subject,and became for the time so many election agents for the-Tory party? Not a bit of it: he patted them O n the back, and encouraged them in their work; and his absurdly virtuous posturing at the present inornent is the result either of sheer forgetfulness or rank hypocrisy. But if it be granted that the Irish peasants are too much under the influence of the Irish priest, what then? Does it follow that they are not entitled to the franchise, to local government, or to Home Rule? it is ridiculous to say so; it might just as well be argued that the Xoglish " softies " who are under the influence of the knights and Dames of the Primrose League ought to be disfranchised as obviously incapable of rationally exercising the rights of citizenship. Ent any stick is good enough to beat a flog with; the dog to be beaten just now is Roman Catho- lic; and Lord SALISBURY thinks he is serving Church and State—and particularly Ulster—by laying on in his own peculiar fashion. Perhaps he Will discover\ that he has made a mistake ; he may find that there are English Tory Catholics who object to see the Irish peasantry and clergy re- ferred to in the spirit of the famous Hottentot Simile; and, further, that he will lose more than he will gain by waving the red rag of religious dis- cord. But be. that as it may, the broad fact re- mains that, while Mr. GLADSTONE seeks to break the last link in the chain of civil disability for reli- gious opinions, Lord SALISBURY is anxious to rivet the chain more firmly upon men who are struggl- ing to be free.
Mr. Brunner THE annual meeting of the North- at wich Division Liberal Association

N'orthwich. was held on Saturday afternoon, and, after the usual business had been transacted, -the member for the division delivered an address O n current topics. Mr. BRUNNER iS a politician of decided views, with a high ideal of progress, and a determination to persist in what he believes to be the right course. .He is devoted to the advance- merit of education amongst the masses, and re- gards it as desirable that there should be equality ~°f opportunity in the struggle for existence. It 48 not, in his opinion, for the rich to say anything about "assisted education," seeing that they Were not ashamed "to take the money that was left by benevolent donors in past days, not for lieh people, but for poor scholars." There is one /natter as to which Mr. BRuNNER uttered a note of warning which inay be misunderstood, and that as to the tendency for the professional and Working classes to apply to Parliament for protec- tion. In so far as this may tend to create close corporations, and thus prevent those who are down stepping upward and onward, it is to be re-f sisted ; but, on the other hand, it is—speaking generally—the duty of the State to protect the 1/....eak against the strong ; and the results of our Xining and Factory Acts show that the principle has been applied with incalculable" benefit to the 'workers as a whole. How much further this pro- cess of protection can be carried, without doing more harm than good, remains to be seen; but 'there is certainly a growing opinion that quite as much can be done in: this direction as has lbeen done. With regard to the licensing question Mr. BRUNNER said he was not a total abstainer, ibut he thought as to houses which were a nuisance to them that they should be "either mended or ended ;"and that was the principle upon which he tad acted in raising the question at Knutsford. is resolution was carried by the votes of fifty- tight magistrates to two; and he is right under the circumstances in concluding that" the proba- 13irit, y was that they would have a change for the 13etter before long." In responding to a cordial '°teof thanks, Mr. BRUNNER said "he beeped he 'would never slacken his efforts until every] family the country had available the comforts and re- finements of life which were now to be had for :',2°° a year." This is a noble saying and worthy aeceptation ; and, assuming that the mem- uer for the North.wich Division does his best to affai . n this end—and we believe he will—it would "e deserving of a place on his monurneutal marble ter what we trust will be a long and usefal career.

THE breach of promise action by yv‘.‘ "people an actress against Mr. HUELBURT, lii the Anglo-American, which occu- ti?(l a judge and special jury for seven days, ter- -lated, on Monday, by the jury saying—" We 4nd there Was no promise of Inarriage." It is much te,artnnented on that the jury said nothing about _ he authorship of the extraordinary letters which Were Put iu evidence, although-Mr. Justice CAVE

specially directed their attention to them as a main feature of the case. The contention of the defence was that, although the handwriting was admittedly very like the defendant's, the letters were, as a matter of fact, written by a Mr. Wilfred Murray, who had been in the employ of the defen- dant, but was not now to be found. The plaintiff's statement was that the defendant himself was Wilfred Murray—that being the name under which he had carried on his intercourse with her. As the letters did not show that a promise had been , made, they were of moment chiefly as exposing the writer who is shown to be "foul as Vulcan's stithy." The Judge commented on the fact that nobody who knew MURRAY had been called; and he added :—" A very valuable witness for the defendant would have been a person who could have sworn that he had seen the defendant and Murray together, that they were two different persons, and that their handwriting was not dis- tinguishable." It does seem odd that MURRAY should have completely vanished; and that there was not even a single person to go into the box as witness and say that he knew of the ' existence of such a man. BROWNING once wrote a poem in which he asked "What's become of Wareing ? " For many years there was no answer ; but WARE- ING did at last appear in the flesh. Will MURRAY ever be seen? It is of great importance to Mr., HURLBURT that Mmutly should be found; for "people will talk." If he should find this extra- ordinary being, it will not of courslibe to employ him again, but to give him into custody for con- spiring to blackmail and defame his former master. Mr. HURLBURT has succ3eded in showing that he did not promise the actress marriage; but the abominable letters—what of them ? He must find the writer, or "people will talk."

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

"Flour Raised Again" says a contemporary; but there is no need of large type, or of a ghost come from the grave, to tell us that. If there was no raising flour again, we should soon be badly off for bread, and, like Nebuchadnezzar, might have to "go to grass."

Mr. Storey,M.P.,has been committed for trial on a charge of perjury in connection with the Silksworth strike ; but when he came out of Sunderland Police Court the inhabitants showed .their view of the case by cheering him. It is to be hoped he will clear himself. A Storey may represent Sunderland, but surely not a story-teller.

With the late chairman for a cnmpetiler, Mr. H. G. Linaker failed to secure the clerkship of the Runcorn Board of Guardians; but, if he has missed the post,he has secured a splendid testimonial from the Board. It is to be hoped that it will be the means of helping him ere long to something as good as the berth he sought, if not better.

The severe winter and late spring have com- bined to increase the bills of mortality, besides lay- ing many people up with prolonged illness: The sun shines, but, as the east wind continues to blow, the weather is deceptive. This year it must be said with emphasis—

div.head: Cast not a clout Till May goes out.
div.p: Cast not a clout Till May goes out.

Mr. Edward Davies and his mother, extensive colliery proprietors in Montgomeryshire, have announced their intention of giving £2,000 for intermedit‘te school scholarships in Montgomery- shire, £2,000 for the Rhondda Valley district, and £l,OOO to form a library, &c., at Barry Dock. Is there nobody in this district to give us a pleasant surprise in a similar way P There is plenty of room for a lift, and plenty of money somewhere.

"Many Happy Returns" to Lord Winmarleigh, who will complete his eighty-ninth year to-morrow (Sunday). Long may his age be "as a lusty winter, frosty but kindly." Sir Uilbert Greenall is a few years younger than his lordship ; but from all we hear it is not likely that he will ever again be in a position to resume his Parliamentary duties. It is a case in which "haggish age steals on and wears him out of act." His best friends would best serve him by inducing him to relieve him- self of responsibility by resigning his seat.

The Warrington Amateur Photographic Society 'continues to make progress. Its annual exhibition is one of the pleasantest gatherings of the season, for there is always something good for the ear as well as the eye. This year the members have made a charge—they could not be expected to give free entertainments for ever—and the result has been very satisfactory. As Mr. Down, the president, suggested, the audience were willing to admit that they had their money's worth. The pictures in little came out splendidly on the screen.

The prediction of the able Correspondent who famished us with "Notes from Manxland" has been verified. The first of the contests in the general election to the Manx House of Keys came off on Thursday, :when the representative of Peel was decided upon. The former member, Mr. A. N. Laughton, was opposed and defeated by Hr. Joseph Mylehreest,who polled 202 votes,which gave him a majority of 63. Mylehreest, who amassed a fortune in South Africa, is known as "The Diamond King;" he is thoroughly generous, and thoroughly demo- cratic.

Critics, with a freedom of speech which has proved of inverse ratio to their knowledge, have now and again had something to say m disparage- ment of the Town Clock presented to Warrington by Mr. John Crosfield. A writer who is" in ii, posi- tion to know" affirms that "the clock goes to a, second or two a month, and that on the rare occa- sions when it has been at fault the cause has always been purely accidental, as when recently it was more than once stopped by workmen engaged in replacing the wind-vane." Just so; it is not the clock—it is the critics who are" at fault."

Mr. Goscnen has taken advice; he has devoted his budget surplus to one main thing and re- deemed his word. As there seems to he some doubt as to how far the Government were pledged to" Assisted Education," it is as well to repro- duce Mr. Goschen's words when introducing last year's Budget. He said :—" We look forward to dealing with the question of assisted education next year. We consider ourselves committed to the questior, and I am afraid that the liability of finding the necessary funds will fall upon me. I trust I shall be able to meet that liability, which, in fact, I must meet."

The Government having resolved to free educa- tion, the question is—How will they do it? From what has been,hinted at, there is reason to fear that it will be done by re-etidowing the sects. But this will be resisted as reactionary. The subject was debated at the Conference of the Unitarian and Free Christian Churches in London on Thurs- day, and it was resolved that "no syst:em of free or assisted education will be satisfactory that does not provide for the establishment of Board schools under public management of a thoroughly unsec- tarian character in every district of the country." This is the proper course to take. Supply and con- trol must go hand-in-hand:

The member for Newton Division in the course of .an address at the Town Hall, on Saturday, alluded to what he called "the defunct temper- ance Ooposals of the Government. They all knew the history of that measure, and they would pro- bably agree with him that it was wreoked by the fanatical opposition of certgain people whose efforts had in all probability succeeded in putting off temperance reform indefinitely." Fancy calling the endowment of public-houses a temperance reform! Temperance men—by which publicans are not meant—will do well to remember that at the next election.
lAI one point Mr. Legh spoke of Home Rule as something that had almost disappeared. Perhaps 'the wish was father to the thought. However,it

appeared later on, for, referring to the next elec- tion, he said" the danger was that they might be so led astray by extravagant promises on the part of the Liberals that they might be induced to vote for Home Rule, and upon that question they would have to make up their minds." Mr. Legh, Tory-like, is not" up to date ;" when he gets a little t more off," he will know that the minds of the electors are made up. What is wanted by the elec- tors is the opportunity of making up their votes. •

It is Byron, is it not ? who sings— . Italia ! Oh Italia! thou who bast The fatal gift of beauty.' But the beauty has another fatal gift or rather habit—and that is the very ugly one of assassina- tion. It is alleged that there are more murders committed in Italyin a year than in Great Britain, France, Germany, and Spain combined. It is not to be wondered at that American citizens have revolted against an introduction of this cut-throat system into New Orleans. If something is to be abolished "Let us," as the witty Frenchman said, "begin with the assassins."

Lord Churchill is going on a little jaunt to South Africa, and was entertained at the Amphi- tryon Club on Saturday evening. As Mr. Balfour was also present, Mr. Asquith made merry by pro- posing that they should in solemn silence, drink "to the undying memory of the-Fourth Party." The Irish Secretary was,however,equal to the occa- sion for he said:—" I do not rise to respond to this toast, for I recollect that when the distin- guished party to which allusion has been made was in existence we all quarrelled as to who was the leader. (Laughter.) If I were now to respond to the toast it would imply that I was the leader, and until that question has been settled by those alone competent to settle it, it would be improper —even indecent—if I were to undertake to speak for it. (Laughter.)" All this was really very well done—" jollycompanions everyone."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 25, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 25, 1891.
RIOTIOTIS CONDUCT AT A RAILWAY STATION.

On Monday at St. Helens Police Court, Thomas M'Gurl (3, Milton-st., Widnes), William Crowe-(24. Cromwell- St., Widnes), John Kelly (11, Tithebarn-st.,(Widnes),and Henry Cosgrove (13, Granfell-st., (Widnes), were sum- moned by the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany for wilfully damaging a weighing machine, at Sutton Oak Railway Station, and Crowe was further charged with assaulting William Spencer, a porter. On Saturday night, the 7th March, the defendants were at Sutton Oak Station, and commenced to pull about the scales, tore down the time bills, and tore them to pieces. They used very abusive language, and on a signal man named Ridgway remonstrating with them they seized him and pitched him across the room* and threatened to "do " for him. Ridgway returned to his box, and the men left the station. Some time later they returned,and porter Spencer saw them creating another disturbance. He spoke to them, and Crowe struck him a severe blow on the chest,causing him to fall backwards against the form. • Each of the defendants was fined 10s. and costs, and ordered to pay is. 6d. each ag damage. Crowe was also fined 10s. and costs for the assault on Spencer. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD ACCOUNTS.

The adjourned ratepayers' meeting to receive the audi- tor's report on the Burial Board's accounts was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall on Thursday night. The Rev. Canon Maitland Wood presided, and Mr. W. Jones (assistant secretary to the Burial Board) presented the balance sheet which showed receipts' as follows :—Balance in bank general account £lO3 ss. 7d.; balance sinking fund account £1 95.; interment fees £449 6s. 4d.; grave burial certificates £25: sale of grass £5 12s. 3111; rent of field £l5 7s. id. Cash from overseers: General fund fir,t ; sinking fund £120; sale of consols £234; dividend on consols £l2 Bs. 4d.; bank interest £2 is. id.; total £1,027 2s. sd. On the expenditure side were the follow- ing items: Interest on mortgages £199 19s. ; salaly and wages £l9l 7s. ; maintenance and repairs £3 Os. 10d. ; rates, taxes, and. tithes £lO Bs. lid.; printing and stationery £26 16s. 6d.; sundries £lB 175.; murtgag,es paid off £3OQ; bank commission 13s. 10d. ; balance in bank general' account £209 16s. 9d. ; sinking fund account £66 12s. 7d.; total £1,027 24. sd. The mortgage debt on the cemetery is £s,oso.—The balance sheet was adopted on the motion of Mr. Digges, seconded by 'Mr. W. Sutton (assistant overseer). 'Emit BY JURY AT RUNCORN.

The University Extension lectures of the past winter, although of an interesting character, and on the whole well attended, have resulted in a financial loss and the Committee require about S3O to enable them to strike a balance. With the object of raising this sum, a grand concert was held in Runcorn Public Hall on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings, and on each occasion there was a large and appreciative audience. The principals en- gaged were Miss Florence Dick; Mr. Thomas Barlow, and Mr. John Allen. The first part of the programme con- sisted of selections by an efficient orchestral band under the leadership of Mr. Duncanson, songs by Miss Dick and Mr. Barlow, and humourous sketches by Mr. Allen • and Mr. Fouldes gave a bassoon solo. The chief interest, how- ever, centred each evening in the complete representation ef Sullivan and Gilbert's popular musical satire, "Trial by. Jury," in which the dramatis person was as follows: —Plaintiff (the Fair Angelina), Miss. Florence Dick; Defendant (the Faithless Edwin), Mr. Thomas Barlow; Judge ("and a good Judge too"), Mr. John Allen; Counsel for Plaintiff, Mr. W. J. Thomas ; Usher, Mr. J. H, Harrison; Foreman of the Jury, Mr. J. Booth; Asso- ciate, Mr. R. D. Maddock; Bridesmaids, Mademoiselles Ainsworth, C. Hatipson, Handley, Mellor, Moss, Sithis- ter, Stubbs and E. D. Wright; Jurymen, Messrs. Booth, T. Fox, Fryer, W. Jones, Lancaster, Morris' Nickson, Nield, Pownall, Savage, Scott and Worrell; barristers, solicitors, spectators, &c. The three principal characters were admirably pourtrayed, and the singing and acting, was throughout maintained at a high level. The amateurs were also highly subeessful in their several positions and the chorus, conducted by Mr. E. NV. Humphreys, did their work in a highly creditable manner. Altogether the per- formance was a highly diverting and enjoyable one. *MANCHESTER ASSIZES.

At these assizes, the business of which will com- mence on Monday next, the 27th'inst., there are only nineteen prisoners for trial. Of these one is charged with murder, three with forgery,three with bigamy, one with attempt to murder, three with burglary, one with a Mint offence, one with larceny, and six with criminal assaults. THE SUBSIDENCE QUESTION. _ •

It was decided by the Committee on Brine Pump- ing Compensation that gas and water companies, county councils, municipal corporations, sanitary authorities, and local authorities, should be ex- cluded from compensation under the bill. On Thurs- day it was proposed on behalf of the Northwich Local Board that brine, as brine, should not be con- veyed, with one exception,to a greater distance than three miles from the pumping station. Nll.Brunner, M.P., intimated that he would move an instruction to that effect in the House. A clause was introduced into the bill authorising the diversion of the fund Of £20,000 provided by Mr. Joseph Verdin for compen- sation for subsidence to technical education and other purposes. The Committee adjourned until Thursday. SWINE FEVER PROSECUTiON : HEAVY PENALTY. At Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, William Littler; St. Helens, was summoned for removing two pigs into a swine fever infected area without a license. Mr. Riley appeared for defendant, and explained that his client was in the employ of a wholesaleilopig dealer at St. Helens, and the employer had in his possession a license for the removal of the pigs. He submitted that it was not absolutely necessary that a scrvant when removing pigs on behalf of an employer should have the license with him. The magistrates said that if a man moving pigs was not bound to have a license in his posses- sion people could move pigs all over the country, and as many as they cared to. They held that there was nothing to show that the two pigs in *question belonged to the person to whom the license had been granted. They considered the case proved, and imposed a fine of £5 and costs. SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. Burros s Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. COLLIERS' DISPUTE AT ST. HELENS.

On Wednesday night, Mr.T. Glover, miners' agent, St. Helens, posted to Messrs. Bromilow, Foster, and Co., of the Ashton's Green Colliery, notices on behalf of the 200 men employed by the firm in the Rushy Park and Little Delph Mines, to terminate their en- gagements in seven days. It appears that fora con- siderable time past the firm, following the usual custom, have deducted from the weight of coal got by each collier a certain amount for the dirt brought up with the coal. Recently the colliery proprietors intimated that this amount. would be doubled and the men raised strong objections. Mr. Glover, the miners' agent has been in communication with the firm, and on Wednesday afternoon, at a meeting of the colliers held near Ashton's Green, he reported that the firm insisted on their proposal being carried into effect. It was unanimously resolved to Come out on strike, and notices were directed to be for- warded as stated. LICENSING IN CHESHIRE.

In Cheshire, as in other parts of the country questions relating to the licensing laws are at pre- sent receiving a good deal of attention. On Satur- day, at a meeting of the Standing Joint Committee for the county, a resolution was passed which was regarded as amounting to a vote of censure on Mr. Speakman,the clerk flr the magistrates of the Nant- wich division, for his failure to see that the magis- trates were represented at the hearing at quarter sessions of an appeal against their decision refusing to renew the license of the Coach and Horses Inn at Bnerton, on the ground that, according to the evi- dence of the police, the house was badly conducted. •From correspondence which was submitted it appeared that Mr. Speakman was repeatedly reminded that the appeal was coming on, but that owing to an error of judgment he took no stops to secure that the magistrates, who were the respond- ents, should be represented by counsel, with the result that the appeal was sustained. •
SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at a. &. W. Durrozes Sankey-st., Watrington.—Advt. MR. Tom STONE'S WEDDING PRESENT.

The " loving cup" which we stated a fortnight ago had been subscribed for as a wedding present for Mr_ Tom Stone, of Canada, a former resident of Newton, has now been received, and as a work of the silversmith's art excels anything which has _

hitherto been on exhibition in garlesiOwn or New- ton." Weighing 130 ounces of solid silver, the cup, when placed on the black ebony stand which ac- companies it, stands about two feet high, and at once attracts the eye by its beautiful appearance. The groundwork of the design represents agricul- tural productions, Canadian fruits, flowers, and eereals being• illustrated. On the cup are four shields, upon which are representations of a cours- ing soene, with hounds in full cry, and the judge on horseback in close attendance, another illustrates a
shooting expedition, whilst the third depicts Mr. Stone's farottrite pastime of putting the shot. The Temainingshield bears the following inscription :
For auld Lang Syne This Loving Cup

Tom Stone from his Newton-le-Willows friends 11th November, 1890. His wedding day. Upon each of the two handles is a greyhound in an upright sitting posture. Surmounting the 141 is the figure of a man in athletic costume, prepar- ing to put the shot, the features of the figure on the close inspection hearing a remarkable likeness to Mr. _ _
Stone, w-hom it is intended to represent.
CHESHIRE CLERGY AND CREMATION.

In view of the establishment of a crematorium at Manchester, the Cheshire clergy in several rural deaneries have discussed the question of cremation, and decided to recommend that where bodies are cremated the ashes shall be carefully preserved for interment in the churchyard or cemetery, and that a service be held at the burial of the ashes and not before. LAWN MOWERS.—Garland, 51. Bridge-st., Warrington, and at Barlestown.—Advt.

div.head: "PURE BUTTER."
div.p: "PURE BUTTER."

At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Samuel Milner, grocer, Buyton Quarry, was summoned for selling adulterated butter, on the 12th ult. Super- intendent Barker said that the article was, bought as pure butter at is. 2d. per pound,. and that the analysis by Dr. Campbell Brown, of Liverpool, showed that it contained 9 per cent. of water and upwards of 80 per cent of fats. Defendant, who pleaded that he bought the article as pure butter, was fined 20s. and costs. cs SPRING FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. THE WARRINGTON FOUNDLING AGAIN.

On Tuesday, John Warrington, aged sixteen, the well-known lirarrington foundling, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment at the Quarter Ses- sions held at Liverpool, for stealing a spade, on The 24th ult., the property of Sarah Potter, farmer, Poqlton, near Warrington. Another Warrington labourer, John Smith, aged thirty,receoived a similar term for stealing, on the sth inst., Ss. the property of Robert Burgess. SPRING FAsruoNs now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankov-st.. Warrington.—Advt.

Rigby rela- tive to the projected Central College of Agriculture for the county. Sr. HELENS AND WIGAN JUNCTION RAILWAY.

There cane, flee other day, before the Commons Committee on Unopposed Bills, presided over by Mr. Courtney, a Bill to extend the time for the compulsory purchase of lands for, certain rail- ways authorised by the St. Helens and Wigan Junction Railway Act of 1885, and the St Helens Junction Railway Act of 1886, and to provide for the issue of preference and guaran- teed shares of stock, and for other purposes. , At St. lie-l;;-13—Town -Hall, on Monday, before Mr. A. Walmsley, Cotham, and Alderman Macechnie, Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., the well-known colliery proprietors, were summoned for having an unjust weighing machine at their liavanno.h Colliery, Parr, on the 11th instant. Evidence was given to show that the machine was 41bs. wrong, and that it was 11Ibs. wrong when tried at 12 cwt. The machine was used for determining the wages of the colliers aecording to the weight of the coals sent up the shaft. It was stated that the machine had been examined on previous occasions and it was fognd correct.—The magistrates imposed fine of £2 and costs. SPRING FASHIONS now Showing .at J. W. DurroN's Sank ey-st., Warrinzton.— Ada. THE NORTH WALES EXCURSION SEASON.

The regular daily service of the passengefsteam- era of the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company to Llandudno and the Menai Straits will commence on the 2nd prox. The accommodation provided for passengers even exceeds the high attainments of last year. Besides the Bonnie Princess the Company have a new steatoer, the St. Tudno, built by the Fairfield Shipbuilding and Engineering Co., a really magnificent specimen of a finely-moddejled paddle steamer, designed express- ly for the new service between Liverpool, Landud- no, Beaumaris, and the Menai Bridge. The arrange- ments are on a scale which will make the new ves- sel one of the most superb and luxurious passenger vessels afloat. Seekers after health and pleasure during the coming summer can thus look forward to making this delightfnl trip by steamers the builders of which have taken advantage of every improvement that could possibly be suggested or that ingenuity could devise, as well as the certainty of performing the journey in an expeditious time. Under these circumstances a very successful sea- son may be anticipated for the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company and its new vessel. SPRING FASHIONS now showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S. Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt.
