PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday afternoon, when there were present Major J. W. Wareing (who was elected to preside pro tern), Mr. F. Stapleton- Bretherton, J.P., Messrs. W. Tyrer, J. Goldsworth, John- son, Buckley Griffiths, Mercer, Ellison, Joseph Birchall, James firchall, E. fireball, Kenwright, Hulme, Whalley, Davies, Ranson, Graves, Marsh. Middlehurst, Leather- barrow, Fisher, Borrows, Daine, Syder, and S. H. Hartley (clerk.)_

THE CUAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMEN.-Mr. Kenwright proposed the appointment of Mr. W. Tyrer as chairman for the ensuing year, remarking that his abilities were well known by the ioard, and he was quite qualified for the post.—Mr. Ranson seconded the motion which was adopted unanimously. Mr. Tyrer acknowledged the compliment, and said he was much obliged for the con- fidence they had shown in him. He trusted that neither himself nor the Guardians would have reason to regret the appointment.—On the motion of Mr. Joseph Birchall seconded by Mr. Ellison, Mr. James Birchen was ap- pointed senior vice7chairman, and Mr. P. Longton was elected junior vice-chairman on th the proposition of Mr. James Birchall, seconded by Mr. Goldsworth. MiscELLANsous.—On the motion of Mr. Wareing seconded by Mr. Mercer. The standing orders of the board were adopted and the various committees were selected.

THE WIDNES AND DITTON RELIEVING OFFICERS.—The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board assenting to the appointment of Messrs. Herbert Flamp- son and Alfred Wood relieving officers for the Widnes and Ditton districts it salaries of £lOO per annum each.

TEE VACANCY AT BOLD.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board intimating that they would proceed to issue an order for the election of a Guardian for Bold in the room of Mr. G. Chadwick resigned. VISIT BY A LUNACY COSjSSIQNEE.—TIIC Local Government Board forwarded a report of a visit made to the Workhouse on the 26th ult. by Dr. Allbutt, one of the visiting Commissioners of lunacy. The report was as tollows :—" To-day I visited the Workhouse at Pres- cot and saw all the inmates save one man, who was out for, the day- All these inmates seemed fit per- sons for detention in a Workhouse and for classi- fication as insane save one woman, named Kelly, who seqpied to me to have recovered. I suggest to the medical officer that the Mite may have arrived for her to be removed from the list. I gave special attention to the two idiot boys, nintioned by one of our board on his visit two years ago and also to a third who recently was admitted. The master in his

kindly desire to benefit these children was desirous of sending these boys to the Royal Albert Asylum if possible. Unhappily in my opinion all these boys seemed incapable of much improvement, and would therefore not make any return for the expense and the trouble of their edu- cation. At the same time I think more might be done to make them more cleanly in their habits. The state of the inmates in respect of food and dress and appearance were satisfactory and their treatment seemed kindly and sufficient. The male patients were just going out fora walk in the country with the attendant on my arrival. A fair number are occupied about the house and wards. THE EMIGRATION OF CHILDREN TO CANADA.—Mr.James Burchall remarked that some time ago a number of children from that union were sent to Canada. and he would like to know if any information in regard to them had been received.—The Clerk said that all the informa- tion he had received he had laid before the Guardians. They had received sonic reports, but they were not of a satisfactory character. If his recollection served him right, they could not find more than one half of the chil- dren sent out, and when they had another application a few months mo they declined to send out any children. They preferred to keep thtm.—The Chairman considered it hopeless to expect more information in re- gard to the children. Mr. Burchall said the reason he raised the question was because someone was making inquiries about getting a couple of the children back from Canada.—Mr. Leathertarrow remarked that he had -received letters front Canada showing that three of the children were doing well.—The Chairman said it seemed a pity they could not trace the children they had sent out.—Mr. Burchall : Must we take it that no news is good news P—The Chairman: I don't know. Let us hope so. The subject then dropped. RELIEF.—The Clerk said the tctal amount of out-relief for the week ending 15th April was £220 2s. 6d against £219 14s. 3d. in the correspond* week last year. —The Workhouse Master reported there were 527 inmates this week, 553 last week, and 544 in the corres- ponding week last year

THE ST. HELENS RELIEF OFFICE.-Mr Mercer, in accordance with notice given moved That the resolu- tion of the Guardians of the 26th March appointing James Litter as messenger, &c., at the St. Helens relief offices be rescinded."—He contended that the appoint- ment was altogether unnecessary and unfairto the other relief districts.—After some discussion,it was decided that the discussion on the matter be postponed until the Local Government Board had sanctioned, or otherwise the appointment. This was the principal business.

FIRST AID TO THE INJURED AT RUNCORN.

Benjamin Ockin, a sailor °on board the schooner Elizabeth, was knocked into the hold of the vessel by the crane bucket, on Monday morning and fractured his thigh. He was conveyed to tho railway station, suffering , a most acute pain and there P.C. Edwards afterwards found him and obtaining a splint bandaged the limb, and eased the pain. Dr. Robinson, who was called in said he could not fix the bandage on any better himself, and the injured man was taken by train to the Liverpool Infirmary. Accidents frequently occur at the docks and it would be of great advantage if a few of the workers there went through a course of lessons under the St. John's Ambulance Association. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT RUNCORN. Before Mr. G. L. Davies and Dr. Steele at Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, John Moore, copper furnace- man, Widnes, was charged with being drunk add dis- orderly and with assaulting P.C. Hughes. The cqnstable took the prisoner into custody on the previous night for being drunk and disorderly, when the prisoner became very violent, kicked the ()Meer savagely on the legs, and during the struggle that ensued esc4ped. The prisoner, however, went to the police station alone, and he there also acted very violently and assaulted Inspector Byer.. The Inspector said he waS the most violent man he had seen in Runcorn.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed for the drunkenness, and he was sentenced to 21 days hard labour for the assault.

RUNCORN WESLEYAN CIRCUIT SUNDAY SCHOOLS UNION. The annual meeting of this Union was held on Mon- day night, in Brunswick vestry, Rev. H. Burson pre- sident, Rev. J. Judson Halton, Messrs. E. Taylor, A. R. Norman, W. Rowe, and R. J. Posnett (the two last mentioned being visitors),were also present with teachers from Mill Brow, Nelson-st., and Halton schools. The secretary gave a ,statistical report showing the average afternoon attendance of 136 teachers and 1,434 scholars for the circuit. The amount contributed and collected or Foreign Missions was £125. A most interesting and valued report was presented by the visitors describing the visit to each school during the past year, and a' considerable discussion foilowed. Mr. W. J. Posnett and Mr. A. R. Norman were re-appointed visitors. ASSAULT'WITH A SLEDGE HAMMER AT WIDNES. _ _ _

At Widnes Police Court on Monday, -171;ofi. Brown-st., was brought up on remand with unlawfully wounding William Lovatt, on Thursday afternoon. The men were employed at the Widnes Alkali works, and on the day inguestion the prisoner accused Lovett of break- ing open a door. Lovatt denied the accusation and with- ont further ado, the prisoner struck him on the nose with a heavy sledge hammer, and also on theJeft side of the body. Lovatt was stunned, and was afterwards taken to Dr. Allen who attended to his injuries. The Doctor informed the Bench that the right nasal bone was frac- tured and the cartilage of the nose was dislocated; and Lovatt would always have a deformity of the nose. The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. The prisoner was brought up at the County Ses- sions on Tuesday and sentenced to 14 days hard labour. SHOCKING RAILWAY' ACCIDENT NEAR WIDNES

On Friday at midnight, Mr. Nutter, the stationmaster at Farnworth Central Station received a telegram from Stockport, stating that the'driver of the 7.50 goods train from Huskisson Station to Leeds, had found blood on the life guard and brake of his engine. The message re- quested Mr. Nutter to examine the line on his section. A, search was made at once, and the body of a man, dread- fully mutilated was found in the tunnel at Farnworth. The head was lying ten yards away. From appearances the body appeared to be that of a foreigner, about 30 years of age and about sft., dark brown hair, dressed in black worsted jacket and vest and brown coloured trousers. He also wore blucher boots. In his pockets were found five American coins and a joiner's pencil. The body was removed to the Griffin Inn. where Mr. Brighouse held an inquest on Monday. The station- master stated that from the time the goods train passed to the time the body was found eleven trains had passed "through the tunnel.—P.C. Almond said the body had not been identified.—An open verdict was returned. The deceased has been identified by means of his clothing as James Greenall Melvine, a pawnbroker's assistant, who had lived at 285, Scotland-road, Liverpool.

div.head: RUNCORN WATERMAN AND HIS
div.p: A RUNCORN WATERMAN AND HIS
WIFE.

On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, before Mr. James Handley and Mr. G. L. Wigg, George Dugdale, mate on a river hopper,who lived in York- St., .waA summoned for assaulting his wife, Mar'i Dugdale. Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, appeared for the complainant, and stated that the parties were married on the 18th February, 1886, at Run- corn Parish Church, she being a widow and lie a widower. There were four children. They had been separated three or four times during the short time they had been married. On Saturday, the 11th inst.,the defendant went to the football match,butsseveral public- , houses were an obstacle to his returning home to tea,and he turned up at half-past nine very drunk. He used most abusive language to her; accused her of having kept him in ignorance of the visit of two cou- sins on the previous day : and then stiuck her two blows in the face, and knocked her over a cradle. When she got up he knocked her about the face with his open hand,and struck her several blows with his fist. She sent one of the boys for a policeman,but the officer did not come. On Sunday he was very violent,and she dared not stay in the house with him,and slept with a neighbour. On Monday morning she went to get his breikfast,when he seized her by the throat and struck her several severe blows.—Mr. Brown wished the Bench to treat the camas an aggravated assault, and grant the woman a judicial separation. He earned 355. per week.—The defendant stated that. he had never struck her in his life.—Complainant said not before this time,but he had ill-used her in other ways.—Defend- ant : am willing to make a happy home, if she would leave her mother.—Complainant: I daro not live with youe—Corroborative evidence of the assault was given.— The defendant said his wife " blackguarded " him fur everything when he came home from the football Match, and refused to make his tea. He never struck her.—The Bench fined him 12s. and costs, 2854 for the assault, and made an order of judicial separation. He would have to contribute 15s. per week towards the maintenance of his wife and four children.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The annual meeting was held at Dutton Work- house on Tuesday. Plesent : The Rev. J. W. N. Tsnner, Messrs. C. Reynolds, J.P.,-Heywood, Aaron, Lewis, Kirkham, Stokes, P. Hall, J. Whitlow, Brandreth, J. Parr, J. -Knowles, W. Whitlow, Bax- ter, Ellison, Edwards, Hewitt, J. Hall, Pickering, Mslntyre, J. Weir, J. Bate, Wikinson, J. Ashton (clerk), H. G. Linaker. •

THE APrOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN. Mr. H. G. Linaker took the chair pro tem, and said the first business was the appointment of a chairman for the ensuing year.—Mr. Rrandreth moved the appointment of Mr. Mclntyre, tin ce-chairman.—Rev. John Tanner secondee ••• marking that no more suitable ma.n could be found. he was a regular attender, and had officiated as chairman, of the Board and the various committees with credit.—Mr. Whitlow said they would have soine great difficulties to deal with this year, and they ought to be very particular as to whom they appointed. He had no objection to Mr. Mclntyre but he thought that they should make a separate appointment for the Rural San- itary authority and the,Board of Guardians. He objected to the system of placing one gentleman in the chair year after year; the chairman should be changed every year and the seat thrown open to the whole Board.—Mr. Knowles proposed the appointment of Mr. Brandreth as chairman.—Mr. Whitlow seconded.—Mr. Brandreth said he would rather retire in favour of Mr. Mclntyre,but Mr. Knowles pressed his motion.—Mr. Mclntyre was elected by alarge majority.—The Chairman thanked the mem- btrs for the confidence reposed in him. He should con- duct the duties of the chair as became a gentleman— (hear, hear)—and he was confident the members would also act on gentlemanly lines—(hear, hear)—and such being the case he thought they would be able to get through the business. (Hear, hear.) IMPORTANT TO APPLETON.

Messrs. J. anci-F.Y:ionstal.l and Co., accountants of Warrington, wrote that Mr. William Bostock, a client of theirs owning house pr i operty n the township of Apple- ton-with-Hull, had the greatest difficulty in getting any- one to empty the privies, and they believed that other property owners were in the same predicament. Messrs. Tunstall suggested that the Authority take into consider- ation the advisability of contracting for the removal of refuse in the township. They thought the owners and occupiers would be glad to pay the cost in the shape of an increased rate.—The Clerk was instructed to forward a copy of this letter to the Guardians of Appleton, and also to the overseers, as it was purely a matter for the ratepayers there.

_ _ FRODSHAM WATER SUPPLY. Mr. Walter Timmins, writing on behalf of the execu- tors of the late Mr. E. Timmins, asked if there would be any objection to a small trial boring being made to test the land on the proposed site of the reservoir for Prod- sham water supply, in order to enable the firm to pre- pare a plan. It would considerably alter the design if rock was met with at a depth of 6or 8 feet. The cost would not exceed £2 25., and the expense could be charged in the account for the plans, &c.—The subject was referred to the Frodsham Parochial Committee. FINANCE COMMITTEE. The following gentlemen were constituted a Finance Committee: The Chairman, Messrs. J. Baguley, J. Hall, J. Knowles, Heywood, Stokes, John Weir, W. Whitlow, and Brandreth.

GOOD NEWS FOR RATEPAYERS. The Chairman said he was pleased to announce that they w?dlei be able to carry on the work of the Sanitary Authority for the next six months without making a call on the ratepayers. WATER SUPPLY AT DUTTON. The Inspector of NuisanAs (Mr. Farrington) said notices served upon Preston Estate, Aston Estate, and London and North-Western Railway Company to pro- v!de a supply of water for their property at Dutton ex- pired on the 13th February. He had suggested that this supply should be provided jointly, and the amount that could be expended under the Public Health Act would be apportioned as follows: Preston Estate, £l7 6s. Bd.; ! Aston Estate, £69 6s. Bd. ; London and North-Western, Railway Company, £34 13s. 4d.; total, £l2l 6s. Bd. The railway company were willing to pay their quota it the Authority would give a guarantee that this would.be 1 the full extent of their liability. The Aston Estate in- tended to object to the scheme; he had heard. nothing from the Preston Estate. He wished for autnority to serve a second notice upon the owners, to give them an

opportunity of stating their objections. In answer to Mr. Baxter, the Inspector said it was very unlikly the amount named would be spent. He proposed that a welt be sunk near the Tunnel Top.—The Inspector's request was granted.
FEVER ouTnREAR. The Inspector said he had heard of an outbreak of fever at the Stone Hills, Halton; and , he would make an inspection of the premises.
IMPROVEMENT AT BUDWORTH.
The Inspector reported that iliTi..Bie;COn Warburton, had provided an admirable supply of water for Great Budworth. It was one of the best improvements effezted since the Authority was in existence.

PAYMENT FOR SERVICES. A discussion took place as to the payment of Mr. H. G. Linaker for his services as clerk from the 25th March up to that day and for attending the audit. After some discussion it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. W. Whitlow, seconded by Mr. Aaron, to grant Mr. Linaker Ll&

div.head: THIN. GS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THIN. GS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.

BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRXSPONDENT. It will be interesting to the ratepayers to know that the cost of the recent election of Guardians in Runcorn Union was £67 55. id. This amount is made up as follows :—Returning officer's fee £2O; Stortkhain and Norton, £1 10s. 3d. Frodsham, 9s. 10d. ; Runcorn £36 ss. Od. The Runcorn contest was by far the most expensive, a fact due no doubt to its extensive area and large population as com- pared with the other townships. The competition for the honour of the Chairman.. ship of Runcorn Union, was more keen than ever. Four gentlemen were nominated, and Mr. John Me. Intyre, a well-known gentleman from Great Bud. worth, was elected by a decisive majority. He has been a guardian for upwards of 30 years, is well ac- quainted with poor law administration,and ought to prove a worthy successor to Colonel Ashton. We congratulate him upon his election.

IC is satisfactory to learn that our anticipations with regard o Mr. Howitt and his seat on the School Board are to be falsifidd. Mr. Howitt intends to hold his seat for at least another twelve months, and the ratepayers will reap the benefit of his services on that body. The County Council election takes place at the end of this year, and the present representa-. tires can make ready for a very severe course of "heckling." The grumbling at the increase in the county rate since the Council was formed, is not only lcud but deep. The present call upon the Runcorn Union is £l,OOO more than it was last year, and nearly double the amount which sufficed the magistrates to administrate the county affairs. There is a pretty general feeling abroad that the Council have created several unnecessary offices and have increased salaries on much too lavish a scale.
;th.. F. H. Gossage with his customary thorough- ness, when his interest is aroused, has promised to subscribe £5OO towards the erec4tion of a Crcmatoriutn in Liverpool.

div.head: BREACH OF THE -LICENSING ACT AT
div.p: BREACH OF THE -LICENSING ACT AT
It UNCOItN.

Before Mr. J. Handley, Dr. Steele, Mr. G. Davies, and Mr. G. L. Wigg, at Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, Thomas Pendlebury, lan llord of the Royal Oak Inn, St. John-st., was summoned on two informations for having supplied liquor to a drunken person named John Nappy and also with unlawfully permitting drunkenness.—Mr. E. W. Humphreys prosecuted for the police and Mr. J. Burton defended. From the opening statement of the advocate it appeared that on the 13th inst. P.S. Gosling and a constable were standing near the Lancashire and Yorkshire Bank, when Nappy and another man passed them. Both were under the influence of drink and Nappy was undoubtedly very drunk. The men went to the Royal Oak, but observing that the officers were watching them they stood on the pavement. The offi- cers then walked round by Bold-st., and ten minutes later visited the house. As they entered, the man whose). name was unknown came out, but Nappy was found leaning against the counter with a glass half-filled with freshly drawn beer. The Sergeant asked the young woman in charge why she had served a man in that state' and she replied that she saw nothing the matter with him. The Sergeant said anybody could see that he was drunk, and the woman admitted that she had sup- plied him with a glass of beer on the-counter. The man refused to give his name was brought to the police station and next morning pleaded guilty to being, drunk and was fined by the Bench. P.S. Gosling and P.C. Dickinson gave eviderkce confirming this statement. —For the defence Mr. Burton contended that there was no permission of drunkenness as defined by the Act of. Parliament, and as to the supplying of drink to a drunken person.the defendant's wife on the afternoon in question was left in charge of the house by her husband. She was upstairs attending te a sick child when the men entered the house, and they were standing against the counter when she went into the bar, and there was nothing in their condition to specially attract her atten- tion. The man who is unknown gave the order, and they were supplied. The defendant had borne a good • character for 14: years and during the four months he had been in this house the police had had no complaint to make of the manner in which he had conducted it.— The defendant, in cross-examination by Mr. Humphreys, said he was manager of the house for Mr. Alfred Ellison, of the Man at the Wheel.—The Bench imposed a fine of 10s. and costs for selling drink to a drunken person, and dis- missed the other summonses. The advocate's fee of 105.6 d, was allowed.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD,
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD,

A meeting of Widnes School Board was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. T. S. Timmis, J.P., presided, and there were also present Dr. O'Keeffe, Dr. McDonnell, Rev. J. Clarke, Major Wareing, Mr. B. Brown. and Mr. S. H. Danby (clerk.). • GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended, in accordance with a report submitted to the Board on March 17th. 1894, that the salary of Caretaker Parsons, of the Simms' Cross Board Schools, be increased from £1 7s. 6d. to £1 10s. per week, the increase to date from April Ist, 1891. The minute was confirmed. DISTRICT EDUCATION COMMITTEE. This Committee reported that during the month of March the number of cases summoned before the ‘Com- mittee were the following :—Applications for payment of school fees, 258 ; for contravention of the Education Act. 191; total, 499. Fees were recommended in 232: cases, 26 were refused, and 20 were prosecuted and con- victed before the magistrates. Some discussion took place on the number of cases which the District Educa- tion Committee brought before the magistrates. The Chairman said he had had considerable experience of such cases, and he had never known one where he was net not satisfied that the prosecution was justified. The minutes were confirmed. THE ATTACK ON THE CLERK. Major Wareing, referring to the remarks made with regard to Mr. Danby, the Board's clerk, by Mr. James White at the township meeting recently held, said he had not intended saying anything on the matter, but it had been suggested to him by one or two members of the Board that the -charges should not be allowed to pass unnoticed. He was not, however, pre- pared to go into the matter that day.--The Clerk : I think you had better adjourn it to the Finance Coin- mittee.—The Chairman said he saw the speech in question in a local paper, and was much surpised on reading it.—Dr. O'Keeffe thought it was very hard to make an attack on a public officer who had not the power to defend himself. It was very unfair.—The Chairman • I think it was a most unfair and uncalled-for- attack. -A speaker has a perfect right to criticise the proceedings of the Board, and to pass strictures. Tne Clerk was simply the mouth-piece of the Board, and be (Mr. White) ought not criticize him.—Major Wareing said it was really an attack upon the Board. He took it as such, aid thought any observations would come better from the Chairman if the members generally recognized it as an attack upon the Board.— The Chairman said if the report was correct, he con- sidered it a most unfair and uncalled-for attack. At the. next election they could turn them out, and put in a more economical body. They had never wasted any of the pul4lic money. The subject then dropped.
TRUANT SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION.

The Clerk read a letter from the Chorlton-on-Medlock School Attendance Committee, pointing out the diffi- culty experienced at present in obtaining truant school accommodation for boys. Inconsequence of this, truants had to be committed to ordinary industrial schools, where they had to associate with thieves, and other objec- tionable characters, which was a monstrous penalty for so trivial an offence as truancy. The letter further so- licited the help of the Board in urging the County CounCil to consider the question of providing truant school accom- modation in Lancashire. The letter was referred to the District Education Committee. This was all the business.

div.p: GWILYM EVANS' QUININE BITTERS
BEFORE THE 31A.GISTRATES.

TRANSFER OF LICENSES. On Monday at a special sessions at the Borough Police Court for the transfer of licenses, the beer license of the George and Dragon, Sankey-st., was on the application of Mr. R. Dobson, jun., transferred from the executors of Edward Pugh decease&to Edward Halton ; an off licen.se in Lord Nelsomst., from Mary Ellen Podmore to Joseph Reed ; an off license in 411y-lane,from Mary Ann Cookson to Martha Keenan; the license of the Hop Pole Inn, Rorsemarket-st.Lfrom Harry Dale to Joseph Cook. UNLAWFUL POSSESSION OF MILITARY CLOTIIING. Samuel Barr was charged at the Borough Police Court, on Monday, with being in unlawful possession of military clothing.—P.C. 14 deposed to the prisoner being found tO be wearing military boots and socks, and a military shirt, on being taken into custody, the number on each boot having been cut out, and that on the shirt partly cut out. He stated that he had bought the articles in Middlesbrough.—The prisoner now asserted that he had bought them in Middlesbrough market. AlAerman Harrison: Don't you know you have no right to buy Military accoutrements ? Prisoner: No. —Alderman . Harrison: You know ignorance of the law is no excuse for breaking it. That is an old. legal maxim.—The pris- oner was fined 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days.

A COMMON NTJISANCE TO THE MARKET. At the Borough Court, on Tuesday, William Yates was charged with being drunk and disorderly the previous night in Corporation-st. P.C. Clough said the defendant was drunk and using very obscene language, and at- tempted several times to put his foot through the win- dows of the Blackburn Arms. Witness requested him several times to go away, but he refused, and he had to get the assistance ot three other constables to take him to the Police Station, as he behaved like a madman. Mr. E. Place, market inspector, said during the afternoon the defendant insulted him, and witness's assistant told him that he had seen him previously with his coat and hat off fighting a stall. He was in the most filthy condition, and was a common nuisance to the market. Sometimes the butchers would take pity on him and allow him to clean their stalls, but if their customersknew they would not care to t tke their meat there. The defendant was fined 20s. and costs; in default a month's imprisonment.
THEFT BY A GIRL.

..41.111r • Al A. .1-1. • Before Alderman Holmes and Councillor Voisey, at the Borough Court, yesterday, Clara Wilson, aged 14,0! Pinner's-brow, was charged with stealing from the back yard of Martin Tearney, 41, Pinner's Brow, between 2 p.m. and 9.30 p.m., on the 14th inst., two cotton shire, value Sc. Detective-sergeant Monaghan said the prisoner's father and the prosecutor occupied the same back yard. The police were informed on the night of the 14th of the theft, but nothing could be ascertained as to the thief until Thursday, when the prisoner went to Mr. • Mather's and wanted to pledge the shirts there for is. 6d., stating that they belonged to7Mary Lamb. Mrs. Mather had some knowledge of the articles, and sent for Mrs. Tearney. The house of the prisoner's father was searched, and the shirts were found under the mattress of her bed. —The prisoner's father was present, and said the child had no mother, and this was the first case of the kind that had occurred in his family, both he and the prisoner shedding tears. Me Bench, in consideration of the pri- soner's youth, decided to record a conviction only. AN OBSTREPEROUS FISH HAWKER. At Monday's Warrington Police Court, Patrick Burke, fish hawker, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Winwick-st., on Saturday night, also with assaulting P.C.'s Amson and Rylett.—P.C. Amson said he was on duty at Town's-end, with P.C. Rylett, when they received a complaint that the prisoner had struck a little boy. Witness went to him and asked him what he did it for, and he replied that it was for taking some fish off his cart. A woman said "No, nothing of the sort, officer," and while he was looking at the woman the defendant struck Rylett in the chest. They took hold of him, and he threw witness to the ground and hit him. Witness, in answer to prisoner, denied that he asked him for a drink and accepted 4d. from him.—P.C. Rylett gave evidence.—Gilbert Berry, a little boy, said he was putting into the defendant's cart some haddock that had dropped out of it, when Burke struck him on the jaw.—The Chairman said it was a most cowardly thing for the defendant to say he gave P.C. Amson 4d. for a drink. Nobody would believe such a tale as that he would take 4d. from a man like him who had been brought UP ten times.—The defendant was sentenced to a month's hard labour. TRAVELLING WITHOUT TICKETS.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Saturday, John Williamson, Anthony Runkinas, and Anthony Rimoyney, all of Widnes, were charged with travelling from Widnes to Warrington by the train reaching Bank Quay Station at 11.15 the previous night, without pay- ment of the fare, 6d. From the evidence of the railway officials and a police constable it appeared that the defendants presented third-class tickets available from Liverpool to Widnes, and refused to pay the extra fare, stating that they had no money. They were then asked for their names, and Williamson gave that of Jones. They refused to explain why they had come on to War- rington. They were asked if they had done SO through being asleep, but said that was not the case. They were given into custody. One of the defendants nwiv stated that he had been asleep in the train, and Runkina.s, a foreigner, explained with difficulty that after being apprehended he had found a shilling in his pocket and the railway officicls would not take it. The third defendant .stated that he was a sailor and was travelling from Liverpool to join his ship at Widnes, and did not mean to come to Warrington. The Bench considered the pri- soners had no motive for defrauding the Railway Com- pany, and dismissed the cases. THEFT OF UNDERCLOTHING FROM A WAR:MOUSE.

James. Toyer was brought up on remand at the Borough Police Court, on Saturday, charged with steal- ing from the washhouse of Mrs. Frances Taylor, Wash- lane, Latchford. on the previous Monday night, one pair of drawers, one singlet, one bodice, and one nightgown. Mary Catherine Hughes. Mrs. Taylor's servant, deposed that she last saw the articles in the wash-house on Mon- day evening, between six and seven o'clock, and did not know they were gone till Sergeant Monaghan informed her. The singlet belonged to her and the other things to tier mistress. Mary Leslie, wife of William Leslie, second-hand clothes dealer, Mersey-st., stated that on the Tuesday afternoon the prisoner offered the articles to her for ss. 5d., saying that they belonged to his sister-in-law. Witness said his sister-in-law never wore such things as those, and he replied that she bought them amongst some other things. Witness did not purchase them:— Detective-Sergeant Monaghan deposed to encountering the prisoner coming out of Leslie's shop, and to his tell- ing witness that he had bought the things.from a woman in Manchester-road for is. 3d. Witness saw him after- wards and asked for a description of her, and he said it was a woman ,with a child. He afterwards admitted that on going to Mrs. Taylor's for a bit of bread he stole the clothes. He was committed for trial. A BRUTAL HUSBAND DBSERVBDLY PUNISBED. John McEvoy was charged at the Borough Court, on Monday morning, with assaulting and beating his wife on the 13th of August last. The complainant a weakly- looking woman, deposed that on the date in question, the defendant heather and threw a bottle at her, cutting her about the head so that she had to go to the Infirmary i to have t dressed. She had kept him idle, but told him though she was willing to provide him with meat, she could not find him moth for drink. He left home on tir day of the assault, and did not come back. In reply to the defendant, she denied striking him with the poker or the sweeping brush and throwing a bottle at him ; nor

did she tell him she had a better man than he, In answer to the Bench, she said he woull sometimes work a week and then it was worse for her : he would drink his money and come home and call her everything.—P.S. Ckandley having given evidence as to complainant's condition:after the assault, the son of the complainant and defendant was called, and stated that on the date in question his father got drunk, and came in and lay on his mother. Witness ran upstairs for the lodger, and on coming down again found that she was bleeding.—The defendant, a mild-looking man, of good address, made a lengthy state- ment charging his wife with assaulting him, and turning him out.--The Chairman said he did not believe this story, and remarked that the Bench generally found the fault on the side of the man.—The defendant had been convicted previously of assaulting his wife, and twice of neglect of family, and he would be sent to gaol for two months' hard labour. Mrs. McEvoy subsequently applied for an order for separation and maintenance, and the Bench acceded to her application, ordering that the de- endant allow her ss. a week on coming out of jail.
AN AUDACIOUS ROBBERY.

At the Borouifi'Police Court, on Wednesday morning, before Mr. Alderman Holmes, Thos, Farrell, Jos. Butler, and Wm. Moran were charged with assaulting James Cunningham, and also with robbing him of 255. at the Higher Angel Inn, Buttermarket-st., the previous night. —lnspector James said the prosecutor had worked as a farm labourer for Mr. Edward Percy, farmer, near Widnes, and had come to Warrington on Monday, and been sleeping at his father's house.—The prosecutor said he was in the Higher Angel Inn on Tuesday afternoon, about four o'clock, and had had some drink. He lad the money in his shirt, in front, and Farrell came and deliberately cut open the shirt with his knife and took his money out, carrying it away with him, and also a piece of the shirt. Witness grabbed at his money, and the prisoner's knife struck Farrell's finger and cut it. The other two prisoners were standing close to him, one on each side of him. Edith Critchley deposed to hear- ing a noise in the tap room and going in and finding Cunningham on the floor having hold off Farrell. Cun- ningham said Farrell had robbed him, and he would fetch a policeman. The other prisoners were doing no- thing. Police-Sergeant Taylor said Cunningham com- plained to him of the robbery, and he found Farrell and Butler in Bank-st. Farrell had his hand behind him, and it was bleeding very much. Witness asked him what was the matter with it, and he replied that he had cut it with a piece of glass in picking a child up in the yard. He denied having done anything to Cunningham. Witness found no money on him, but he had in his coat pocket a piece of a shirt corresponding to that cut out of Cunningham's. Witness took the three prisoners into custody. They all on being charged denied their guilt. -,-Butler and Moran were discharged, and Farrell was remanded till Saturday.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT
SATURDAY.—BeforE.!, Alderman Chandley and Councillor

Voney. VAGRANCY.—Thomas Browne was charged with sleep- ing, at two o'clock that morning, in an outbuilding be- longing to Mrs. Monks, of Arpley, and was fined ss. in- cluding costs; in default seven days.—The Chairman (to the prisoner) : We must make that lodging a little more expensive to some of you. It has been a common

convenience for some time. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman R.W. Francomb and Aldermen Harrison and Sutton. Dnmirs AND DISORDERLY.—Thomas Larkin, in Butter- market-st., on Saturday afternoon, and William Farrell, Cloth Hall-yard, and Edward Griffin, in Bank-st., on the 13th inst., each fined 5. and costs ; Benjamin Shepherd and Thomas Atherton were charged with be- ing drunk and disorderly in Winwick-road, 9n the 11th inst. The two ccinstables who gave evidence, said the defendants were fighting. Shepherd was not fighting with Atherton, but with another man, and Atherton called a witness who said it was a man named Povey, whom Atherton much resembled, who was fighting with Shepherd. Shepherd was tined ss. and costs, and Ather- ton was dismissed ; Thomas Mannion, 23rd appearance, *lnd Peter Cartledge, 18th appearance, drunk and disor- derly in Turner-st,, on the 11th inst., were fined ,I.os. and costs each. EMULATING THE LIVERPOOL CORNERMEN.—Peter Ford was eharged with being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-st., on Saturday night, also with assaulting Thos. Howard in Scotland-road. P.C:s 23 and 45 and Howard proved the charges. The last-named said he asked the defendant to allow him to pass, and the man then began to curse and assaulted him. The Chairman told the defendant that he was imitating the Liverpool cor- nermen's style. He was sent to gaol for a month. A SATURDAY Niontr Row.—Patrick Jennings, Patrick Mulcairn, and James Mulcairn,were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-St. at twenty minutbs to twelve o'clock on Saturday night, and Abram Shaw Was charged with obstructing the police by at- tempting to rescue Patrick Mulcairefrom their custody. P.C. 10 said he was in Buttermarket-St. at the time mentioned, when he saw Jennings and the Mulcairns in company with a crovvd,drunk, and quarrelling with some females. He stopped them, but they commenced again, and did not seem to take the slightest notice of him. He and P.C. Amson then took them into custody, but Patk. Mulcairn cqmmenced to struggle with P.C. Amson and they fell to the ground. P.C. Hollingsworth then gave assistance, and the men were all taken in custody. P.C.'s Amson and Hollingsworth gave corrobarative evidence, and Amson" stated that outside the Bridewell Shaw came up and attempted to rescue Patrick Mulcairn. In reply to the Bench, as to what Shaw did to constitut an attempt at rescue, P.C. Amson stated that ha put his hand on Mulcairn and appeared about to rescue hirn,aqd witness had to get P.C. Hollingsworth's assistance to take the man into cdstody. The Bench considered that there was a doubt in Shaw's case,and dismissed him,but fined the other defendants ss. and costs each. DRINK AGAlN.—Elizabeth Lawrenson and Margaret I Riley, drunk in Buttermarket-st., about two o'clock on Sunday morning were fined ss. and costs each.—John McCormick, drunk in the Market Place on the 11th inst., was discharged on promising not to offend again. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF A 'Bus.—William Matthews, drunk in charge of a horse and 'bus in Buttermarket-St., on the 14th inst., was fined ss. and costs. INDECENT BEHAVIOUR.—Mary Annie Fairbrother, of Naylor-st., for indecent behaviour in that street on Sun- day morning, was sent to prison for 14 days' hard labour. PITCH AND Toss.—William ,Riley, for playing at this game for money in Winwick-st., on the 13th inst., was fined 2s. 6d. CIMINF.YS ON FlRE.—Mary Ellison, widow, 15, Smith- st., and Ellen Usher, Morris Court, Church-st., were each fined is. and costs for having their chimneys on fire. TuFADAY.—Before Messrs. E. J. Guest (chairman). and E. M. Crosfield.

LODGING-HOUSE OFFENCES.-Mr. Norman, sanitary in- spector, prosecuted in the following cases :—Ann Farrell, 5, Cloth Hall Yard, was charged with omitting to keep proper utensils at her lodging-house, also with allowing married couples to sleep in a room without having a proper screen .—The defendant was fined 10s. and costs in each case, 345. in all, and on the application of Mr. Norman her license was withdrawn,—Eliza Marshall, 13, Pinnees Brow, for not keeping her lodging-house clean was fined 55., including costs.—Francis Robinson,lodging- house keeper, 93, Tanner's-lane, and bird merchant, Winwick-st., was charged by six summonses with keep- ing his lodging-house and an outbuilding in an unsanitary condition.—Mr. Norman said the place was left with a deputy, who did nothing but smoke and sit with the other lodgers.—The defendant was fined 2s. 6d., %elud- ing costs, in each case, in all 159.—Mary Clark, for omit- ting to remove filth from her lodging-house before 9 o'clock in the morning of the 10th inst., was fined 2s. 6d. UNSANITARY OUTBUILDINGS.--SOIOMOD Bentley, and R. Kennedy, 1 and 3 Crossley-st., for allowing outbuild- ings to be in an unsanitary state, were fined 2s. 6d. each; or seven days in default. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—The following cases were dealt with at the instance of Mr. Riley, school attend- ance officer :—John McCone, forgeman,Friars Green,and Moses Williams, forgeman, Pierpoint-st., were fined ss. including costs, each. Patrick Leonardy, forgeman, Warburton-st, ; had an order made against him for his son to be sent to St. Anne's industrial school, Liverpool. Wm. Barton, forgeman, Pierpoint-st. ; T. Berry, labourer, Silver Square; J. Travis, forgeman, Silver Square; M. Bennett, Pierpoint-st.; and Thos. Ryder, forgeman, Edward-at. ; were each fined ss. including costs. In the case of John Gotton, News Agent. Latchford, the Bench ordered his son to be removed to the Workhouse.he being an incorrigible truant. F. Lee, of Garden-st., employed at the Whitecross Works, was fined 25., and John Ward, forgeman, was fined 10s. THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman) and Captain Ridgway. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Patrick Horan and John Kelly, hawkers,were charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Percival's Fold, the previous night. They were creating a disturbance outside a lodging-house in order to get in. They were fined ss. each, including costs, in default? days.—Bridget Douse, wife of Thos.t Douse, late of Wombwell, was charged under a vvarrand with not appearing to a summons for being drunk an disorderly on the night of the 16th of August last. She was fined us., including costs.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. W. H. Bleckly. ALLEGED THEFT.—Nathaniel Morgan, was charged with stealing from the person of Henry Smith, a boy ten years old, a bag containing the stun of 16s. 2d. The prosecutrix stated that on the 3rd inst., he had just received his father's wages, and was on his was home from a colliery at Haydock, when the prisoner met him. The prisoner asked him to allow him to take care of the monev, "for fear he should lose it." The latter gave up the money to him. They walked together for a short distanc,e,whon the prisoner called at a house on the way. He shortly afterwards rejoined the boy, and ultimately called at a farmhouse. He afterwards told the prosecutor to go back to the first calling place, where he (prisoner) had left the money. The lad did so, and was informed by a woman living there that the prisoner had simply called to ask his way to St. Helens, and had left no money with her. The prisoner in the meantime had made his escape, but he was subsequently apprehended at Blackburn by Constable Booth. The prisoner was committed for trial.

WARRINGTON v. KENDAL HORNETS
The return match between these clubs took place ac. Wilderspool on Saturday. Since the Kendal men made

their first visit to Warrington, when it will be remem— bered they rather astonidhed the homesters by their uni- que passing, and inflicted a two goals defeat, their visit to this district, has been annually awaited with interest.
The Hornets have long been noted for their fine displays,
and it is from the Kendal distriot that Lancashire have
captured one of the smartest half backs they ever pos- sessed, in Berry. The first match this season resulted in favour of our local team, and in order tagive the visitors

a chance to. bring their best teatn, the kick-off. was delayed until five o'clock. Warrington, who were arrayed in different jerseys, were withot4 the services of Fair Turner and Jolley, but Kendal had all on.

Losing the toss, Warrington defended the pavilion goal against a slight breeze, and from Frank Turner's kick-off, some exchanges between Battersby and Evans saw play at neutral ground. A display of passing by the home half backs and threequarters saw Daniels running strongly along the/molder sifie, the tackling of Armstrong pulling him up about five yards from the line. Ndvins struggled over, but the point did-not meot with approval. Holmes tackled well, and prevented relief, but eventu- ally, Wilson led the visitors ,en with a dribble, Boscow staving off the determined rush by a fine punt. Some sharp play by Berry. Ashton, and Frank Turner was supplemented by useful kicking on the part of Evans and Roscow,but. Battersby fielding the oval grandly, the home goal was threatened, and Warrington was forced to defend'. The two Rates gained a trifle of the lost ground, and Evans kicking welt, the Kendal 25 was reached. A response was made by Battersby, Allan, and Armstrong, and Bell had a shot at goat, but Berry responded in tine style. A kick by Allan was charged, A.nd James Bate hadextremely hard lines in not registering a major point. A concerted piece of play by Hall, Battersby. and Allan led up to another attack on the home citadel, and a minor- was conceded. Play was still confined to the home quarters, and a spell of exchange kicking between Barnes and Armstrong found the former judiciously kickincy in touch beyond the half-way flag. The visitors were determined, and some loose play tak- ing place opposite the grand stand; Bell kicked across 0 Armstrong, and the tatter, slipping- Daniels and Bosco*, scored nem-the corner, Belt placing a fine goal. Frank Turner. Holmes, POvey. and Denohne showed up pro- , minentiv in a combined dribble to the Kendal 25, but Barnes failed to make ground from a Pass by Holmes, and then from some grand passing, Handles failed in the finishing touch, and a certain score was lost. Favoured by this slice of hick, the Kendal men once more relieved, and Donohue in stayinr their progress was foully tackled. Some dispute arose over this, and during the altercation Hall took advantage of the temporary disorganization, and gained a somewhat easy try, Bell placing the second goal. Daniels was prominent with some smart work soon after the restart, and it was now the VVarringtonians' turn. Ashton and Nevins were to, the fore in causing Kendal to defend, and the two Bates were exceptionally smart at this juncture. but Hine ldeltity made his mark when in difficulties. It did not avail his side much, for short passing by the Bates, Ashton, Nevin, and Handles was held by the latter a trifle too-long. However, James Bate succeeded a monient later in defeaang his opposing half, and scored a pretty try near the posts',. Boscovv fail- ing. Evans met the dron-out, and Battersby having a kick charged, the Kendal goal narrowly escaped dipaster. Some passim, bY Evans and Barnes took the ball to the line. hut Hine pluckily saved, andtlie score at half-time read—Kendal Hornets, two goals and two minors; War- rington, one try. The second half opened greatly in favour of Warrington. and their forward's plhyed a deter- mined game.rarely allowing the visitors to pass the quar- ter flag. Nevins, who was now deputed to act as an extra three-quarter. was prominent with clever work, and smart exchanges between the two Batestharassed the Kendal defence. Allan temporarily relieved, and James Bate ran down the open, and was pulled up just on the verge of scoring. A protracted series of scrimmages found J. T. Bate fruitlesslt endeavouring to force his way over, but the tackling of the Kendal men was like so many leeches, for no sooner was the hall in his possession than hail-a-dozen of the Northerners grassed him. By degrees the oval was worked away, hut Daniels made an effort, being held before he gronnd.d, and in the struggle he was injured. taking no further part in the game. His absence seemed to inspire the hnmesterg to greater exertions, and another attack by the forwards ended in Berry scoring, Barnes placing a neat goal. Ev.ns met the restart, and the visitors all but scored straight away, a minor being con- ceded. This was their last chance. for Warrington, combining grandly, literally forced themselves to the pavilion end, and Frank Turner, Ashton, ind Dillon were very prominent. Bandies tackled well on two occasions, but the off-side tactics of the visitors were especially noticeable at the point, and being penalized on one occasion, Nevins placed the ball for Frank Turner, and to the surprise and delight of spectators and players he landed a grand goal from the hall-way flag. With the sores equal, Evans forced a minor, and then from a dribble by Berry and Handles, Battersbv Saved. War- rington continuel to have the best of it till the close, and a grand passing display by Berry, James Rate, Evans, and Barnes, found the latter preferring to drop, another minor occurring. An interesting game resulted in a draw the scores7eading—Warrington,2-1-3- ;.Kendal Hornets,

2-0-2. Teams :—Warrinton : J: Boscow, hack ;. J. W. Evans, T. Barnes. and W. Daniels. three-quarters ; J. T. Bate, and James Bate, half-backs ;H. Ashton, W. Nevins, W. Bandies. T. Donohue, Frank Turner, W. Povey, E. Dil- lon, W. Berry, and J. Holmes, forwards. Kendal Mor- nets :—T. Hine, hack: J. Armstrong, J. Allan. B. Bell, and G. Battersbv, three-quarters; W. Hall and E. Braithwaite, half hacks; W. Parsons, F. Hexley, G. Hexley, W. Wilson, J. Mitchell, J. Whiteley, Thompson, and Jackson, forwards.

RUGBY.

ST. HELENS RECREATION V. RinsconN.-_—About eight thousand persons assembled on the Recreation ground, St. Helens, on Saturday afternoon, to witness the match between the Recs and Runcorn. At the end of March the Rees went to Runcorn. but were beaten by two tries and three minors, and in the return it was expected that the Rees would make every effort to keep their winning record on their own ground intact. roe following were the teams.:—Recreation—T. R. Jackson, full back; J. Ellison, J. Seddon, and T. Hodson, three-quarter backs; J. Pilkington, and J. Turt2n, half hacks; W, Parr, 'J. Dolan, J. Hankinson, J. Mousdale, W. Dean, P. Fildes, R. Fildes, T. Winstanley and J. Briers, forwards. Run- corn—S. Houghton, full back; T. H. Davies, J. H. Crompton, and H. May, three-quarter backs; Abrahams and W. Antrobds, half backs; W. Hughes, W. H. Broady, 0. Hughes, H. Williams, W. Shaw; A. Hampson, J. Gayter, R. Dolan and G. Lee, forwards. Broady kicked off for Runcorn against the wind, and play for a time was ot an open nature. Mousdale, Hodgson, and Seddon put in some effective work and Jackson was then called upon. A scrimmage followed the line out. The ball was heeled out by the Runcorn backs, but Parr picked it up and made a short kick. The ball was charged down,but Pilkington secured, and dashed over near the touch in goal flag, Briers mak- ing a good attempt to convert. Play then became of a give-and-take character until from a scrimmage in the visiters" 25, Pilkington gave a nice pass to Ellison. who just managed to get over the line, Houghton colliding with him and having to retire for a time. Briers again missed the kick. After the drop nut Pilkington passed to Seddon, but Crompton intercepted the pass,and, evading Jackson neatly, had an easy run in. The, same player took the place, but failed. From now to the call of hair time the Recs.had tlie best of the plav;and Seddon scored the first minor from'a long kick. With the wind in their favour in the second half,it was expected that the visitors would make a more effective show, but the game in this half was not by any means of as fine a character as in the first half. Pilkington got another try,which Jackson failed to improve upon, and when the whistle sounded the score read—Recs., three tries and three minors; Run- corn, one try and one minor BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS V. WIDNES.,—The Widnesians made a first appearance at the St. Anne's ground, Bir- kenhead, on Saturday afternoon, in delightful weather, the attendance being unusually large. It was fully 35 minutes past the time appointed for starting when noble kicked off from the centre, and a feeble return being made, the play for a time was located in the visitors' half. At this early period there were frequent informali- ties of play, the referee's whistle being frequently heard. At length Ellis Hurst made a dash, and losing the ball a minor was scored. On restarting the Widnesians momen- tarily gained a footing across the half-way, and Ingham having relieved. Peters made a dash 'on the left, and looked like forcing a passage until Conning intervened. A breach of rules now enabled the Widnesians to take up a commanding position, but eventually Conning got the ball away to the home 25. Still' the Wanderers were heavily pressed, and on Ingham's kick .being charged down, Holt crossed the line and scored an unimproved try. On restarting Nosworthy made a fine 'strategical run, but was unable to get through the vigilant Widnes backs. Again Nosworthy secured the ball and located play in the visitors' 25. Desultory play ensued, during which hi a succession of stages the visitors reached the central line, where the ball lay when the interval was reached. Half-time result! Widnes, 0-1-0 ; Birkenhead Wanderers, 0-0-1. On restarting Ingram returned,where- upon Watson and Nosworthy made successive efforts to reach the line hut both failed, and the ball was worked hack to mid-field. Here scrimmaging ensued, from which Widnes made headway. but, mulling when a splendid chaSice presented, the Wanderers were enabled to ease the pressure. At this juncture play was suspended for several minutes, owing to one of the players being in- jured. On restarting Ingham was called upon to con- cede a minor point, which, however, proved of advant- age, as the Wanderers, went away to mid-field, where: Hartles took a free kick. Brennan made a determined effort to break through, but although the effort failed, the visitors held their ground. Now a series of free kicks were taken, and the Widnesians added a minor Point to the score. At this time scrimmaging was frequent', and the game was not interesting from a spectator's point of view. The Wanderers, however, played a pluckily up- hill game, conspicuous among them being Ellis Hurst, their captain,who ran strongly on the left. Although the ball was lost owing to an abortive pass, the homesters continued to make headway until -the referee brought the game to a close. Final result :—Widnes, 1 try, 3 minors ; Birkenhead Wanderers, 1 minor. WARRINGTON" A "v. RGCTIDALE ST. CLEMENTS.—The Warringtonians were decidedly lucky in escaping from a severe defeat in this match at Rochdale, as. to complete the team, they had to press into their service four sub- stitutes, whilst to make matters ?verse, Lally was very unwell, and had to. play in his ordinary attire. War- rington, playing with the wind, at once made a raid, a , grand loose rush headed by Barnes, Molvneaux, and Hackett carrying the ball over the line. Hayes scor- ing a try. Rowe returned the drop-out, and a dribble by Bailey, Isherwood, and Lawless supplemented matters, a minor quickly following. After this a long kick by Potts was grandly follo-ved by Barnes, but a miskick allowed the homesters to get to midfield. Soon after- wards Barnes, Lawless, and Hackett dribbled to the line,_ and Hayes secured another try., the place failing. With such a poor team these successes came as a welcome sur- prise, but disaster for the Saints did not end here, for within a minute afterwards Lawless got grandly away and passed nicely te Heesom, who had no difficulty in scoring, and enhanced the point by kicking a goal. A grand tackleby Heesom stopped Greenwood, but a fine run by Isherwood caused the play to flutter about the Wa rington line. Potts and Sampson showed up, anda rare bit of exciting play ended in Warrington teething down. Then ensued a grand bit of passing amongst the home hacks, the outcome being a try to S. ims's credit. Warrington were soon beateo back after the drop out, until a fine rush by Bailev,Molyneaux, Rowe, and Hackett carried the leather into their opponents' 25. Some rare tackling by Rowe and Isherwood was supplemented by , a kick from Lally, only to see Sims get right away, a magnificent tackle by Sampson ending his career; and half time arrived with Warrington 1-2-1 to 0-1-1. Re- . starting, a dashing run by one of the subs was followed L by passing between Rowe. Lawless, and Potts, the latter running into the home quarters. This was nullified by some capital transfers amongst the Saints' backs, and a minor conceded. The homesters were now having the hest of matters, but after Sampson had cleared his lines beautifully. Heesom intercepted a pass, and ran ta mid- field, where his pass was mulled, and a long kick forced a further minor. Again the attack was renewed, and a try obtained by Grandidge. Then Warrington had a look in, Rowe kicking to Greenwood, and Sampson tackling, Isherwood dribbled to the line, and had hard lines in not scoring. A rush of the Saints' forwards car ried the oval to neutral territory, but the ground was quickly regained. as Potts, receiving the balj from Law- less, ran speedily into his antagonists' 25. The same player directly after almost dodged through, but a bungle being made, Fisher got the "all and kicked down the field, the ball being forced over the line, and a try claimed, from which a goal was kicked, and the game ended Warrington 1-2-1 to 1-2-3. WARRINGTON v. STOCKPORT.

The football season in Warrington was brought to a conclusion on Monday evening, when the local team, easily accounted for Stockport. The Cheshire club, it will be remembered, last September defeated the. War- ringtonians by a pal (dropped) and a try to a try, but any pretensions they had of repeating the dose must have had a serious drawback when they arrived at War- rington three short of their full combination. Able•sub- stitutes, however, were forthcoming, G. Wainwright (Runcorn) and Lawless and Rowe (Warrington) filling the vacancies. The homesters had a fine team up, Antro- bus being again seen in the ranks. Playing with the wind,the VVarringtonians at the onset pressed. So accu- rate was the passing, that it required all Bailey's efforts in the first few minutes to prevent a score. By the aid of Darn, a fine dribble removed hostilities to half way, but Donohue, Bate, Ashton, and Fair Turner passed with a freedom which did them credit. Barnes spoiled the chance offered by a pass just a trifle too high for Potts, Rowe relieved, but a strong rush headed by Berry and Donohue saw Jolley struggling near the line, but being impeded in his progress he handed over the charge to 3 Bandies, and a try was the result. Barnes failed to augment. This was only the forerunner to a series of successes on the part of the locals, for after Wainwright had dribbled to Boscow, the latter promptly replied to the Stockport 25. From a scrimmage here Bate got clear of a pack, and passing neatly to Potts, the latter dodged Lund finely, and a really clever try was the result. Frank Turner failing at the difficult place. Warrington still kept up the pressure, and another spell of passing led up to Berry manipu- lating a try, which Evans converted. Nor did the scoring end here, for after Fair Turner and Holmes had put in grand individual pieces of play, a spell of passing between Antrobus and James Bate found the latter run- ning in his own peculiar style, and being pressed near the line, Bandies received the oval, and the fourth try was chalked up, Barnes doing the needful. The visitors were completely out-manceuvred, and Warrington, tak- ing advantage of the weakness of their opponents, at times turned the game into more of a farce.. Evans was to the fore with some sterling runs, Out a fine run by Dain enabled Stockport to reach the haif way flag for the third time. Their stay here was but brief, and Potts, although pressed, got the oval away in fine ityle. Another passing movement in which nearly the whole of the homesters participated had a futile ending, and al- though Morton relieved, Donohure, Fair Turner, and Jolley took play once more under the Stockport posts. By degrees the oval was worked away, and Barnes in response put in one vas his characteristic runs, and War- rlngton still attacked. Near the call of half time Antro- bus computed the scoring of this half, and the kick at

WAllzden. have now played n latches 'in the West Lancashire League competition, and have won, 10 and drawn I—points, 21. They are unquestionably the League champions, and by consistent form have proved themseltres the winners of the Cup for the present sea- son:

It is not often possible for a leading Rugby riub in Lancashire to,win every home fixture in a season but St. Helens Recreation by defeating Runcorn on • season, but have accomplished this feat. It was the winners' twenty-eighth,victory, and Pilkington's brace of tries made his,total into 25. Seddon, the centre, has dropped seven goals and placed 3CP others.

The formidable Hornets from Kendal, says the "Athletic Icews," can still put a rattling good team in the field despite the constant migration of many of their best known members, and on Saturday they gave War- rington something to do to make a drawn game or . a well contested'match. Battersby is still a terror amongst the backs, and keeps up his form most amazingly. The team travels with a touch judge that can gain more yards on the line than any three forwards, What he mast have been when umpires were allowed on the field is really fearful'to•imagine.

The ordinary football spectators who attend the War- rington enclbsure were in a dreadful state of mind over the scoring intricacies in the game. The visitors had scored a. couple of tries, from which goals had been kicked, .while Warrington had notched a goal from a try, and one froma penalty kick, besides an unimproved try. Although these-figures looked beautiful on the big scor- ing board, there were a lot of unsophisticated' fellows who believed that Warrington had won, and backed their opponents against the more knowing ones, with the consequence that there was considerable- weep- ing and gnashing of teeth in the neighbourhood of the Roebuck-flotel after the match was over.

CRICKET. The Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club, formally ',opened their season on Saturday afternoon. There was no set match, but a number of members turned up to practice. The pitch was not in first-class condition, but with a continuance of the fine weather which has been experienced during the past week it will be in goad order by to-day, when the first Eleven will play • the next Six- teen. Owing to a great increase in the membership the thirditeam will be a permanency this season. Mr.F.Wil lia.mson, Thelwall. has been appointed captain

div.head: CYCLING
div.p: CYCLING

Kensington Oval, on Saturday, was the scene of the first meeting of this season promoted by the Surrey BicycllYClub, and 20,000 spectators availed themselves of the privilege of witnessing the four events included in the programme. In the mile race for the Sydney Challenge Cup, A. Du Cros (the Irish Champion) won very cleverly by about a length, in fairly fast time. The ten miles race was, however, the most interesting, the finish being a magnificent one. Round the lAst bend Du Gros was leading at a terrific Oace, but SaTon made a splendid spurt, and, coming up on the outside, Just de- feated the Irishman on the post, whilst Fentiman, of the CatfOrd Cricket Club, was only a foot or so bebind in the third place.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The Liverpool gymnastic team, which met the Dundee eight in Kinnaird Hall, Dundee, on Saturday night, in the semi-final heat for the challenge shiekt of the Inter- national Society, have reason to feel proud, not only at gaining a decided victory, but of the enthusiastic recep- tion accorded them by the ladies and- zentlemen who crowded the hall to witness the contest. Between 2,000 and 3,000 persons were present. On the horizontal bar, the teams were pretty well matched,,bnt the exercise finished with Liverpool seven points ahead. Standwell and Jones for Liverpool, and Rogeraibi Dundee, each. had the maximum of twenty marks. The jumping had scarcely begun when the superiority. of Liverpool was apparent, only :Crowe showing to advantage against them. He, however, had to succumbat 51t. 2in., lea-7- imp. Mason and Cookson still in. Mason cleared sft. sin., and Cookson sft. (iin. Liverpool gained thirty points, and were thus thirty-seven to the good. At rope climb- ing, Dundee reduced the lead by lipoints, leaving Liver- pool victors:by 39,. points. Cooksoa,with a total of 451, was highest for Liverpool; and Betsworth, 441, for Dun- dee. The team totals were :—Liverpool, 327; Dundee, 2911. Cookson, after his -rope climbing,was so exhausted that on coming down he fell to the floor, and lay for a short time before v.:covering.
