div.p: ASSOCIATION.

_ WESTON POINT (SHIP CANAL) V. VirA.TIRTNGTON Assoct- 1 ATlON.—These teams played their return fixture at Runcorn in grand Weather, bofore a fair number of spectators. The visitors kicked off with the wind in their favour; and'pla.y was kept in midfield for a time, until Powell and T. Mather getting possession, raced away towards the home goal but the defence was too much for them. Some give and take play ensued, each end being visited in turn,. Clayton and Onions making several good attempts to score, but half-time arrived with no score. Onions.retired injured having wrenched his knee just before half-time. After the re-start the home team went off with a dash, only to be pulled up by Phillips and Parry who were playing a strong defence. They,how- ever, returned to the attack and kept Jones busy, Phil- lips, Parry and Mather,. all putting same good work in. Eventually, after about twenty minutes' play in the second portion of the game, the home team sent in a well directed shot,which,glancing off the foot of PhilliPs, went through. This livened the visitors up, who, re- starting, playectup with renewed vigotir. From a pass by J. Mather, Cornforth raced away, and, crossing to T. Mather, that player equalised with a splendid goal. No further score being added,the result was a draw game— Warrington, I goal Welton point, I. Warrington team : —Goal, Jones ; backs,Phillips and Parry (captain) ;half- hacks, Ayling,, Warburton and J. Mather; forwards, Clayton, Onions, Cornforth, T. Mather, and Powell.

div.head: PRIMROSE LEAGUE.
div.p: THE PRIMROSE LEAGUE.

A business meeting of the Grand Habitation of the Primrose League was held, on Monday, at Westminster Town Hall, Lord Radnor presiding. The report of the council shbwed a steady increase•of members and marked progress in the activity of the habitations; but there had not been a corresponding increase of the tribute paid to the Grand Council. The admissions since the formation of the League had been 63,251 knights, 59,773 dames, and 887,968 associates.

div.head: LORD SALISBURY AT COVENT-GARDEN.
div.p: LORD SALISBURY AT COVENT-GARDEN.

Lord Salisbury, presiding on Tuesday at the annual meeting of the Grand Habitation of the Plimrose League, at Covent-Garden Theatre, said that great meeting was a tribute to the exertions of the League and the great success by which its efforts were attended, the member- ship being now a million. There was a small general election going on at present, and a larger ene was pend- ing. There were certain social questions at present exer- cising great influence on the electors. He was glad of the appointment of the Labour Commission, though it might not lead to a party victory. He believed the Iris b ques- tion was the one this generation had to solve, and the eyes of the electorate would not be drawn from it by any other temporaky occupation. He could promise that the other party would have no rest on the Irish question. Thanks to Mr. Balfour they had had five years of reso- lute government, and no one would venture to say it was impossible. It had given tranquility, and peace td Ireland. Referring to Mr. Parnell, he said he thought of him exactly as he had done three years ago. All the transactions showed that Mr. Parnell was still allied with the most violent of agitators, and the experience of the last five years had skown the seamy character of Irish heroism and the men who agitated
LINUM CATHARTICUM Plias, agreeably aperient 94c1., 2.5..9d. Of all Chemists,—Advt. A Lloyd's telegram from Finieterre reports the wreck of the English steamer Skyro, at Meixede •
NEW BOOKS, &c.
The late one-volume edition of the works

of Lord Tennyson is published by Messrs. Macmil- lan and Co., price 7s. 6d. It has for frontispiece a finely finished portrait of thepoet laureate, and the volume itself is one of over 800 pages. As there are two columns to a page it will be seen that the 4uantity is great—to say nothing of the quality. It has been the fashionof fate in some quarters to de- cry Tennyson as a veteran who lags superfluous on the stage • but no person •of judgment and taste can read his later works Without still feeling the presence uf tile master mind. There may be a lack of the force and fervency of earlier days.; but there is something in every poem to show that the hand has by no means lost its cunning. There can be only Om" Charge of the Light Brigade"; but if it had never been written we shotild have made much
of" The charge of the Heavy Brigade" horn the same pen—with such thrilliug,lines as :

Pell like a cannon shot, Burst like a thunder-bolt, Crusted like a hurricane, Bi.oke through the mass limn. below, • Plunged up and down, to and fry, Rode flashing blow upon blow,. BraNe Inniskellens and Greys, Whirling their sabres in circles, of light! "A Ballad of the Fleet" is, in a similar way, swift and . .
• powerful, while in "The Northern Crobtrier " we have the humour and skill in the use of dialect whieh de-

lighted everybody in " The Northern Farmer." It must be admitted that Tennyson has not succeeded as a dramatist; but,. if his plays are not all: that could be wished for acting purposes, they amply repay the reader. What there cleverer in its way than .the das- eription in " Queen Mary " of the Pope as— , The Eternal Mier of the changeless chair,. Crown'd slave-of slaves, and mitred king of Isiings Again, Shakespeare has nothing finer than this To do him any' wrong was to beget A kindness from him for his heart was rich, Of such fine mould, that if you sow'd therein The seed of Hate, it bloesom'd Charity. Vireeannot hope to• have more than a few linessnow and again from the poet who has turned eighty' ;. but we have every reason to-be proud of the literary wealth he has- created. The eight Ba,mpton,Lectures delivered in 113 W by the Bishop of Ripon, and published with the title of " The Permanent Elements of Religion," have reached a: second

edition and are published by Messrs. Macmillan. & Co., price '6h. The scope of these lectures is wide • and the treatment is tlaoroughifrom. the lecturer's point .of view. He enters into an exhaustive comparison of" three uni- versal religions "—lslamism,BUdclhism,and Christianity; and proceeds to show that there are certain essential ele- ments demanded by man in religion, chief among whicli are dependence, . the' need. of fellowship, and the need of rogress. While admitting all that is good in Islamism and BudOisms. he argues that Christianity best supplies the needs of man's, nature; and that, the survival of religion being probable, Christianity fulfils the conditions needful for survival. Dr. Boyd Carpenter speaks, as might be expected, aseme holding a brief for a particular client, but thereis no denying that his state- ment is onthe whole as fair as it is thoughtful. Th( lectures are enriched by somel3o pages of notes, and ther is besides-a copious index. The tanners of this district will doubtless welcome _work by the late Mr. John. Nayfor on " The practice., theory of tannin." It is Published„price 55., by Messrs. Waterto2 Bros. &. Leyton Limited, London. Mr. Nay- lor. we !learn, at different periods in his lifetime filled positions of importance in tanneries-at Warrington, New- port (Salop). Newcastle-under-Lyne, and other places -; and in consequence of his extended experience, to which he added by diligent study of the scientific or chemical r.spects of his business, he gained the reputation of be- mg a considerable authority in tanning. The work cannot be said to be a text book on tanning, and yet-it is a technical treatise written by a most ° experienced man. He commences by saying" Tannin or tannic acid is the astringent prineiple of plants. It is not the bitter principle. The bitter principleis scarcely-perceptible in pure tannin'. It is called tannin on account of the pro- perty it possesses of turning: skin into leather ; and on account of its medical properties it is called an astring- ent principle." In the twelve chapters which compose the book Mr. Naylor treats, amongst other things, upon tests for tanning, soft and hard tannages, skin, water, acids, preparing for tanningesoftening dry hides, lining, bating, and heats. in tanning. The fourth and last part isto hand of" John Bull and his other island" by Mr. Arthur Bennett, of Warrington. Like the previous issues, this detailed account of visits to Ireland is well written ; and, apart from the anti- Home Rule sentiment which pervades it, it is good read- ing. Mr. Bennett seems to have met a sensible Irish doctor, who said he had not any wish to see Ireland treated differently from the rest of the United Kingdom, but be thought that a federal' system would be the out- come of the present dilemma, in which each portion of the kingdom would have,Homeßule in purely local affairs, coupled with perfect union fell. imperial purposcs. This, it seems to us, puts the case for Theme Rule in a nutshell, and is much more valuable than the summary which Mr. Bennett has green of his own views on the political situation. It should be added that there is a considerable. amount of livelyincident in the volume, and that the descriptions of scenery are admirable. The " Westminster Review " is strong, as usual, in well thought out and carefully written papers. There is a second paper by EMily Glole Miss on "The fetish of charity," which ought to be read and re-read by all who are in the habit of 'Contributing to benevolent institutions. Amongst other papers we- have "The rear-guard of the Christian army,"" Women and negro suffrage," 4' Geolegists among the idealists"" Ibsen's Brand," and; in the independent section, "In Darkest England and the Way out." The review of contemporary lituaturee deals with science, philosophy, and theology, sociology, history, and biography, and the.b'etfea lettres. The "Century Magazine" has for frontispiece a beautiful engraving of Mona Lisa, by Leonardo da Vinci. The first article illastrated is on "The Salons of the Revolution and the ,EMpire." Amongst other illustrated papers we have A' Fetishism in COngo-land," "Cold cheer at Camp Morton," "Two •EkpeclitiOns to Mount St. Elias," and "To California by Panama in '49." In addition there is a good supply of bric-a-brac, open letters, and story and verse. The" Manchester (learterly," which is published for the Manchester Liberal Cluh4 by Mr- John Heywood, has Mr frontispiece, a portrait of the Rev: W. A. Connor, B:k., followed by an article-which gives an account of his life and work. "A visit toqtalv." which is contributed by Mr. W. Clough, is adorned with bee) most charming 'l views of Lake Come. from, photographs by F. Edwards. Other articles are on " Efeelish Rhythm," " The poetry:of Dante Gabriel Rossetti.' " The works of Robert ' Browning," "concluding with a, poem on " The voice of Nature," by Mt. J:B: Oldham. The "English Illustrated Magazine" for April, leads off with an interesting sketch of' William James Linton, engraver, poet, and-politica/ writer. There is a splendid portrait of Linton, and there are some specimens of his engravings, which- are unsurpassed for artistic treatment. An artiele on" The Harrow School "is amply illustrated, and we have " The true. history of the Koh-in-ur," with illustrations. The contents also include ' The lepers of Robben Island," "Girlhood in Italy," " The. Monas- teries of Meteora," and a further instalment of "The Witch of Prague,"by F: Marion Crawford. The" Ladies' ' Gazette of Fashion " (6d.) is; furnished' with two highly finiehede full page, coloured plates, and a large number of fashion engravings. There is a needle- work supplement of chair and sofa backs in applique,. and amongst the contents we have "Spring. fashions in. Paris," "Society and Fashion," "The drawing-room table," "The uses of bamboo," "Round the Shops.' "Housekeeping notes." &c.

div.head: TERRIBLE EXPLOSION IN ROME.
div.p: TERRIBLE EXPLOSION IN ROME.
FIVE PERSONS KILLED AND 60 INJURED..

ROME, THURSDAY, 1(1 A.M. An explosion occurred early this morning at the powder magazine at POMO Pantaleo, about two miles and a half from this city,acl- joining the fort, to which is annexed the Vigna Pia Farm and school tor bays. At a few minutes past seven the inhabitants-were startled by a loud report, resembl- ing a thunder clap, and the greatest; excitement pre- vailed. Windows were broken in vauious quartets, and the detonation Awes heard for many miles round. On hearing of the disaster Kin.' Humbert proceeded at once to the • scene of the explosion with Signor Nicotera, Minister of the. Interior, and was quickly followed by Marquisdi Rndini , the Premier, an&other Miniztera. An immense crowl soon collected, and! the troops-were des- patched from the Porto Portese to.nnaintain order. ROME, TUE.YDAY, 1 P.M.—lt is believed that the full extent of the disaster at the foclis now known. Five persons are believed to be killed,but all the bodies have not yet been. recovered. Aboxt €0 are wounded, and these aro chiefly peasants. About 40 smaMruaral houses situated within about one miloof the fort are, completely wrecked. Fortunately, at he time of the. explosion the inhabitants were mostly at work in the fields. The soldiers in the fort had dimly notice of the disaster, by hearing the preliminary warning, and saved their lives by throwing themselves on the ground. One captain and two soldiers are severely wounded,, and this is be- lieved to be the extent a the injuries among the troolis.

A gun, 'which it is believed will prove of some assist- an.ce in elucidating the mystery surrounding the murder of Mrs. Morrall, at Matlock Bath, recently, was favard on Thursday morning in the river Dervrent. On Thursday morning a man named Healy fired a shot at his wife at Loanhea.d, Midlothian. The shot struck her on the cheek, and Healy immediately after shot him- self dead. Deceased and his wife had not been on good terms for some time. The woman Is 'in a critical condi- tion.

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

A meeting of this Board was held at the Work- house on Wednesday morning. There were present, the Rev. G. F. Roborts. Alderman Harrison, Messrs. Clarke, Kilshall, J. Houghton, Swinton,Owen, Jolley, Davies, Heat on, T. Jones, Au kl and, Dobson, Kilshaw, Hibbert, Gill, Mather, Ratcliffe, W. Houghton, Hum- phreys, Turton, Hood-Wright, Balharry, Smith, Warburton; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant Clerk), C. H. Ward (workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (superintendent.of Padgate Schools.) ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN. The CLERK having taken the chair pro tern., Alderman HARRISON, the retiring chairman, rose to propose a chair- man for the ensuing year. He thought it would not be considered presumption on his part, because, in the first place, he was afraid that he was the oldest member of that Board.—(The CLERK: No, Mr. Kilshall is the senior member of the Board.) Well,he was quite willing to give up that honour to somebody else. (Laughter.) He thought that was about the 57th time the Warring.ton Board of Guardians had met for the purpose of appoint- ing a chairman, and although he had not had much per- sotral intercourse with Mr. Balharry—for that was the gentleman he was about to propose—he knew him by re- Putation, and he thought a more worthy man than Mr. Balharry was not to be found amongst his predecessors. (Rear, hear.) Mr. Balharry had been a successful man,and bad worked himself up to a position of honourable inde- Pendenee. He had devoted his spare time towards fami- liarising himself with duties of a parochial character, and if it could not be said that he had rendered the State some service, it could at all events be said he had ren- dered his neighbours some service. (Hear, hear,and ap- Plause.)—The Rev. G. F. ROBERTS, in seconding the pro- Posal, said it had been his intention to propase Mr. Har- rison for re-election to the chair, but as Mr. Harrison had proposed Mr. Balharry, he would most gladly second the proposal.—The proposition was supported by Mr.' zteaton and Mr. W. Houghton, and agreed to unani- lacmsly. Mr. Balharry then took the chair and returned ‘uanks for his election. APPOINTMENT OF A VICE-CHAIRMAN.

On the proposition of Mr. HEATON, seconded by Mr. RIBBERT, Mr. G. Ratcliffe was re-elected senior vice- Chairman. On the motion of Mr. HIBBERT, seconded by Mr. W. WARRINGTON AMATEUR PHOTO- GRAPHIC SOCIETY.

This Society held its fourth annual exhibition of lantern slides in the Co-operative Hall, 4ankey-st., on Tuesday evening. There was a large attend- ance. The President T. J. Downs), in opening the proceedings said the slides they were showing that night were all the work of the members of the society. They had been carefully selected, and he believed he was right in saying had not been Publicly exhibited before. In addition to the lan- tern slides they had, fortunately been able to pro- vide them with a rich musical treat. Mrs. W. B. Roberts, of Wilderspool, Mr. and Mrs. R. H. Pearson, and Mr. W. S. Howard having most kindly promised their assistance. These names were familiar to most of them as household words, and it needed no words of his to recommend them to their notice: their great musical ability was so well known and $o highly appreciated in Warrington. They had made a slight change this year in regard to admis- sion. In previous years the admission had been free, but this year they had ventured to make a small charge. The fact was, they were some- what hampered for want of money. They had a large number of members but the annual sub- scription was a small one. That was all the source of income they had, and it was only sufficient to keep their heads above water by the exercise of strict economy. They felt their society had done in the past some useful work by bring to a focus, as it were, the various amateur photographers in the town and neighbourhood, and that it had also been the means of creating an interest in photography generally such as did not previously exist. (Hear, hear.) But it was their desire to make the society even more useful, and for this they required money. It was for that reason they had made a slight change that evening, but he telt quite sure that, at the close of the evening's entertainment they would all feel that they had got their money's worth, and they would also have the satisfaction of knowing that they had had helped on what he honestly believed to be a most deserving society.' (Applause.) The programme of the evening was a varied and interesting one. The exhibition of lantern slides was interspersed with musical selections, vocal and instrumental, of a high order. The slides, as mentioned by the chairman, were all by members of the society. There was the greatest possible variety in the subjects treated,and it is no exaggera- tion to say that in no instance was the treatment of an inferior order. Many of the slides, in fact, could hardly have been better than they were, and, speaking of the exhibition as a whole, it afforded conclusive evidence that the society contains members, amateurs though they may be, who are _capable of turning out work of the best kind. The members of the society who ex- hibited slides were Miss Harding, Messrs. H. N. Houghton, J. Smith, jun.. J. Chorley, jun., P. Pearson, W. Robinson, Kirby, J. Hallowes, J. Pritchard, C. Yonge, J. Skelton, and J. Harding. A word of high praise is due to Mr. H. N. Iloughton and Mr. J. Harding for the manner in which they manipulated the lantern during the evening. Many local scenes were shown on the screen including views at and near Stockton Heath and 'Walton, at the Isle of Man; and in Ireland. There were also 80131 e fine landscapes which had been photographed ,bY members of the society in differenttparts of -"gland. The musical pa,rt of the programme was texcellently arranged, and gave a pleasing diversity e the proceedings. It is needless to say that the Solos on the piano by Mrs. W. B. Roberts were thoroughly appreciated, the approval of the audi- ence being particularly hearty after a fine perform- ance of Gottschalk's "Pasquinade.". Mrs. Pearson _gave a successful rendering of the song "The last larewell," and Mr. Howard's song " Fetters of Gold," with a violin obligato by Mr. R. H. Pearson was also warmly applauded. A duet, for piano and "Lucia de Lammermoor," by Mrs. Roberts and Mr. R. H. Pearson, was in keeping with the rest of the proceedings which were altogether success- ful. The programme was brought to a close with the singing of "God save the Queen."

Sir,—As the statement of accounts for the past year, in connection with the above Church, was not allowed by the Chairman (Rev. G. Allton) to be read to the parishioners at the vestry meeting held on Wednesday, Ist day of April, at ten o'clock in the forenoon, I wish to ask the churchwardens, through the medium of your valuable paper, whether it is their intention te .submit a statement to the ratepayers of the Parish. Speaking for myself I am a little bit curious about 'the matter seeing that the Vicar so strongly objected to the accounts being read over to the full meeting, although the greatly-respected people's warden, Mr. R. T. Smith, (who was also treasurer), was present with the report and quite expected being called upon to read it'to the meeting. It is quite evident that Mr. Smith anticipated this, as I heard him ask the chairman several times whether he was going to have the accounts gone 'through. I have read in the papers the proceedings at a great number of vestry meetings in this town' and its vit:inity, and failed to find the odd one where the accounts were not submitted. I venture to express a hope that the churchward6ns may see their way to getting a few report& printed and circulated amongst the parishioners, thereby afford- ing an opportunity of the same being perused by those wishful to see them. Thanking you in anticipation for the insertion of this letter.—Yours, &e. A RATEPAYER OF THE PARISH. April 24th, 1891.

INVERTED VERITAS. Sir,—Your correspondent,figuring under the non-nom en of "Veritas" has been good enough to advise me "to pause for a moment and reflect whether my own state- ments can test criticism." Well, sir, I have paused and

reflected that my statements will not stand criticism, if my critic begins by inverting my statements. I Wave chal- lenged criticism;if conducted logically and reasonably; but a complete inversion and perversion of what 1 have said is too much for me. And this is exactly what "Veri- . tas" has done most completely. I must apologise for over-rating his literary capacity ; I ought to have adopted the reading-male-easy style and not put things before him which his limited capacity was unable to grasp. The mind that conceives optics and acoustics as mechanical sciences is capable of any puerility, and so 'requires some little indulgence and consideration. This is the history of the mare's nest, over the finding of which " Vanitas non Veritas " gets prematurely jubilant! Your inveri- table correspondent himself dragged the name of New- ton and Herschell into this discussion, in a letter dated February 9th, 1891, with the contention that what con- tented "these eminent men" as to the identity of the •God of Creation and of Genesis ought to be sufficient also for us moderns. So this brilliant idea, this utter begging of the question,originated with the genius who now turns round and accuses me of it! It was as a corrective of this absurdity that I penned tho sentence which has so disturbed him—" An idea of his fitness for the task he has assumed may be gathered from the fact that he instances Newton, Herschell, and other eminent inter- preters of nature as being uninfluenced by the disturb- ing influence of geology and biology upon old beliefs." Am I not then warranted in saying that an idea of his unfitness for even elementary authorship maybe gathered from his entire inability to see the drift and purpose of so plain a statement? But, in erder still further to prove his utter incapacity in this work, "he commits hi in self as.follows" :—" It is rather startling to be told that Newton was influenced by the disturbing influences of geology and biology, considering, that these influences did not come into existence for many a year after his day." Precisely. If anybody had told him this it would be startling. No one did tell him that ; but he was startled himself by allowing his perfervid imagination to overpower his unweaned judgment. It would be in- teresting to a student of mental science to inquire, how far these aberrations may be attributable to the early training of " Veritas." I regard turn as a type. There is a class of men, who, while shrewd and successful in the crdinary business of their lives, are quite at sea and astray when they enter the region of theology ; for here they abandon the system of logical and rational treat- ment which led them to success in their every-day busi- ness and intrust themselves to the unsafe guidance of heresay and tradition. Assuredly the hypothesis of re- vealed religion must he in a bad way if it can send no more efficient champions to do battle for it than this 'inverted " Veritas."—Sincerely yours, 'JOHN PEERS.
Penketh.,l9-4 1891

div.head: WARRINGTON MAGISTRATES AND THE
div.p: THE WARRINGTON MAGISTRATES AND THE
BIRCH ROD.

am much pleased to find that my recent letter GU the subject of illegal procedure on the part of Warring- ton magistrates in sentencing the boy Dunbobbin, Gri his father being summoned for not sending him regularly to school, to chastisement withthe birch rod, has been the means of bringing upon the magistrates concerned the well-deserved animadversions of so high an authority as the "School Board Chronicle." But that paper points .out that, since the appearance of my letter, the matter has assumed a new phase, the Town Council, which is at present—thanks to the pernicious influence of a narrow, antiquated, and fossilized type of humanity at present lying like an oppressive dead-weight on Warrington— our local substitute for a School Board, having endorsed the action of the magistrates. I should like to ask how it happens that the Mayor, the Corporation—in- cluding several lawyers—and the Town Clerk, could allow such a preposterous piece of illegality to be ap-

proved by the Town Council. As to the acquiescence of the Mayor and the other justices who have seats in the Council in this approval, I might point that it has this significant import—it amounts practically to a public declaration of their readiness, supposing a case like that of Dunbobbin came before them, to pass prezisely the same sentence as was passed in that case. The Corpora- tion, therefore, including all the magistrates who were presentiat the Council meeting, as well,as those immedi- ately concerned,now stand identified with the culpability of the notorious birehing sentence. In your report of the case there was no record of the magistrates' clerk, or the deputy who, it appears performs so often the func- tions for which his employer is so well remunerated, advising the magistrates against the sentence. Hence I presume that he did not so advise them audibly to the press; or that if he privately gave them such advice they choose to ignore it as the Warrington Bench are accus- tomed, at their convenience, it seems, now and then to do. I might ask, too, how it was that our zealous School Attendance Officer, who-can lay down the law to the magistrates, on occasions,, was so ignorant of the Education Act; or so careless as to the observance of it, as to allow such a sentence to pass unchallenged. I said in my last letter that an action for assault could have been sustained against both the magistrates and police for their part in the boy's chastisement and deten- tion. But I will now put the matter more plainly. Any man in Court would have been free to intervene to re- lease the lad from the clutches of the police, and it would have been at their peril if they had laid a hand upon him to prevent him or to take him into custody. It would have been at the peril also of the magistrates if they had subjected him to any penalty for his intervention. Yet, despite all these facts, despite the severe denun- ciations in the press of the conduct of our local Dog- berries in this matter, we have it reported in your last impression that the Bench at the Warrington Police Court, on the previous Tuesday, had the cool audacity to threaten another boy, whose father was summoned for not sending him to school regularly, with a birching if his parent were brought up again for the offence. I have now most emphatically to warn them and all their col- leagues in the local magistracy that if Dunbobbin or any other boy whose father is summoned under the Educa- tion Act be birched in future, I will take care that the "School Board Chronicle" is duly apprized of the, cir- cumstance and will do my utmost to bring the perpetra- tom of such an unsconscionable outrage—for the plea of ignorance of the law can now be no more admissible— into merited obloquy and contempt, both locally and throughout the country. I shall consider it my duty, indeed, to endeavour to create an agitation for the removal of men who can so scandalously abuse judicial anthority and contravene the law, from the commission of the peace. I have to say this, too, that if the Town Council &I not take steps at their next meeting to redeem them- selves from the compromising position they have placed themselves in of giving the direct stamp of their autho- rity to a piece of flagrant magisterial lawlessness they will be most remiss in their duty, and will stand discre- dited in the eyes of the town.—Yours truly, MANLIUS.

THE INCREASE OF RATES IN WARRINGTON. IMPORTANT EXPLANATION. Sir,-There is so much inquiry in town, and so many erroneous impressions on this matter, that I deem it a duty to make the following simple statement of facts, as to how it comes about the Finance Committee and the Overseers have had to increase the rate they originally proposed to levy. First let me clear away all doubts as to what the rate will be. It is in everybody's recollection that the over- seers first determined to levy a rate at is. 81 in the 2- a reduction of 10d. upon the rate of last year. The Finance Committee proposed to levy a rate at 2s. 10d. in the £ an increase of 4d. upon last year;and to levy a sewer rate of 2d. in the £, a reduction of 2d. upon last year, making in all 4s. Bd. in the £, or a general reduction of Bd. The Overseers have since increased their rate from is. Bd. to 25., whilst the Finance Committee propose to make their rate of 2s. 10d. into 35., bringing the total amount to ss. 2d. being a reduction of 2d. only upon last year. When the Oferseers at the annual town's meeting announced their intention to reduce the rate for the coming year by 10d. in the £, everybody rejoiced, and most people scanned the papers for the reasons which justi- fied them in taking this course. Everything seemed clear and justifiable, but from what I learn they had assumed the borough call for the present year would not exceed the call of last year, whereas, unfortunately for their calculations,it amounted to £10,304 9s. 11d. or £2,174 6s. in excess. Many ratepayers have very naturally enquired how this increase comes about. In the first place we had last year £l,OOO from the gas department which we must not expect this. We have also to make up the balance of the cost of the application to Parliament for our Extension and Water Bill. The increase of the library rate, and an adverse balance instead of a large surplus as last year at tho bank, easily accounts or the in- crease. With respect to the borough 6'r improvement rats several of the Committees have fortunately only made slight increases in,their estimates, but the Market Com- mittee, compelled to alter the lighting arrangements, asks for £222 6s. extra; the Street Improvement Com- mittee, which contemplates altering and improving one or two thoroughfare requires £638 extra; and the nor- mal increase of the expenditure of the Sanitary Com- mittee (owing solely to the extension and growth of the town) is £389 11s. 3d. These three Committees, for perfectly legitimate purposes, require £1,240 7s. 3d. extra. , A very heavy deficit from the sale of manure during the year, made up_ as hereafter shown, and a reduction of £lO4 for the use of the hospital and sundry small items make a total of about ;£2,200, necessitating the imposition of the extra 4d. put on by the Finance Committee. The deficiency in the manure account is as follows : In March 1890, we brought farward as owing for manure (taking round figures alone), £620. The Committee estimated the value of manure then in stock at £2,320 ; and they estimated to make £2,400 worth during the year ;a total of £5,340. The cash actually received for manure during the year was £1,510, the manure sold but yet not paid for amounts to £750, and the original esti- mate...2f the value of the manure in stock this March was £2,2111 making altogether£4,s2s, or an actual deficit of £Bl5. The Sanitary Committee, having some doubts as to the weight of the manure at Longford, had it carefully examined, and instead of there being, as originally esti- mated, £2,265 worth, the amount was found to be only £1,460. They at once communicated this fact to the Finance Committee, and though they very naturally urged the Finance Committee not to increase the rate if possible, the Finance Committee having no margin could not do other than increase the rate, and therefore at the last Council meeting they withdrew their suggested rate of 2s. 10d., and at the next Council meeting- will move to increase it, as before stated, to 3s. Notwithstanding all this trouble and anxiety there is room for congratulation because we shall pay off the balance of the cost of obtaining the Act of Parliament. We shall clear off the deficiency on Longford. We base our estimate for the manure on a reduced value, and, if the error should occasion a more watchful care over this department in the future, the result may be most beneficial. I cannotplose without calling attention to the fact,that, in spite of everything the croakers say about the Borough and its general management, the rates have been gradu- ally decreasing, for in 1889 they were 53. 6d., in 1890 ss. 4d., and this year but ss. 2d., tho latteibeing the lowest rate levied sincelB7B.-Yours obediently, J. SHAW GREEN.

div.head: E GOSPELS AND TIIEIR AUTHORSHIP.
div.p: E GOSPELS AND TIIEIR AUTHORSHIP.

Sir,—Mr. Gandy has certainly a very original method of parrying the force of evidence. In his letter which appeared on the 28th March in reply to my statement that between the Apostle John and Irenmus there only stands one man (Polycarp) from whom Irentens would receive all information as to the writers of the four Gospels,"—he thinks it a sufficient answer to say "that it lea7s out anything that Polycarp may have told Irenmus ! " He then clenches it by an assertion—" We have not a tittle of evidence to show that Polycarp knew anything' about the Gospels, or that he was even aware of the existence of the Gospel of John.",! ; To begin with the former part of the latter assertion—it is evident that Mr. Gandy is not very well acquainted with his subject when ho states that Polycarp knew nothing about the Gospels; for in an epistle which is now extant, and which.is acknowledged as genuine by all critics of any importance of every school, Polycarp quotes passages from both Matthew and Luke, thouali as usual generally with 'the writers of the 2nd century, he does not mention his authors by name. Yet, when he writes as 'follows—" The Lord has taught us saying judge not and :ye shall not be judged,, forgive and ye shall be forgiven; be ye merciful and ye shall obtain mercy; for with the same measure tbat ye mete withal, , it shall be measured to you again • and blessed are the poor and they that are persecuted for righteousness' sake 1 for theirs is the Kingdom of God "; aid further," beseech- ing the all-seeing God not to lead us into temptation ; as the Lord hath said the spirit is truly willing butithe flesh is weak,"—l think it will be admitted that —Polycarp knew very much more about out Gospels, than my friend knows about Polycarp. Again, can Mr. Gandy possibly' have faced the absurdity of his statement that •6 there is not a tittle of evidence to show tnat Polycarp was even aware of tin existence of the gospel of John" ? What, when it lc even admitted by Dr. Martineau that this gosi3el as we have it may have appeared at least 25 years before Poly- carp'Sdeafh, and according to Renan 40 years before, and a reputed work Of his Master's been in circulation throughout all 'Asia Minor; in which district he lived, Polycarp "not beaware of its existence "P Believe this who can! Lastly in reply to his assertion that we have nothing left us to show "what Polycarp may have
PENKETH.
THE NEW BATHS.

During the past few weeks the young men em- ployed by the Penketh Tanning Company, Limited, have been busily employed in preparing for the pro- posed baths. The course of the brook has already been diverted, and the excavations for the baths have now attained a great depth.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL .25,1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL .25,1891.

told Irenseus," I need only say that common sense does not require us to produ& any actual written statement of Polycarp's to this effect. It should surely go without saying that the intimacy of Irenteus with Polycarp is quite sufficient of itself to prove that he could never have accepted the three synoptics, and the Gospel of John as the production of their reputed authors unless he had positively known that his master Polycarp had also received them as such. But Irehreus did receive them, and therefore Polycarp must have received them also, and the Apostle John must also have acknowledged the three synoptics, or Polycarp cciuld not have acknowledged them—whilst he would as certainly hand down his own Gospel to the custody of Polycarp and all the ohurches. This brings me now to the false setting of the testi- mony of Irentens, and to the consequent false reasoning thereon. Mr. Gandy tells us that " Irenseus engaged in controversy with certain .persons who declined tr acknowledge the fourth Gospel, and what does hi do? Instead of proving the historical authority ol that Gospel by simply stating what he knew about its historical origin, on the testimony of Polycarp, the 'personal disciple of John, he employs the absurd argument that there must be four Gosugls because there are four winds." Now this is a most incorrect, and in its general aspect an aboolutely untrue statement. In the first place Irenceus does not set himself " to prove the historical authority" of the fourth or any other Gospel. His contention was with the false doctrines of his Gnostic opponents. In the next place his here- tical antagonists, the Valentinians, with whom he deals in his Third Book, and to which the quotation above refers—actually accepted these same Gospels, paying, as Dr. Lightfoot says, "especial deference to the Fourth Evangelist,and accordingly he argues with them on this basis " ! "But they also superadded other writings to which they appealed, whilst heretics of a different type, as Marcion for instance, adopted some one Gospel to the exclusion of all others. He thereforesurcres not only that four Gospels alone have been handed 'down from the beginning, but that in the nature of things there could not be more nor less than four." Now lam now not concerned with the fanciful analo- gies of Irenveus ; we have to do with his facts ; and to in- sinuate that Irenteus could not have indulged in an imaginative flight by way of illustration without imperil- ling his credibility, or giving anyone kround to suppose that he had no other historical evidence fcr his facts than his fanciful analogies—this. I say, is truly an "imbecile" kind of logic, of which no such specimen can be found in Irenams. Neither the inferential evidence, therefore, to be drawn from Polycarp, nor the direct testimony of Tremens is touched by any showing of Mr. Gandy. The testimony of Irenteus is not his merely,but the witness of the whole Church of Christ in every part of the world for the entire 2nd century to the authorship and truth of the four Gospels. There is no need to continue this discussion wifh my friend any further. He can tell us nothing which has not been refuted over and over again.. I ha've not pro- duced a tithe of the evidence which is furnished by the writers (either referred to or quoted) of the first and second centuries.

To revert to the point from which we started,Mr.Gandy has no standing place—for his assertion—aboutthe value of the teaching of Christ's disciples,and of St. Paul. The gospels and acts of the former. and the epistles of the latter are Christ's own tel chino an 1 messages to the church and •to the world, and we are under the obligation to receive, them as such. For my friend to talk of Count Tolstoi's vagaries, touch- ing the doctrine of redemption not being the teachings of Christ, is utterly absurd. It is infinitely worse than leav- ing out the part of" Hamlet" from the play of "Hamlet" The a hole Christian ages are a standing witness against the falsehood of Tolstoi's utterances. For myself I can only regard it as the concentrated esse,nce of untruth, and only matched by the impious falsehood uttered by the father of lies himself in the garden of Eden. Yours &c. Penketh, 21st, April, 1891.
JNO. DIGNUM.
[We agree with our Correspondent as to the time having arrived for bringing the discussion on this subject to a close. With Mr. Gandy's reply, it must terminate— at any rate for the present. ED. Ex.]

div.head: 6,ICKET.
div.p: 6,ICKET.

The cricketing season was opened at Penketh on Saturday, when a match was played between the Friends' School and Penketh Recreation on the ground of the former, resulting in a victory for the Recreation by five runs. Robinson did good service for the home team, taking seven ickets in quick succession. The remaining three were bowled by McTear. For the Reareation .Hobson bowled With great effect. The scores were as follows :—Penketh Recreation, 21 ; Friends' School, 16. A TIMELY RESCUE.

A boy, about 3 years of age, named Mughes, was playing near what is known as the spring pit, on Wednesday night, and fell in. A boy witnessed the accident, and after ineffectually trying to rescue Hughes went and told his mother. She immediately ran to the pit and was just in time to save, her boy who was completely exhausted by his fruitless struggles to reach the land. Remedial measures were at once employed, and he is now progressing favourably.

div.head: FRODSHAII.
div.p: FRODSHAII.

FnonsnAm PRIMROSE LEAGUE.—The annual general meeting of the Frodsham District Habitation (No. 1662), was held in the Town Hall, Froeisham, on Monday even- ing, when Mr. James Reynolds, J.P., ruling counaillor, occupied the chair. Mr. A. l'homas, J.P. (trea.);reported that he had a balance in hand on the general account of £36 2s. 10d., and on the excursion fund account of £l4 63. sd. Colonel Ashton (warden) reported that the number of persons enrolleri as meathers of the habitation was-19 knights, 20 dames, and 663 associates, making a total of 703, which showed an increase of 98 on the previous year's record. Dr. Weaver proposed a vote of thanks to the ruligg councillor, the officers, and execu- tive council, for the admirable manner in which the work of the council had been carried on, which was carried non con. The following officers were unanimously re- elected for the ensuing year : Ruling councillor, Mr. .4mes Reynolds, J.P. ; hon treasurer, Mr. .A. Thomas' J.P.; hon. secretary, Mrs. Ashton; warden, Colonel Ashton ; Executive Council, Messrs. E. A. Wright, J.P., R. Watson, and S. Davies; Mesdames Reynolds, Weaver' Thomas, H. Reynolds, Murray, White, Steele, Dunsford, H. Lowe, Barff, and Broady; Misses Wright, E. P. Wright, and Laycock. The ordinary busi- ness having been transacted, a toy symphony by mem- bers of thehabitation, conducted by Mr. H. Tiley, was given, and heartily enjoyed. On its conclusion a leeture on "The Irish Question," was delivered by Mr. F. Smith-Barry.

DR. W. G. GRACE.

Dr. Grace—the G.O.M. of cricket—was barely eight years old when he played his first match. It was not an infants' match either,for his side bore the im- posing title of West Glouces- tershire. He was only a mere youth, his age being but fif- teen years, when he put on the phenomenal score of 170 in the first innings and 58 (not out) in the second in- nings of a match against the gentlemen of Sussex, at Brighton. At the same age, be actually took part in an All England match, and also

.ppearance at that most classical of grounds, Lord's, for his county against M.C.C., and against some first-class bowling put on 50 runs. Great honours awaited him the following year, 1865, for he was twice selected to play for the Gentlemen against the Players, a position to which many ar- dent cricketers have striven for years to attain without reaching the goal of their ambition. What other cricketer of this or any other generation can point to such a performance as that of Grace's,when, at the age of seventeen, he put on 224 (not out) in the England and Surrey match of 1866. Four weeks after the great display of batting skill he ran up another mammoth score-173 (not out)—in the Gentlemen v. Players of the South match. It has been the lot of but a small number of cricketers to score upwards of a century twice in one match,but Grace has performed that very great feat, and did so at the early age of 20 years,viz :-130 and 102(not out). Mr. Grace has made some tremendous scores in his time, but took the wind out of everybody'e sails in 1876, when he ran up the following figures: --400 (not out), 318 (not out),and 344. In the year just named he scored no fewer than 3,908 runs dur- ing the season, and between 1864 awl 1879 he made 20,842 runs in a total of 415 innings. His exploits as a batsman, fielder, and bowler were so famous that the title of " champion " was spontaneously conferred upon him. No amateur or professional has ever reached the batting averages credited to Mr. Grace, and on July 22m:, 1879, at Lord's the en- thusiasm of his admirers took the form of a presen- tation of the value of £1,400. It should be added that Dr. Grace was born at Downend, near Bristol, in 1848. He is just a year and five months younger than that other great amateur. Mr. A. N. lkornby, who has fought side by side with him or against him in honourable battle foT the greater part of their career.

div.head: , SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE , SHIP CANAL.
OPENING OF THE WESTON kARSII LOCK:

The first lock-connected with the Ship Canal, that at Weston Marsh, which is to take the traffic be- tween the Weaver and the Ship Canal, was opened 'on Thursday week. • There were present Mr. S. Platt (chairman of the Works Committee), Alderman W. H. Bailey, Councillor 11. Boddington, Mr. J. K. Bythell, Mr. Leader Williams, Mr. Abernethy, jun. (resident engineer of the section), and Mr. J. Weston contractor's agent), who has executed the work. The party embarked on the con- tractor's steamtug, and the gates being opened, steamed into the lock. The lock, which is 315 feet long, 42 feet 6 inches broad, and 16 feet deep, has three pairs of gates, the intermediate ones dividing the basin. The gates are worked by hydraulic power, obtained by using the water of the Weaver Canal, and are put into gear by friction cones. The machinery has been constructed by Messrs. Cleghorn and Wilson, Weaver Foundry, North wich. Boats can pass through the block in from three to four minutes. The gates, which are made of the finest greenheart wood, have been tested by the Weaver Trustees, and are as tight as a bottle. Eventually they will be handed over to the chaige of the 'Trustees. In the course of the day, the party visited Eastham section, and were highly gratified at the rate at. which progress is being made. In the course of a month, it is expected, the monster lock at Eastham will be in working order. All the gates are now hung.

KILLED ON THE CANAL AT ECCLES. • On Friday afternoon, Mr. F. Price, held an inquest touching the death of Richard Knight, 26 years of age, late of 15, Barton Grove, Patricroft. Deceased was em- ployed as a labourer, and on Monday last was at work in the Eccles cutting. He endeavoured to pass between the boiler end of a working steam navvy and the "" face" of some rock, when he was caught between the frame work on which the boiler stood and was severely crushed by the moving of the navvy against the rock. He died from his injuries on Wednesday. A verdict of accidental death was returned. THE NEW BILL.

div.head: NON-COMPLIANCE WIWI STANDING ORDERS.
div.p: NON-COMPLIANCE WIWI STANDING ORDERS.

The petition of the Manchester Corporation and the Ship Canal Company for a bill to enable the Cori:Oration to subscribe £3,000,000 to the undertaking of the Com- pany, was on Thursday before the Examiner of Standing orders in the House of Commons. It was reported that the usual notices had been given, but that they were all too late in the session. The Examiner said he should, of course, have to report that tbe petition had not somplied with standing orders. The sublet now stands referred to the Standing Orders Committee, who will doubtless dispense with the formalities in this case and allow the bill to proceed in the usual course.

ACTON GRANGE. Much time has been of late 'eXpended upon the con- struction of bridges and railway embankments, and those who are in a position to judge agree that the work is being well and substantially done. The arches and bridges are in a great majority of cases very elegant, and no One can lay it to the charge of the company that the work is being done in a slipshod fashion. On all sec- tions of the canal operations are being carried forward with considerable . activity, and nowhere is this more apparent than at Acton Grange. The:stonework for the girder bridge is being fixed rapidly, while at Walton Arches the timbering has been taken down frozii the river bridge, thus showing its light and graceful propor- tions. The bridge is now being constantly used for the purpose of conveying the loads of spoil across • the river, and it is used to make the bank for the deviation rairway into the town. Near the girder bridge at Acton Grange, men are engaged on the railway embankment in Rying down the chairs. and sleepers for the perman- ent way. - --------

•-•-, • THE RECENT FATAL ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. , The adjourned inquest on fienry Ankers, aged 26 (son of Thomas Ankers, 13, Queen-st., Runcorn). who died-in consequence of injuries received at the Ship Canal works at Runcorn, on the l'Oth inst., was held by Mr. H. C. Yates, coroner, at the Ship Canal Hospital, Latchford, on Wednesday afternoon.—Mr. P. Davies attended on behalf of the Ship Canal Company, and Mr. Wynne Hum. phreys, of Runcorn, on behalf of the deceased relatives.- .—Elenry Jones, of 14, Grosvenor-St., Runcorn, said he was engine driver for the pile driver on which the de- ceased had been employed. On the morning of.the 10th inst., witness was putting the pump of the engine in order, when he heard the foreman shout" lower the ram on the pile." Witness told the fireman Henry Barnes to lower the ram steadily on the, pile, and he did so, there being no jerk. Just as the ram hit the pile the chain broke. He knew then. there was something wrOng. When he turned his"head to look he saw the deceased in the water. lie did not see him struck. !Tarries had lowered the ram before, and never had an accident. He had been viith him nine months, and he, considerisd him careful, and well acquainted with the work. The shaft broke before, about five weeks ago—he did not know why—but nobody was hurt then.—The Foreman (Mr. Davidson) thought that the deceased ought to have had medical advice sooner than he had. It was a very strange thing that the man who got such a knock over the head , and then tumbled into the river .should be brought eight or nine miles in his wet clothes before he pot medical assistance. He must have been almost, perished.—The Coroner said he did not think there was anything in that. It was pretty evident what would be the result of a great thing like that coming on his forehead, that he was: un- conscious the whole time from the minute he was struck. —Cross-examined by Mr. Humphries. the witness Jones , said he could not say whether a new shaft was put in after the breakage five weeks ago,or whether the old one was welded, though he remembered a shaft being put in since. A new " monkey " or ram, had been provided. He thought it was heavier than the old one. The mon- key was changed about a week before the accident.— Henry Barnes, aged 14, said he was what was called fire- man, and lived at Runcorn. The last witness was his driver. Witness did not hear the foreman tell him to lower the ram. The driver told him to lower very steadily, and he did so. As he was doing this, when the ram was close on the pile he heard something fall, and stopped his engine directly. He had driven it many times without an accident. Witness did not see the de- ceased hurt.—By Mr. Humphreys: When I was first as- ked about this matter I said that the driver had been driving it, not me at all, but I forgot what I was saying. —Mr. Humphreys: Are you sure you are not fotgetting what you are saying now ?—Witness: No. sir. —By Mr. Davies: Witness had seen Mr. Humphries before.—ln reply to Mr. Humphries, he said he had never spoken to him before.—Mr. Humphries asked if he might call a witness.—The Coroner: No.—Mr. Hum- phries witness who can give material evidence.—The Coroner: You are not the person who is getting up this
CtIANGES AT RUNCORN CHEMICAL WORKS. PRESENTATIONS TO MESSRS. KO WITT, KNOWLES, AND REID.

An interesting gathering took place in the cooper- age of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Works,on Satur- day evening. Mr. J. J. Howitt (engineer an:l gene- ral manager), Mr. J. Knowles (Leblanc Works mana- ger), and Mr. Reid (ammonia soda manager), have each severed their connection with the company, to undertake responsible and more lucrative positions under a company formed for the purpose of con- structing a large works at Northwich on the Brun- ner and Mond principle, and the officials and work- men determined to show their appreciation of the charac- ter and services of these gentlemen on their departure. Three handsome silver tea and coffee services were ob- tained, and the workmen assembled in large numbers to witness the presents formally handed over to the reci- pients, and to wish thein every success.—Mr. J.J. Speak- man occupied the chair, and said it was an occasion of pleasure and sorrow—sorrow that they were losing old and valued friends, and pleasure that they were im- proving their position in life. Their three friends had risen by energy, and research, :'and perse- verance, and their connection with the, works had been of a most pleasant description. (Applause.) —Mr. John Ince, in making the presentation, remarked up6n the value of friendly intercourse between master and men, and said they wonld miss tha genial kindness of Mr. Howitt—(applause)—the quieter but none the less real greeting of Mr. Knowles—(applause)—and the warm impulsiveness of Mr. Reid. (Applause.) Amid much applause he handed the service to the recipients and stated each bore an inscription showing they had been presented by the officers and workmen of the Com- pany as a mark of esteem.—Mr. Howitt, who was cor- dially greeted. said he received the present with some sort of regret because he was about to leave the Com- pany's works and the many friends he had gained there. He had always had the interests of the workmen at heart —(hear, hear)—he did not say that with any egotism, but with some amount of pride. When confidence existed be- tween employers and men work went more smoothly, he had striven to that end, and to a great extent had suc- ceeded ; and it was with great regret he left the work- men who had done their duty admirably. (Applause.) He wished to tender his heartiest thanks to the men for the assistance and co-operation he had received in help- ing him to carry on the works. (Applause.) When he came to Runcorn he found that labouring men were working for 25. 80. a day, and he thought it was mon- strous as that would scarcely keep body and soul together (Applause.) He did not believe in starving men ; he believed in paying them n honestly and fairly for the work they did (applause) and he had striven from the com- mencement to get men paid fairly well. He was anxious , that no man should earn less than 3s. per day. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. J. Knowles, in returning thanks, said he was pleased to tell them that the strike amongst the coopers had beeft amicably settled. (Applause). He had only done what he thought was right. From the bottom of his heart he thanked those present for the kind comments on his long connection with them. They I had been eleven years together, and they had experi- enced fine and dirty weather, ,but owing to the con- fidence which existed they had worked amicably together both at Runcorn and Weston. (Applause.)— Mr. Reid said although he was sorry to leave the men, he hoped he was going to do better. (Hear, hear.) He could say this that if Mr. lit owitt had not come to Runcorn he did not think they would have met that night under the same conditions. (Applause.) Mr. Howitt had been principally instrumental in bringing about the success of the Company, and had been the means of making everything comfortable and agreeable, and of creating a better feeling between masters and men. (Applause.)—Speeches appropriate to the occasion were also delivered by Messrs. Bealey, J. Turnbull, J. Poole. T. Riley, D. Bisbrown, Wm. Davies, McCullock, and T. Watson. A vote of thanks havinc, been passed to the chairman the proceedings terminated'. A COMPLIMENTARY DINNER. On Monday a complimentary dinner was given to Messrs. Howitt, Knowles.and Reed at Riley's Cocoa Caf6 and the proprietor provided a capital repast. There was a large company present, and amongst others besides the guests were Messrs. S. Taylor (chairman of the Board of Commissioners), H. J. Grice, J. J. Speakman, James Turnbull, Wm. Armstrong; Thomas }Vile, Thomas Moores, John Roberts., , Thomas Watson, Wm. Rushton, James Tudo J. W. Kearsley. Wm. Manghcan. Samuel Dodd, John Sefton, Fred. Wilson, John McCulloch, John Ince, James Garner. Mather. McClard, .Tohn Fletcher, Ralph White, William Twaddel.—After dinner,yr. Speakman presided'and pro- posed the customary loyal and patriotic toast,Coleur-Serg.. Poole, and Mr. Thos. Pickering responding for the "Army Navy, and Reserve Forces." The Chairman tlien proposed the Toast of "Health and success to our guests" and said it was with great 'regret that they were parting with their genial friend Mr. Hewitt, who was almost always in a merry mood. Whatever his inner feelings might be Mr. Howitt's exterior had always been one of a pleasant nature. and in his (the Chairman's) opinion thisrwas one of the things that had helped him through the great diffi- culties he had experienced since he came to Runcorn. (Hear, hear.) But Mr. Howitt had not been all shop. He and Mr. Tayler had laboured together on the School Board for education of a wider scope and had been instrumental in forming evening classes which had been. mined on with great success. (Applause.) As to Mr. Knowles, he had known him for Tit or 15 years and he had watched him rise to the position he new occupied. That position had not ben a bed ef roses, but his endeavour had been to bring to the best possible results the process of which he had the control. (Hear, hear.) Then there was their friend Mr. Reid. who was of a volatile but still sturdy nature and he had a true British heart within. him. (Hear, hear. \ ThOtoast was drunk with much enthusiasm and "For he is a jolly good fellow "was heartily sung.— Mr. Reid, Mr. Knowles, and Mr. Hewitt made suitable re- sponses.—The Chairman proposed " Our, local governing hod v," and in an interesting mannerpointed out the change which had taken place in the town 'during the past forty vears.—The toast was coupled with the name of Mr. S. Taylor, and was drunk with musical honours.—ln res- ponding Mr. Taylor said he (lid not think there was a town of its size that had made greater progress than Run- corn had during the past ten yes rs.T-The Chairman pro- posed the town. and trade ef Runcorn and Mr. Ince responded, and the toasts of "The press" "The host and hostess 7 and "The Chairman 'concluded a most enjoy- able evening. Songs and recitations were contributed by the company. On Monday afternoon a number of workmen metin-the -fitting .shop to say good-bye to Mr. Ralph White, the fore- man engineer, and to present him with a token of their respect and esteem. On behalf of the men, Mr. S. Mat- thews (chemist) presented Mr. White with a handsome marble timepiece, inscribed as follows :—" Presented to Mr. Ralph White, by the workmen of the Ammonia Soda Plant of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Works. April2oth, 1891." Mr. Matthews delivered a few appropriate re- marks,and speeches were made by Messrs L Turnbull,W. Maughan, J. Kersley, and J. Jump, who all bore testi- mony to Mr. White's good qualities. In acknowledging the gift,, Mr. White said his connection with the work's had always been of the pleasantest character, and he hoped they would treat his successor in the same way they had treated him. He would treasure the timepiece as a memento of their good-will.

Samuel Howe, farmqr,Woodley,Cheshire,was on Tues- day committed for trial by the Bow-st. police magistrate on a charge of forging a cheque for £1,275 and a promis- sory note for £2OO, also committing perjury in the recent action Howe v. Burcbardt.

inquiry, but I am the persan.—Thomas Morris, iron- works manager for the Canal Co., then gave evidesee as to the results of his examination of the broken shaft, produced, and described careful and elaborate tests to which he had subjected the iron, all of which he said it had stood remarkably well. He had detected a flaw of the depth of about three-sixteenths of an inch, but it could not have been discovered by an expert on exam- ination of it. If he had examined it on the morning of the day of the accider...there was plenty of time for such a flaw to develope before the accident. The monkey weighed 20 te 21 cwt. and the shaft would have borne 20 times that load if there ' had been ho flaw.—The Coroner said though he had• declined to allow Mr. Humphries to bring any more evidence, he was very loth to hide anything from the jury, and if they wished to have more evidence they could have it, but he failed to see the necessity of it.—Several jurors agreed that it was not necessary, and another thought some- , thing might be gleaned from it, but there was no general expression M opinion on the Point.—The Coroner (to Mr. Humphries) : Who is this witness P—Mr. Humphries: He was here last time, but it was from him that I ascer- tained that it was the boy who was driving not the other.-- The Coroner: That is admitted.—Mr. Humphries said his witness had broken in when the lad was giving evidence last time with the remark "You know that is a lie," and but for him they would never have got the facts out.— The Coroner : That is assuming -n great deal, but still I think this evidence of Mr. Morris clears up the whole thing.—Mr. Humphries: My witness will prove that the machine was not worked in the easy manner you have been told.—The Coroner: Mr. Morris says distinctly it weighed only 21 cwt. and a jerk would not affect the flaw.—The Coroner then proceeded to sum uip. He ex- pressed the opinion thaA, Mr. Morris's evidence had satisfactorily explained tire matter. He remarked that had it been supposed that the deceased was so seriously injured medical assistance would have been obtained im- mediately ; but under the circumstances he should have thought that hospital, where there were good medical men and the best medical appliances, was the best place to bring him to.—The jury returned a verdict of acci- dental death, coupled with a recommendation to the company not to allow a boy so young to lower the ram I in future.... •

div.p: IRUN ERALS. MESSRS. MAGINN BROS beg to I: inform their numerous pitrons and the public that they are now prepared to execute funeral orders in the best and most economical manner. They have spared no expense in acquir- ing the most elegant and modern hearse and carriagbs, and superior matched pairs of horses either blacks or bays can be supplied as desired': Customers can rely on their orders being carried out to their entire satisfaction, and in a style which cannot be excelled in this district. Inspection invited. MAGINN BROS., PARK MEWS, SANKEY-ST., WARRINGTON.

div.head: LAT 'EST NEWS.
div.p: LAT 'EST NEWS.

THE HARBORO' ;ELECTION. The Harboro' election nomination is fixed for May 2nd. The polling takes place on May Bth. GRAVE CHARGE AGAINST A CURATE. At Maidenhead, yesterday, the Rev. James Pilling, curate of Winkfield, was remanded, charged with car- nally knowing a girl aged 15. FATAL FIRE AT PUTNEY. A fire occurred at Mr. Ballasis's Laundry, Putney, yesterday morning, and on the flames being subdtied,the charred remains of John McGee, aged 19, were found. THE POLITICAL SITUATION. A DISSOLUTION bUDGET. The " Standard " states that, after the Budget last , night, a number of telegrams were despatched from the House, warning local political agents to be prepared for an early dissolution. The "Times" says: A few Conservative members are opposed to the whole principle of free education,, and it is stated that they-will hold an informal meeting next week to discuss the situation. CAPTAIN VERNEY, M.P., BROUGHT UP AT BOW-STREET. At Bow-street, yesterday afternoon, befOre Sir John Bridge, Captaiin Edmund Hope Verney.M.P..surrendered to further answer the charge of conspiring with a woman named Rouiller, to procure a girl named Nellie Basket, under age, for immoral purposes. Mr. Avery, who pro- secuted for the Treasury, mentioned that several addi- tional facts would be brought against the defendant. Miss Basket went into the box. She said that when she saw defendant in Bridge-st., Westminster, he was wear- ing the same clothes as in France. She also recognised him by a limp in his walk: After other•evidenee, the case was adjourned,and the sane bail was then accepted. THE WHITEHAVEN CONTEST. The polling commenced at Whitehaven yesterday, to fill the vacancy in the parliamentary representation caused by the death of the Hon. George Cavendish Ben- tinck, Conservative. The candidates are Mr. H. G. Shee, Gladstonian Liberal, and Sir James Bain Conser- vative. The few carriages used principally displayed the colours of the Conservative candidate. Nearly half the voters had already polled at noon. The result was as follows : Bain (C) 1338 Shoe (L) 1105
Conservative Majority 233 It the last election, in 1886, the Cohservative majority was 206.

YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the Woolsack at a quarter-past four. THE MANIPUR MASSACRE.—In reply to the Marquis of Ripcn, Lord CROSS deeply deplored the loss sustained by the Government of India at Manipur and promised to lay despatches on the table, Lord Lansdowne might be trusted to treat the natives with justice and mercy. BILLS ADVANCED.—The Drainage Acts Amendment Bill passed through Committee.—After a brief discussion on state-aided emigration the Merchandise Marks Bill passed through Committee. The House adjourned at quarter to seven. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past two o'clock.

div.head: PORTUGUESE IN AFRICA.
div.p: THE PORTUGUESE IN AFRICA.

Sir J.FERGIISSON, answering Mr.Labouchere said com- plaints had been made by the Portuguese Government of a violation of the modus vivendi on the part of the Chartered South African Company, but it had not been shown in what respect. Only one complaint had been made of the imprisonment ani deportation of Portu- guese officers by the agent of the company, and that re- ferred to th& reported arrest of Lieut. Friere. The company denied the arrest, but further inciiiry was being made.

div.head: LAND PURCHASE BILL
div.p: THE LAND PURCHASE BILL

Tne House went into Committee on the Purchase of the Land and Congested District (Ireland) Bill. After a long discussion clause 2 was added to the Bill. Clause 3, which provided for a guarantee fund under the di- rection of the Treasury, was next discussed. A proposal to abolish the cash portion of the guarantee was defeated by 185 to 113. Mr. LABOUCHERE moved to omit from the clause the words" and a contingent portion as re- garded the guarantee fund," but it was rejected after a discussion by 196 toll 3. Mr. KEAY moved to omit from the contingent portion of the guarantee fund the Irish share of local taxation customs and excise duties, but on a division it was negatived by 173 to 95. Progress was reported, and the Chairman obtained leave to sit again on Tuesday at two. The sitting was then suspended.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The annual meeting was held on Tuesday, at Dutton Workhouse. Present : the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. C. Reynolds, J.P. J. Bate, Wilkinson, Hewitt, J. Weir, Heywood, Tay- lor, Lewis, Edwards, Kirkham, Stokes, P. Hall, Aaron, Lightburn, J. W. Baguley, Pickering, Bre- therton, J. Hall, Smith, Knowles, Baxter, Ellison, W. Whittaker, Brandreth, Parr, Lea, J. Baguley, Mclntyre, J. Ashton(clerk).

div.head: RACE FOR THE CHAIRMANSHIP
div.p: THE RACE FOR THE CHAIRMANSHIP

Mr. H. G. L:naker, as retiring officer, presented his certificate of the recent election, and said, the first busi- ness was the appointment of Chairman. Rev. J. W. N. Tanner proposed Mr. Mclntyre in complimentary terms. Mr. Stokes proposed Mr. J. Brandreth, Mr. Pickering seconded ; Mr. Aaron proposed and Mr. Weir seconded, Mr. H. E. Heywood ; Mr. j•lin Whitlow proposed, Mr. W. Whitlow, seconded, Mr. J. Knowles. It was decided to vote by ballot and the result was as follows '.—Mr. Mclntyre 15, Brandreth 10, Knowles 5, Heywood 4. .A second vote was then taken, when Mr. Mclntyre received 20 votes and Mr. Brandreth 14. Mr. Mclntyre was therefore declared elected and took the chair, and said he hoped it would never be tarnished while he was the occupier of it, and that he would be able to hand it down to his successors as pure as he received it.—Mr. Bran- dreth expressed his pleasure that Mr. Mclntyre had re- ceived the appointment. For the position of vice-chair- man the voting was as follows. Knowles 16, Brandreth 7, Heywood 3, Tanner 2. Mr. Knowles was declared elected.

THE ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE. On the proposition of Mr. Aaron the ex-officio members of the Assessment Committee were re-elected, Messrs. E. A. Wright, J.P., Charles Reynolds, J.P., Henry, J.P., Nield, J.P., and A. Thomas, J.P. On the selection of 8 Guardians being made, Mr. P. Hall said Runcorn was very badly represented. Mr.Speakman had very seldom attended.—Mr.Taylor said Runcorn was not represented. The town was assessed at one-fourt.h of the rating of the whole union, and lie thought Runcorn ought to have two representatives, and Weston one. Runcorn was assessed at about £45,000, and Weston at about £16;000. He moved that Runcorn have another representative.—Mr. Wilkinson seconded.—By 17 votes to 12 it was decided that Runcorn do not have an additional representative.— Mr. Taylor moved that Messrs. Aaron and Speakman re- present the Runcorn district.—Mr. Lea seconded.—Mr. Brandreth moved, and Mr. Wilkinson seconded the ap- pointment of Mr. Taylor and Mr. Aaron. Mr. Taylor wished to withdraw his name,but the mottion was passed, and Messrs. Taylor and Aaron were appom ted*by a- very large majority. The other members of the Committee were selected as follows :—Messrs. Lewis, P. Hall, Knowles, J. Weir, W.Whitlow, and Mclntyre.
A CHURCH /CND CH ,PEL bISPUTE

On the appointment of the School Attendance Commit tee, Mr.lieynolds aSked that the name of Mr. Heywood should be added to the Frodsham Local Committee, as the'number of members had been reduced by various causes.—Mr. Heywood said he was willing to act, but there was at the present time a dispute between Church and Chapel, and he,, as a representative of the Church, would not be acceptable to some of the ratepayets -of Froosham.—Mr. Reynolds: I don't think this Board takes any notice of such a thing.—The Chairman said that was so, and the names of Mr. II eywood and Mr. Edwards were added to the Committee..—Dr. Gastaldi was added to the Weston Local Committee, •

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY.— There is no material change in the market since the opening. and- theirade do!ng does not exceed very moderate dimensions. Spinners can held theirown for the ''eat spinnings, but common yarns are in abundant supply—are troublesome in fact—and buyers refuse to be tempted to take' quantity.
